#5580. An Insurer Paid Me $6.73 to Save a Teen's Life

— The No Surprises Act allows me to keep saving others

In October 2023, a 19-year-old came into the emergency department with a perforated appendix. By the time I got him to the operating room, his abdomen was full of pus. A surgery that normally takes me 15 minutes took an hour and a half due to the amount of inflammation distorting his anatomy. I rounded on him in the hospital every day for a week until he was stable for discharge, then followed him for another 2 months until he had fully recovered.

For that surgery, the week of inpatient care, and 2 months of post-op follow-up, the insurance company sent me a check for $6.73.

This wasn't a clerical error -- it was the contracted rate the insurance company had set for the procedure. Laparoscopic appendectomy, like most operations, falls under a 90-day global period, which meant I couldn't bill separately for any care delivered in the 90 days after surgery. As far as the insurer was concerned, $6.73 was full and final payment for treating a teenager with sepsis from a ruptured appendix.

This is precisely this kind of payment that makes the federal No Surprises Act's (NSA) independent arbitration process so important to physicians like me. The law gives us a way to challenge inadequate insurer payments through a neutral process, helping independent physicians keep our practices open so we can continue caring for patients and saving lives.

I opened my own practice in 2023 after several years in academic medicine, where I had learned exactly how little say a physician can have over her own patients, her own schedule, and her own worth. I wanted to make medical decisions based on what my patients needed, not on what a hospital system's spreadsheet required. I did not expect that the fight for that independence would move from the hospital administration to the insurance companies.

When I first opened my doors, I kept a part-time position at a county hospital to make ends meet while I built a patient base. When that wasn't enough, I added emergency general surgery call at another hospital for $40 an hour. For about 6 months I was working four jobs. My savings dwindled. I started drawing from my 401k. As a single mother and the sole provider for my two daughters, I was doing the math every month to make sure I could pay my staff, office rent, medical malpractice insurance, and my mortgage. For 2 years I did not pay myself, and I wondered whether staying in medicine was still something I could afford to do.

Lately, I find myself wondering whether I can keep practicing independently, because that $6.73 check was not an outlier; it is part of the pattern. A few months after the teen with the perforated appendix, another patient came in with severe anemia and a bowel obstruction due to a large colon tumor. I performed a robotic colectomy to remove the cancer, relieve the blockage, and stop the bleeding. The insurer denied the claim, stating the operation was "not medically necessary."

This is where the NSA arbitration process became critical to my practice. When an insurer and a physician can't agree on payment, each side submits an offer to a neutral arbitrator, who picks one. It isn't a settlement. It's one of the only checks that exists on an insurer's ability to set whatever price it wants for care the patient has already received.

Physicians win these disputes more than 80% of the time, and some critics have pointed to that number as evidence the system is broken. It isn't. It's evidence of how low insurers' offers actually are. An analysis of nearly 160,000 arbitration cases found insurers offered $0 to the physician in more than 20,000 cases. In the fourth quarter of 2024, roughly a quarter of all disputes were resolved by default, seemingly because the insurance company provided incomplete information or failed to make an offer at all. When one side offers nothing, or next to nothing, an arbitrator does not need to search hard for the fair number.

I did not go into medicine and open a solo practice in a saturated Houston market because I thought I could get rich. Sixteen years of education and training to be paid $6.73 for emergency surgery is a terrible way to build wealth, it turns out. I built my practice so that I could provide accessible surgical care while maintaining autonomy and agency over my life and professional choices. Every solo and small-practice physician I know who now uses this process was doing the same math I was doing at my kitchen table over the last 3 years, wondering if it was truly possible to practice medicine independently, outside of large institutions and private-equity-owned medical practices.

Arbitration is one of the only tools we have that puts a solo surgeon and a multibillion-dollar insurer on anything resembling equal footing.

The numbers show what happens when that tool disappears or is weakened by suggestions that doctors are the ones driving up costs. The share of physicians in independent practice fell from 37.8% in 2019 to 22.4% in 2024, with more than 75% of physicians now employed by hospitals or corporate entities. Every one of those doctors who left independent practice took something with them: continuity with patients they'd known for years and the ability to make a clinical decision without checking it against a corporate metric.

No physician is asking for sympathy. We are asking that the next time someone suggests that physicians are "gaming" the NSA, she instead asks why an insurer's opening offer for a week of care after a ruptured appendix was $6.73, and why it took a federal arbitrator and an 8-month process to make that number make sense.

The law was written to protect patients from surprise bills. What's often left out is that it also protects physicians who are trying to practice independently, because we are not interested in 5-minute visits and being told to double-book patients. Take this protection away and let end-stage corporatization and consolidation of healthcare finish the job, and we will witness the end of the independent practice of medicine in America.

Cigna Group Foundation making $31.5M in grants available to community organizations in 10 states" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Cigna is making $31.5 million in grant funding available over the next three years to nonprofits in 10 states that are aiming to tackle several key community health priorities.

The company said that funds will be made available through its philanthropic arm, the Cigna Group Foundation, with applications open now through Dec. 18. Cigna said in an announcement that it's looking for organizations tackling youth mental health, veteran wellness and the impact of complex health needs on patients and their caregivers.

Cigna said the program seeks to deepen the company's community health strategy to address critical challenges.

The company first launched a new approach to community health and engagement in 2024, and since then has deployed more than $30 million in funding to 190 nonprofit organizations. Projects backed by these grants have reached at least 321,000 people, Cigna said.

"Over the past several years, we’ve seen the tangible impact we can make when we invest in strong nonprofit partners and come together to help communities achieve better health and vitality," said Melissa Skottegaard, board chair of The Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. "We’re building on what’s working, bringing together funding, collaboration and the skills of our employee volunteers to address some of the most pressing health challenges facing communities across the street and around the world."

Cigna will allot $10.5 million to each of the three focus areas under the initiative, per the announcement. Youth mental health, for example, has been a leading topic at the company for some time, and the company said it will also continue to build on its partnership with the Boys and Girls Clubs of America in this area.

In that partnership, Cigna has helped build out trauma-informed care services to 90% of clubs, reaching 11,000 employees. The company said that these efforts have supported 1,600 youths, and that its workforce has contributed more than 2,000 hours to local clubs.

Eligible organizations can apply for two-year, $250,000 grants to support programs in the three categories. The funds will be available to groups in Arizona, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Missouri, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Texas, per the announcement.

Cigna said its foundation will also continue to support community health through its Health Equity Impact Fund.

"Community organizations can be a powerful source of support for people navigating complex health conditions,” said Matt Perlberg, president of Evernorth Pharmacy & Care Delivery and board member of the Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. “By helping patients and caregivers connect with resources and overcome barriers to care, these organizations can provide important support alongside essential medical treatment, helping people navigate their health and care journey.”

#5577. 5 Of Today's Best Exotic SUVs, Ranked By Horsepower

Like it or not, building a performance SUV is almost an obligatory part of being an exotic car manufacturer right now. Pretty much every major supercar brand has one. Even McLaren, which once swore that it would never make an SUV, is officially working on an SUV. They're huge when it comes to helping these brands keep the lights on, and still usually really flippin' fast.

In a straight line from a dead stop, most aren't that far off from their "real" supercar stablemates. Furthermore, in the case of new, four-digit horsepower, all-electric ones, they might even beat some actual supercars to the finish line. We've assembled five of today's best and most notable exotic SUVs from brands like Ferrari, Lamborghini, and Porsche, ranking them by pure horsepower. And guess what? There's a trend that, appropriately perhaps, purists are going to absolutely hate: The fewer cylinders there are, the more power there is.

Case in point: the Ferrari Purosangue is simultaneously the SUV on this list with the most cylinders and the one that makes the least power. We let that slide on sheer charisma, though, because what it's working with is a naturally aspirated 6.5-liter V12 — no turbos, no hybrid motors, just 12 cylinders of practical Italian fury.

It is weirdly one of only two cars in Ferrari's lineup that still uses a V12 (the other is the 12Cilindri grand tourer), but its mere 715 horses puts it on the back foot in terms of power compared to pretty much all of its chief competitors. That said, it's likely the best-sounding car of this group, having a redline of 8,250 rpm. Ferrari quotes a zero-to-62 mph time of 3.3 seconds and a top speed over 193 mph. It gets coach doors (the rears open backward) and starts at around $440,000.

Coming in above the Ferrari in terms of horsepower by the thinnest of margins is the 717-hp Aston Martin DBX S. The most powerful variant (so far) of Aston's SUV makes 20 more mechanical hp than the 697-hp DBX707 (the number in that car's name referred to metric hp, not mechanical), while weighing almost 104 pounds less thanks in part to a center-of-gravity-lowering carbon fiber roof.

That power comes from a 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8 borrowed from Mercedes-AMG, although Aston says some turbo tech, such as the bigger compressor wheel diameters, are taken from its own Valhalla supercar. Zero to 62 mph takes 3.3 seconds, and it tops out at 193, which are both identical to the Purosangue. Coincidence? Highly unlikely. When we drove it last year, we wrote that it "might be the best-driving SUV on sale." The DBX S starts at $274,500, but considering the one we tested had a final invoice of more than 400 grand, "starting prices" are sort of academic in this neighborhood of the market.

Given Audi's ownership of Lamborghini, it's perhaps not surprising that the first electrified entry on this list is the Urus SE Performante. Those familiar with Lambo nomenclature will already know that this is the pumped-up version of the plug-in hybrid version of the brand's very popular SUV. Like the Aston Martin DBX, this car uses a 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8, albeit borrowed and adapted from its parent company, Audi. The SE part of the equation adds a hybrid electric motor that results in a total of 801 horsepower.

Comically, however, it's not any quicker than its un-electrified rivals and just barely faster than its Aston Martin counterpart. Electricity is mighty, but also heavy. Zero to 62 mph takes 3.3 seconds (exactly the same as the DBX S and Purosangue). In comparison, the Urus SE Performante's 312 km/h (194 mph rounded) top speed is one mile higher than the DBX S' 193 mph, but Ferrari is more vague with reporting the Purosangue's top speed, simply listing the SUV as capable of exceeding 310k m/h (193 mph rounded). The Urus SE Performante's starting price has not yet been confirmed.

When it comes to raw horsepower and speed, though, gas-powered entries are sort of fighting for silver these days because all-electric offerings like the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric are putting out horsepower figures with commas in 'em. This specific Porsche makes 1,139 horsepower from two electric motors. Zero to 60 mph takes 2.4 seconds (almost an entire second quicker than its gas rivals), but top speed is just 162 mph (more than 30 mph down from internal combustion), which speaks to what performance EVs are good at and what they aren't. The electric Cayenne Turbo features nifty side aeroblades that deploy outward to reduce drag.

In the more exotic-looking Coupe form, this car starts at $170,350, magnitudes less than the other vehicles we've seen so far, but that likely speaks more to the Porsche's "exoticness" than abilities. To those who question whether Porsche even qualifies as an "exotic" automaker, though: if a 1,139-hp car with moving sideblades and optional gold wheels isn't an "exotic SUV," I don't know what is.

In a similar vein, if the Urus with its VW Touareg underpinnings is obviously an exotic SUV, then the new Mercedes-AMG GT 63 SUV and its relation to cars like the old GT Black Series should count, too. It definitely counts on accelerative merit: three axial flux electric motors drawing energy from a Formula 1-derived 800-volt battery deliver 1,153 horsepower. Zero to 60 takes 2.4 seconds with a one-foot rollout and 2.6 seconds without. Top speed stands at an electronically limited 168 mph, precisely 6 mph faster than the Porsche but still not in the same time zone as the 190-plus mph gas rivals.

The AMG GT SUV is one of those electric performance cars that mimics the sound of a gas car engine — specifically an AMG V8 — with simulated gear shifts and corresponding seat vibrations also present. As of this writing, the electric AMG GT SUV is too new for us to have driven it yet, but we recently had a go in the sedan and found it mind-blowingly good. The SUV, then, shouldn't be far behind. Mercedes-AMG's GT SUV pricing has not yet been confirmed for the U.S.

#5576. Ford Begins Producing Its Own LFP Batteries

Ford is now a battery producer. Yes, it’s using battery technology licensed from CATL, but it is now producing EV batteries it is going to be using in its own vehicles. In fact, it is reportedly doing so in a really fast, advanced way. “The BlueOval Battery Park Michigan assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, making it among the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly lines outside of China.2 That pace helps drive down battery costs, and the facility has capacity for more. But speed must go hand in hand with quality,” Charles Poon, vice president of hardware engineering at Ford, writes.

“The first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells are rolling off the line at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan and headed to Louisville Assembly Plant to power Ford Fathom prototypes. With this milestone, Ford is now in the battery business and will be the first to deliver LFP batteries in the U.S. for mainstream consumer automotive use,” Poon writes. He goes on to explain further in a recent article why Ford chose to produce LFP battery cells and a bit on how it is doing so. Here’s a bit more from that article:

“The shipment caps years of work by the team that designed, built, and launched the plant on schedule. Ford now delivers cells at a plant it owns and operates, building expertise to support more affordable electric vehicles (EVs) and Ford Energy’s battery energy storage business in Kentucky.

“Why Start with LFP Prismatic for Fathom?

“When Alan Clarke, vice president, Advanced Development Projects, first joined the development team that created the Universal Electric Vehicle Platform, he issued a clear challenge: find an efficient LFP prismatic battery. The goal was to make EVs significantly more affordable.

“We talked to battery companies around the world. We wanted a technology that was proven in the field, ready to manufacture at scale, and suited to what we were building. That led us to the world’s leading battery manufacturer, CATL, whose batteries power 30 million vehicles across the globe.

“A battery is one of the biggest contributors to an EV’s cost and weight. So, we asked: How do we get more out of the battery without simply adding more cells? Our answer was efficiency over excess.

“LFP chemistry uses no nickel or cobalt, which helps hold down costs. It also holds up over years of charging and use. That durability is valuable as we give customers ways to use their battery beyond driving. For example, AC bidirectional power lets a vehicle receive electricity from a properly equipped home and supply power back to it.1

“This milestone is about more than shipping our first cells. We’re building the expertise to produce high-quality batteries at scale — for more affordable EVs and a new energy storage business.”

It looks like a serious effort and serious progress toward making more affordable, more competitive electric cars at Ford. The aim has been to get as good as making electric cars as Chinese companies are. How effective and successful will this new path be for Ford? We’ll see.

#5575. Metformin and Long COVID; Lp(a) Lowering for Cardiovascular Disease

— Also in TTHealthWatch: retatrutide for knee osteoarthritis

TTHealthWatch is a weekly podcast from Texas Tech. In it, Elizabeth Tracey, director of electronic media for Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore, and Rick Lange, MD, president of Texas Tech Health El Paso, look at the top medical stories of the week.

This week's topics include intensive blood pressure lowering in people with diabetes; metformin for long COVID; lowering lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), and cardiovascular events; and a triple agonist for knee osteoarthritis.

0:50 Lowering Lp(a) and cardiovascular disease

1:50 Pelacarsen administered subcutaneously

2:50 More risk factors you reduce the better

3:15 Retatrutide for knee osteoarthritis and obesity

4:15 Did reduce knee pain as well as reduced weight

5:15 Almost 38% reduction in placebo group

6:00 Intensive blood pressure lowering in type 2 diabetes

7:00 Doesn't reduce major cardiovascular events

9:50 Looked like a benefit with metformin

Elizabeth: Can metformin prevent the development of long COVID?

Rick: Does lowering Lp-little-a levels prevent cardiovascular events?

Elizabeth: A GLP-1-plus agonist for knee osteoarthritis in patients who are overweight.

Rick: And is there a benefit to intensive blood pressure lowering in people with type 2 diabetes?

Elizabeth: That's what we're talking about this week on TTHealthWatch, your weekly look at the medical headlines from Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center in El Paso. I'm Elizabeth Tracey, a Baltimore-based medical journalist.

Rick: And I'm Rick Lange, president of Texas Tech Health El Paso.

Elizabeth: Well, Rick, because the AHA [American Heart Association] meeting has been ongoing, we're talking an awful lot about cardiovascular disease this week. And so why don't we turn directly to the New England Journal of Medicine? And I'm going to toss the ball to you. Which of those two you served up would you like to talk about first?

Rick: Well, let's turn to the one that I think is most surprising. And that is the question, does lowering Lp(a) levels reduce cardiovascular events? Now, for people that aren't familiar, Lp-little-a, or what's called lipoprotein(a), is known to be a risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. And on many different levels, it's been shown to be associated with atherosclerosis. For a long time, we've not had any really good way of lowering it. Until recently, we have a number of new medications that have been shown to very effectively lower it, as much as 75% to 90%. And the presumption was, if you did that, you'd lower the risk of cardiovascular events.

But that really wasn't tested until this study just came out in the New England Journal of Medicine. Pelacarsen, it's an antisense oligonucleotide, which is very effective at lowering Lp(a) levels. And they administered it to about 4,100 patients subcutaneously on a monthly basis. And they followed these individuals over the course of 4.7 years.

Those that received pelacarsen had a significant decrease in their lipoprotein(a), over 70%. They looked at death, heart attack, stroke, or someone needing coronary revascularization. There was no difference at all in those that received pelacarsen and those that received placebo. What about those that had a baseline Lp(a) that was a little bit higher? Even in that group, there was no benefit with regard to decreasing cardiovascular events.

Elizabeth: I think a lot of the analysis of this trial are just really fascinating for people speculating on why in the world didn't this work. Is this just a stand-in for something else? And the other thing is, even in people who have that genetic predisposition to elevated Lp(a) levels, these folks were already on other things to try to keep them at lower risk. And so maybe the delta just wasn't high enough to show up.

Rick: We know that when you reduce cardiovascular risk factors, the more that you reduce, the better outcome you get. And so it was hypothesized that, sure, we could get your cholesterol down, but lowering Lp(a) would even be more advantageous. But apparently, it doesn't appear to be so. There are other agents that are being tested. It'll be interesting to see whether they have any benefit.

Elizabeth: More to come. Let's turn then to retatrutide once weekly in adults with knee osteoarthritis pain and obesity.

Retatrutide is an investigational triple agonist of GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors. Sort of this idea that if we take a multifactorial approach to all of these things, is that going to result in a better outcome? They enrolled adults without diabetes who had painful knee osteoarthritis and a BMI [body mass index] of at least 27. They were randomly assigned to receive once-weekly subcutaneous injections at a couple dosages of this med or placebo. And they were looking at the change in their pain score as far as their knee osteoarthritis was concerned, and the percentage change in body weight at week 68. They had 445 participants in one arm of the trial, 574 in another.

And what they showed was that, sure enough, the retatrutide was able to have a significant impact on this knee osteoarthritis score. And clearly, they also had percentage changes in body weight that were significant as well. Sure enough, if you use this triple agonist in patients who come in with painful knee osteoarthritis and obesity, you reduce both their pain score and you reduce their obesity. For me, this trial really harkens to that same question of which is it, chicken or egg? Is it that you unweight the knee and therefore you result in less painful symptomatology?

Rick: Yes. This particular agent lowered weight and reduced knee pain. You're not terribly surprised because anything you do that reduces weight reduces knee pain. You could argue that it's that effect alone and nothing else. Although when you decrease fat cells, you decrease inflammation. I'd be interested in knowing if you took people that weren't obese and gave them this agent, would it reduce knee pain? Is there anything in here that surprised you at all?

Elizabeth: In the retatrutide group, they had a reduction of at least 50% in their pain score, but that was compared with 37%, almost 38%, reduction in those in the placebo group. And we've noted this in the past.

Rick: Yeah. Placebo effect. That's why all studies to assess whether a treatment is effective has to be compared to some placebo.

Elizabeth: Right. And of course, we have to note that we see the same side effects that we see with almost everything that's relative to the GLP-1s: nausea, diarrhea, constipation. For the most part, they resolved over time.

Rick: And they're usually associated with dose escalation. For people that are taking a GLP-1, I usually advise them, "Listen, as we increase the dose, we're going to do it slowly and methodically. You may experience these." But as you mentioned, it's usually mild and it will go away if they'll persist with it.

Elizabeth: OK. Still staying in the New England Journal.

Rick: This is the third study that I'm aware of that looks to see whether intensive blood pressure lowering is beneficial in people with type 2 diabetes. It follows on two other studies. One was the ACCORD study, and it showed that intensive blood pressure lowering, trying to get it below 120, was not beneficial. And they followed that with a study in China that did the same thing. And it showed just the opposite effect, primarily by reducing strokes, which are more prevalent in the Chinese population.

This study was done in Brazil, about 9,400 individuals, ethnically diverse. About two-thirds were women that had hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and a high cardiovascular risk. And they randomized them to blood pressure lowering to either get it below 140 versus 120, and followed these individuals over a mean follow-up of 4 years.

There was really no significant difference. So in this ethnically-diverse population, it appears that intensive blood pressure lowering in people with type 2 diabetes really doesn't reduce the occurrence of major cardiovascular events.

Elizabeth: Of course, what we know is that when we attempt these intensive blood pressure-lowering regimens, people object to polypharmacy, and particularly those who already have diabetes and are already taking other meds.

Rick: Yeah. In fact, for the individuals that were taking the less intensive, the median of 2.3 different medications, and those on the more intensive, 3.2. This was so well done. Oftentimes, when you get really intensive therapy, you have more episodes of hypotension and syncope falling out, sometimes fractures. But in this particular study, not. They approached it very methodically. It's just that it just didn't really help.

Elizabeth: Let's turn to the Journal of Medical Virology. I think this might be the first time we've ever actually talked about a study that was in this. They were looking at metformin at the time of COVID-19 infection and the risk of long COVID. And this, they identify as a target trial emulation study. They were looking to evaluate the impact of metformin prescribed at the time of COVID infection on the risk of developing long COVID, and they did it by examining electronic health records.

They conducted a new-user analysis of metformin, prescribed within 6 days of documented infection with COVID, versus experimental controls. And those were prescriptions for fluvoxamine, fluticasone, ivermectin, or montelukast. They had to have, as their inclusion criteria, a clinic visit in the 0 to 6 months and 6 to 12 months before infection. They excluded all folks who had had metformin or control within 12 months, and their primary outcome was long COVID development or death.

The number that they actually came up with was 248 in the metformin and control groups with an average age of 53. They had 4% in the metformin group develop long COVID or death versus 8.5% in the control group, seeming to show that there's a benefit of prescribing metformin when somebody presents with a new COVID infection.

Rick: As you mentioned, this was a different kind of study. It's an emulation trial. Usually, we look at randomized controlled trials as appearing to be the gold standard.

So in this particular case, individuals with COVID, some of whom received metformin, and then the other group, let's give them some medication that is not known to be beneficial with regard to COVID, because there are some in vitro and in vivo studies that suggest there is a benefit of metformin in people that have COVID. So those are the active comparators. They used an antidepressant, an anti-inflammatory, an anti-parasite, and then a respiratory drug. It looked like there was a benefit, a reduction in long COVID symptoms attributed to the metformin, because they didn't see with any of these other medications. So that's how this emulation study was done.

Elizabeth: Based on this study, Rick, would you say that you would, especially as we see different variants emerging, if one emerges that's going to be more severe, would you use metformin in patients with a new diagnosis of COVID?

Rick: That's an important distinction. So first of all, it's a new diagnosis. So they were given this within 6 days of the diagnosis. I would be inclined to offer it to the patient and say, "We're not going to be on this long term, but there is some data that suggests it can reduce the risk." I'll let the patient be involved, but I would not have any qualms about it. There's no harm associated in any of the studies. And again, there's pretty convincing data that it reduces the risk of long COVID symptoms by about 50%. So the answer is yes. Elizabeth, let me take it back to you. Would you take it if I prescribed it?

Elizabeth: Oh, I would take it for sure. I would also note that they used a phrase in this paper that I was completely unfamiliar with. They say, "An experimental control reduces unmeasured confounding, such as the likelihood of engagement with healthcare, immortal time bias, and the placebo effect." I've never heard of an "immortal time bias" before.

Rick: That has to do with when the diagnosis is made, when things are given. I'll give you a great example. If we're looking at how long people live and you have a patient group that's 5 years old, they're likely to live for another 80 years. If you start with people that are in their 80s, they're likely to live 5 years. Is there a mortality difference? It has to do with the time that the patient is enrolled in the trial, not the long-term outcome.

Elizabeth: Thank you for that. And on that note then, that's a look at this week's medical headlines from Texas Tech. I'm Elizabeth Tracey.

Rick: And I'm Rick Lange. Y'all listen up and make healthy choices.

#5574. Memo To Musk: Denial Is Just The First Step On The Long Road To Recovery

Tesla CEO Elon Musk made headlines yet again last week, when he publicly denied any affiliation with US President Donald Trump’s “MAGA” movement. If Musk intends to stage a sort of political recovery, he still has a long way to go. Denial is just a precursor to recovery, which begins in earnest when you stop denying the reality of your situation and start admitting you need help from a higher power or some such. And in fact, a higher power is coming for Musk —  if not in spiritual form, then in the form of Congress, where the incoming Democratic majority plans to exercise its authority, and call Musk to account for manipulating SpaceX satellite services in Ukraine.

During an interview for the New York Times DealBook Summit last week, Elon Musk claimed that he was not affiliated with MAGA, though he did not apologize for supporting MAGA candidates this year, or for supporting Donald Trump in 2024. Musk simply said he “felt foolish” for wasting his money on losers.

In the same interview, Musk insisted — falsely — that Russia was the aggrieved party when Russian President Vladimir Putin invaded the Donbas region of Ukraine back in 2014. Justin sayin’…

For those of you wondering why Elon Musk’s politics should be a matter of concern to CleanTechnica, that’s a good question, and here’s the answer: Elon Musk sailed into clean tech history on the coattails of the EV startup Tesla Motors (soon to become simply Tesla) in the early 2000’s, only to emerge in more recent years as a champion of the far right alongside President Donald Trump’s notoriously racist, fossil fuel-supporting “Make America Great Again” movement, thereby setting back the US decarbonization movement by years if not decades.

Musk has also made his own contribution to the resurgence of fossil fuels in the US. His new xAI data centers are well known for deploying loosely regulated (or illegal) on-site gas generators, and his SpaceX venture has been gobbling up natural gas for rocket fuel while laying plans for future expansion.

So much for Elon Musk’s footprint on the US energy profile. Let’s move over to Ukraine, where rich fossil energy and mineral resources in the nation’s Donbas region prompted Russian President Putin to send unmarked soldiers — aka the “little green men” — to annex that portion of Ukraine in 2014 (see clarification/correction below). A ceasefire temporarily calmed the situation until February of 2022, when Putin sent a fully equipped convoy to the Ukrainian capital city Kyiv, aiming to take over the entire seat of government in one fell swoop — literally, in one day.

The effort failed, both militarily and in terms of Putin’s energy goals. Ukraine promptly cut Russia off from its electricity grid and hooked up with the European grid, a complex effort assisted by the Biden administration. Ukraine also set the wheels in motion to join the European Union as a significant source of clean energy, including green hydrogen gas alongside its copious potential for clean power including biomass, wind, and solar power.

To put that into perspective, consider that Ukraine is almost 90% as large as Texas, which has staked out a leadership position in wind and solar power among the 50 US states.

With Ukraine as a leading renewable energy supplier, the EU would have a fresh opportunity to meets its decarbonization goals on schedule while also reducing imports of fossil energy from Russia… And… Well… That’s where Elon Musk enters the picture.

Musk first emerged as a full blown MAGA supporter in 2020, when he helped Trump stir up conspiracy theories and confusion over the federal response to the COVID-19 crisis, in a failed effort to support the President’s bid for re-election that year. Had Trump won, he would have continued to implement a key part of his foreign policy agenda, namely, withdrawing the US from NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Alliance. NATO formed in 1949 as an effort to curb Russian expansion in Europe, an effort Trump has upended on account of his longstanding friendship with Putin.

The election of Joe Biden in 2020 did not prevent Musk from providing additional aid and comfort to Trump. Musk used his media-grabbing public profile to undercut the authority of President Biden at every opportunity, including on the world stage as well as here at home. The stream of insults extended into January of 2022, even as the reality of a fresh round of Russian expansion into Europe began to materialize.

Musk had an additional opportunity to challenge Biden’s authority in January of 2022, when the so-called “Freedom Convoy” of truckers barricaded government offices in Canada, ostensibly in protest of a vaccine mandate. Musk gleefully cheered the effort, which disrupted transportation systems and distracted public attention in two key NATO allies — Canada and the US — even as Russia began ratcheting up its plans to take over Kyiv.

However, once it became clear that Putin’s one-day takeover of Ukraine was a failure, Musk about-faced. He took credit for providing “free” communications aid to Ukraine in the form of satellite services through the Starlink branch of SpaceX.

JK! A later assessment revealed that other sources shouldered about 85% of the cost of Starlink terminals initially supplied to Ukraine, including USAID here in the US (not a typo — that’s the US Administration for International Development, the same agency that Musk later destroyed in 2025).

Poland and other groups also contributed initial assistance to purchase  the terminals alongside an estimated 30% of connectivity costs. In addition, by September of 2022 Musk was making the case for US taxpayers to foot the bill.

Don’t just take my word for it. In 2023, the Belfer Center for International Affairs at Harvard recapped SpaceX’s negotiations over payment for its services to Ukraine during the previous year, concluding that “we can assume the U.S. government agreed to pay some, if not all, of the costs for continued operation of the technology.”

“SpaceX, and particularly Musk, was able to play the role of wartime hero, showcasing the power and value of the technology products the company developed, while simultaneously avoiding sustained and hefty bills,” Belfer Center observed.

US Department of Defense contract or not, by 2023 SpaceX was already making unilateral decisions that restricted Ukraine’s ability to deploy the technology, with SpaceX CEO Gwynne Shotwell publicly insisting that the company never intended for Ukraine to use it “for offensive purposes.”

Of course, “offensive” is in the eye of the beholder. Since Ukraine is the invaded party seeking to assert its rights over internationally recognized borders against Russia, one could argue that every action Ukraine takes is a defensive one until Putin agrees to concede defeat and cede back his illegal claims over Ukrainian lands.

Of course, that’s not how Musk portrayed the situation in his DealBook interview last week. Nevertheless, one also could argue that the US government, not the vendor, controls the use of contractually obligated resources. Be that as it may, Musk raised the bar considerably in October, when he — or Trump — or both — once again dialed down satellite service in Ukraine, exposing that country to further attacks.

Musk attempted to mollify bipartisan outrage over the debacle with yet another publicity stunt for SpaceX. However, service interruptions have continued into this week. Meanwhile, Trump has spent the same week cozying up to both Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, aided and abetted by an obedient Republican majority in Congress.

That majority will evaporate, though, in January 3, which is just around the corner. The incoming Democratic majority is already gearing up for a fight. In a letter dated November 20, the incoming Chair of the House Intelligence Committee, Jim Himes (D-CT), demanded an in-person briefing from senior SpaceX officers, seeking an explanation for the disruption of military-grade Starshield service in Ukraine. As leverage, Himes warned Musk that a Democratic majority in Congress will do what the Republican majority failed to do, namely, exercise its constitutional authority over federal contracts.

Referring specifically to SpaceX’s military-grade Starshield satellite services in Ukraine, Himes warned Musk that his entire suite of present and future SpaceX security contracts with the US government is at risk. “SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes explained.

“For that reason, it is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX- developed, government-owned systems until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes continued.

Will Musk simply ignore the request for a briefing? After all, as Himes notes, Musk failed to respond to earlier requests. Stay tuned…

Photo credit: Kyle Field via CleanTechnica archive.

Clarification/Correction: Russia initially annexed parts of the Donbas in 2014 through its support for a separatist movement, later acknowledged to be a Russian military operation. The “little green men” refers more specifically to the annexation of Crimea during the same period.

#5573. 7 Cars With The Smallest Trunks You Can Imagine

No single car can deliver everything that every driver will ever want from it, and they all come with at least some compromises. Performance cars often aren't that fuel efficient, huge trucks and SUVs with impressive towing capabilities are not the most nimble for around town, and — as this list will prove — a variety of city and sports cars also need to compromise on trunk space, in order to prioritize other key traits.

That doesn't make them inherently bad cars, they just excel in other areas. The list includes various city-slick models like the Scion iQ and Renault Twizy – if these cars were equipped with cavernous trunks, then the smallest parking spots and tightest city streets would likely be best avoided. Similarly, sports and supercars, like the Fiat X1/9 and Audi R8 featured below, sport mid-engine layouts, which naturally make incorporating decent trunk space quite a tricky ordeal.

For this list, we've singled out seven cars with laughably small trunks. If you know of smaller, feel free to drop them in the comments below, although it's probably important to point out that we've deliberately avoided models with zero trunk space — so, no BAC Mono or Morgan Plus 4 models to be found here. Likewise, not all trunk capacities are listed by automakers, so any models we could not reliably verify — such as the Veyron Grand Sport Vitesse's supposed 1.3-cubic-foot trunk — have also been avoided. With that aside, here is our selection of seven notoriously impractical trunks and the cars they belong to, listed in size order, with the largest featured first.

The first entry is an Italian classic that does things differently. Whereas most mid-engine sports cars hailing from Italy boast impressive engines and lofty outputs, the Fiat X1/9 instead makes do with a tiny inline-4. It sports just a 1.3-liter capacity, and power peaks at 67 horses, with 68 pound-feet of torque for good measure. Even with a 2,200-pound curb weight, it still takes around 15 seconds for the little X1/9 to crack 60 mph from a standstill.

As those figures suggest, this is a small car — its wheelbase is just 86.7 inches, which is over 4 inches shorter than that of the Miata below. As a result, there isn't a whole heap of room left for a considerable trunk — the X1/9's frunk provides owners just 5.1 cubic-feet of space.

However, here's where the X1/9 actually impresses, as, despite the diminutive proportions and mid-engine configuration, it actually manages to incorporate a traditional trunk, too. Here lies 4.1 cubic-feet of storage space, so in total, the tiny Fiat actually provides 9.2 cubes — very impressive, considering the space available in other mid-engine efforts. That frunk is typically used as stowage space for the removable targa roof panel, but, of course, with the roof in place or left at home, it could be used for whatever.

This list covers many city-centric little runabouts and exotic supercars, but here instead, we focus on something that lies somewhere between the two. Mazda's timeless MX-5 Miata is a back-to-basics sports car that refuses to follow the status-quo. While other sports cars have resorted to larger dimensions, heftier curb weights, turbocharged engines, and higher engine outputs, Mazda instead continues to focus on simple driving pleasures.

That's perfect for drivers chasing a fun drop-top to enjoy on a local back road, but it does mean that, once again, trunk space takes a back seat on the priorities list. At least, due to Mazda adopting a traditional front-engine and rear-wheel drive configuration, the Miata sports a proper trunk. It only offers 4.6 cubic-feet of actual space, though, so it's never going to be a great touring companion — at least not without owners having to make some sort of packing compromise or opting for an external luggage rack. The cabin isn't particularly clever in terms of extra storage either, with no door compartments to be seen and no traditional glove box.

Interestingly, the current ND-generation MX-5 Miata sports less luggage space than its predecessor, so Mazda clearly did not feel that trunk space had ever been much of a sticking point with Miata buyers in the past. In fact, we recently advised you all to buy a Miata and said that you'd likely never regret it, so we also feel the sports car's limited storage space is nothing too concerning either.

Lamborghini is the only automaker to appear twice on this list, although we doubt being called out for limited cargo space is going to damage the Italian supercar manufacturer's brand image all too much. The Temerario continues the baby supercar bloodline, following on from the Huracan and Gallardo before it, and unlike the Aventador-based Countach further down your page, it's an all-new and fresh design.

There is a pattern emerging here, too, as much like the Countach revival, the Temerario is another mid-engine supercar, and another to sport hybridization technology. Naturally, that leaves no space for a traditional trunk, so it offers a frunk as its primary storage solution. It also matches the capability of later Audi R8 Coupe models, with only 4 cubic-feet of space given at the front end. That's perhaps enough for a few backpacks for a weekend getaway, but certainly not ideal for longer trips that may require multiple larger bags.

It doesn't matter how you spec a Temerario, it's never going to be a great grand-tourer with that little in the way of storage space. An Urus or front-engined model from another exotic brand would be the better bet there, but at least Lamborghini provides owners with enough space to stash away a few essentials for weekends away.

Audi had never made anything that truly verged on being a supercar, so when it pulled up in the late 2000s with a true 911 competitor, with a naturally aspirated and midship 4.2-liter V8, 6-speed manual, and quattro all-wheel drive, the motoring world sat up and paid attention. By all accounts, it was a sublime car, although, thanks to its mid-engine configuration, cargo space has always been at a premium.

Second-generation cars, which ran from the 2016 model year until Audi's supercar became one of the many nameplates that got the axe in 2024, came with a total of 8 cubic-feet of storage space behind the seats, while the physical frunk itself sports 4 cubic-feet. As for those first-gen models, the total frunk space matches that of the Toyota iQ, at only 3.5 cubic-feet. There is no mention of classifying the space behind seats as official stowage space here, so perhaps doing so was just a smart marketing trick of the later cars to make the R8 look like a more complete 911 rival. Either way, there is surely space for a pair of shades or a short novel in the cabin of first-gen models somewhere.

Moving back away from performance cars, the next entry on our list is another cleverly packaged city car. The Scion iQ, or Toyota iQ, as it was known in other markets, was a dinky little four-seater, the first four-seater, in fact, to sit at less than 3 meters (9.8 feet) in length, although it was certainly more conventional in its approach than the tandem-seat Twizy, detailed below. In truth, the Scion iQ was an excellent little car that nobody wanted to buy, produced from the 2012 through 2015 model years, and powered by a naturally aspirated 1.3-liter inline-4 engine.

While it did have the capacity to seat four, those rear seats were particularly restrictive and better treated as an additional storage area. Just as well, as the designated storage space in the trunk was equally as restrictive, at just 3.5 cubic-feet. While the little city car certainly has its fans, not everyone loves it: Consumer Reports called it "slow, noisy, and uncomfortable," in addition to "less-than-enjoyable to drive."

Still, it probably made good sense for those who commuted solely within packed city centers. Furthermore, if those buyers had far deeper pockets and wished for a more upscale ownership experience, they could always opt for the iQ's posher sibling, the Aston Martin Cygnet. The British luxury carmaker took the back-to-basics iQ, furnished it with a sublime interior and refinished the rear end, in addition to many other cosmetic and quality updates. It commanded around three times the price of the iQ, was never offered for sale in the U.S., and, although undoubtedly far nicer to sit in, it likely still made do with the same measly 3.5 cubic-feet of trunk space.

At the complete other end of the spectrum, cargo space isn't far removed from what the city-centric Scion iQ has to offer. To celebrate the initial 1971 release of its Countach, Lamborghini released a modern-day Countach built on the Aventador's chassis. A hybrid V12 powertrain pinched from the Sián FKP37 hybrid hypercar was selected as the motivator, and, as a tribute to the original prototype's LP-112 model designation, just 112 were assembled.

Cargo space likely was not at the forefront of the designer's mind, and neither was it a key priority for buyers either, we can safely assume, as the Countach LPI 800-4 offers just 2.2 cubic-feet of it. That's roughly enough room for two standard milk crates — great news for big milk drinkers, then, but not ideal for road trippers or those who fancy an exotic daily driver.

The Aventador Coupe, on which the Countach is based, manages to boast 5 cubic-feet of cargo space, so more than double, which might make the Countach's lack of available space seem tricky to understand. While Lamborghini (rightfully) doesn't feel the need to explain the Countach's cargo space, which is actually frunk space rather than trunk space, we can assume it's due to the Countach's differing lines and the fact it also boasts a hybrid system, whereas the Aventador is without electrification.

The Renault Twizy was not sold in the U.S., as it likely wouldn't sell well being such a diminutive electrified city runabout, and restrictions would render it pretty difficult to use anyway. And that's if it ever worked its way around the required crash tests in the first place. Having said that, Scoot Networks did temporarily employ a fleet of them around San Francisco for rental use, but that's not why it grabs the spotlight today.

Instead, it impresses — or rather disappoints — with its ludicrously compact trunk capacity. It offers just 31 liters of space, which, for reference, works out to around 1.09 cubic-feet. To put that into perspective, a standard milk crate measures up at 0.9 cubic-feet. So, the Twizy is ideal for grabbing a few gallons of milk, but that's about it.

In truth, it would be rude and missing the point somewhat to blast the Twizy over cargo space. It's designed to be as compact as possible, suitable for two occupants in tandem and, well, nothing else really. So, for city-center commuting and securing the last parking spot that nobody else dares to entertain, this quadricycle is absolutely ideal. Just be careful about the size of your packed lunch before heading out to work.

#5572. The Insurance Affordability Crisis: Risks, Resilience, and Solutions

NRDC resources on insurance affordability, market availability, climate risk, resilience investments, and strategies to protect homeowners, businesses, and communities.

For property owners, insurance provides a critical financial safety net that protects homes, businesses, and other assets from unexpected losses, helping owners recover and rebuild when disasters occur. Beyond individual protection, insurance is fundamental to the resilience of communities and local economies, enabling faster recovery, supporting continued investment, and reducing the long-term financial impacts of shocks. As risks become more frequent, severe, and costly, access to affordable, available, and reliable insurance is increasingly essential, not only for safeguarding property owners but also for maintaining overall property affordability, economic stability, and the resilience and prosperity of the communities in which they live and operate.

The frequency and severity of losses are increasing faster than insurers can sustainably price and absorb them, leading to higher premiums, reduced coverage availability, and, in some cases, the withdrawal of insurers from certain markets. This trend is eroding the affordability and accessibility of insurance, increasing the total cost of property ownership, and placing additional pressure on housing and business affordability while leaving individuals, businesses, and communities more physically and financially exposed.

However, the insurance sector is increasingly recognized as a key component of resilience, incentivizing risk reduction through pricing and support for adaptation measures that can help moderate long-term insurance costs. When functioning effectively, insurance enables communities to not only recover from shocks but also to better prepare for future risks while preserving access to coverage.

Linked below are reports, expert blogs, and other resources that examine the insurability crisis and how insurance can play a key role in advancing housing resilience and adaptation.

NRDC’s director of insurance and financial risk, Alfonso Pating, breaks down how homeowner’s insurance works and why climate change is making it unaffordable.

More reports and resources on this topic here.

Article originally published on NRDC website.

NRDC is the nation's most effective environmental action group, combining the grassroots power of 1.3 million members and online activists with the courtroom clout and expertise of more than 350 lawyers, scientists, and other professionals.

#5571. Buick GSX Stage 1s Are Super Rare Muscle Cars, But They're Common Compared To Stage 2s

If you take a moment to think of some classic-era American muscle car brands, names like Chevrolet, Pontiac, and Dodge immediately come to mind, but "Buick" doesn't. Buick occupies a market segment just under luxurious Cadillac within the GM hierarchy of automakers, making athleticism something most wouldn't associate the brand with. Regardless, the marque was responsible for building one of the most torque-happy muscle cars of the classic era, with 510 pound-feet of torque on tap alongside 360 horsepower.

The model responsible is the 1970 Buick GSX Stage 1. At the time, the GSX was locked in direct battle with more well-known adversaries such as the Pontiac GTO and the Dodge Charger, but even when it was new, few knew about it. It was one of the rarest of muscle cars — only about 400 were produced in 1970. To boot, it became even rarer as time went on, with just 24 built in total for the 1972 model year.

However, "Stage 1" was only part of the GSX's performance story. There was also the incredibly fabled "Stage 2" iteration. Only a couple of fully fledged examples were ever produced  — making it one of the rarest Buick muscle cars to ever grace the pavement.

If you fancied a hot Buick muscle car in 1970, you could simply pop down to the dealership and buy something like the GS 350 or GS 455. Your most desirable choice, however, would have been the flagship Buick GSX, carrying a sticker price of about $4,880. It boasted the poise and presence of a tried-and-true muscle car with its black striping and lack of chrome trim — something rarely seen in a Buick of the time. The Stage 1 package was offered for just $199, adding 10 horsepower and things like a higher compression ratio at 10.5:1 versus the GSX's standard 10.0:1, a more aggressive camshaft, and larger valves.

If you took a walk back into the Buick dealer's parts department, though — and also happened to be a drag racer — you could build yourself an even more powerful GSX with Buick-bred components that were off the standard books. This marked the initiation method for procuring a Stage 2 kit, and it needed to be special-ordered through dealers, rather than from Buick itself. The package consisted of a litany of upgrades over the Stage 1 version. Because it wasn't available to the public at first, the Stage 2 upgrade went without an RPO code.

The Stage 2 kit carried things like an 11.0:1 compression ratio and 2-inch circular exhaust ports, allowing the engine to breathe much more efficiently. A gigantic Holley carburetor sporting an 850 cubic-foot-per-minute flow rate sat atop an Edelbrock intake manifold, and a set of high-strength forged pistons handled the engine's combustion.

All told, the Stage 2 GSX was thought to have roughly 100 more horsepower than Stage 1 models. To test its Stage 2 creation, Buick drummed up a pair of GSX prototypes outfitted with the complete kit, one of which was sent to Doug Jones and Dave Benisek — a pair of drag racers — for some stress testing, with the duo managing to achieve quarter-mile times under 11.7 seconds at trap speeds nearing 130 mph. Jones and Benisek continued to race their prototypical Stage 2 GSX throughout the 1970s, going undefeated during the National Hot Rod Association's 1972 season.

That very same year, Buick finally made the existence of its Stage 2 project public, letting regular customers special-order parts from the program. As for the rough number of Stage 2 kits built, it's thought to be just about 75 pairs, the vast majority of them produced in 1972. Sadly, looming changes to American emissions standards rendered the factory-sponsored Stage 2 program moot before it could get really off the ground.

1972 was a pivotal year for the classic American muscle car. Horsepower outputs had dropped dramatically by that time, and the GSX Stage 1 was no exception. While the 1970 model boasted 360 ponies, the '72 GSX Stage 1 made just 270. Fitting, then, that Buick's Stage 2 GSX dream would effectively flame out that year — right around the time emissions standards and rising fuel costs began to render the classic American muscle car a thing of the past.

#5570. Are GLP-1s Enabling Disordered Eating?

— Safe weight loss requires limits and attention to extreme restriction

I often open my obesity medicine visits by asking "How are you feeling today?" Today the answer was, "I feel like the medication is finally working!"

I checked the chart to find that the patient was down 21 pounds in 3 months, or about 6% of bodyweight. When I dug in and asked about dietary intake, she reported that after switching to tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) 2 weeks ago, she spontaneously decided the best way to take control of her life was to start a water fast. She was currently on day 13 of only water and diet coke and stated she felt "amazing." I reviewed her vitals and her heart rate was 127. After a few questions, she admitted she wasn't sleeping due to stress and then burst into tears. She told me she wanted to go up on both her GLP-1 and her oral weight loss medications so she could continue water fasting indefinitely.

Based on my level of clinical concern, I discontinued her weight control medications, referred her to the local eating disorders center, scheduled her a visit with the dietitian, and scheduled a close follow-up to ensure she was receiving these additional forms of care.

On another occasion, my phone rang. It was an emergency doctor who I've known for years: "Hey, I need to curbside on a patient."

The doctor told me that a patient was brought into the emergency department after fainting and hitting her head. She reported feeling fine but not drinking as much water as usual. The patient's husband reported that she had been receiving a GLP-1 receptor agonist from the local med spa and "was working out 2 hours a day and only eating an apple and a protein shake a day" while at a body mass index of 21. Lab work revealed the patient was deficient in numerous electrolytes, including potassium, magnesium, and phosphorous. After receiving fluids, he reported that "the patient left and stated she had no plans to stop the medication."

Obesity is a chronic disease that affects over a billion people globally. For five decades, there were no highly effective medication options for treatment, with safe options providing only limited benefits. Over the past 6 years, that has radically changed: multiple long-acting medications for chronic weight management have been approved by FDA and widely adopted. GLP-1s have more than doubled medical treatment efficacy compared to prior medication options. Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide reduce spontaneous food intake by hundreds of calories a day, on average, and can produce weight loss of up to 30% of bodyweight in some individuals.

However, with this substantial breakthrough comes the risk of over-suppression of appetite. The speed of weight loss is akin to driving a fast car down a highway: it's done best with limits and attention to safety concerns.

The wide variability in individual responsiveness to GLP-1s produces a challenging clinical scenario for chronic obesity treatment in some patients. While a minority do not lose weight on GLP-1 medications, others may experience profound reductions in hunger and food-related cognitions (also known as "food noise"). On the extreme end, I have witnessed some patients spontaneously lose nearly half their bodyweight. This variability is reflected by field-leading clinical trials. With a drug this powerful, every individual must be monitored and medications tailored to their needs.

Based on the experiences of patients described earlier, I strongly counsel my patients on health and nutritional intake to avoid malnutrition, especially for patients suffering gastrointestinal side effects, including nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Because GLP-1s can limit the thirst reflex as well, raising the risk of dehydration and acute kidney injury, it is imperative that patients understand proper hydration.

Meanwhile, a recent meta-analysis showed that approximately one third of patients seeking medical obesity treatment report binge eating behaviors. The lifetime prevalence of eating disorders in the U.S. ranges from 0.6-2% for anorexia nervosa, 1-4.6% for bulimia nervosa, and 0.6-4.5% for binge eating disorder, with younger adults with obesity at significantly higher risk and females at higher risk than males. The evidence that GLP-1 medications will curb hunger does not guarantee these behaviors will be modified, and their presence requires especially careful guidance, understanding, and clinical support.

So, what are clinicians to do? A joint publication by leading medical societies detailed recommendations for nutritional support of patients on GLP-1s, including the need to ensure adequate hydration, protein, fiber, and micronutrient intake. In addition, a 2024 Obesity Reviews publication I co-authored specifically discussed managing these complications.

In my practice, I no longer tell patients to aggressively reduce calorie intake. When I prescribe GLP-1s, I instead instruct them to drink at least 60 oz of water a day, get at least 60 grams of protein a day, and focus on vegetables and solid foods. I also recommend patients consume at least 1,000 calories a day. In our clinic we are fortunate to have dietitians who work with patients on medical therapy to personalize an approachable eating pattern.

Additionally, we ask about history of eating disorders or other psychiatric comorbidities that may indicate risk of disordered eating, while encouraging patients to avoid fasting or excessively restrictive eating schedules. Instead, we focus on patients eating two to three healthy meals a day with adequate nutrition.

For patients who reported current restrictive eating, medications are closely monitored and may be decreased or stopped if those symptoms are worsening or leading to excessive weight loss. For patients with emotional eating as a coping mechanism, we regularly refer to psychology for cognitive behavior therapy and other supportive modalities to help coping behaviors.

More than 100 million patients in America qualify for medical weight loss therapy. At the same time, the rates of eating disorders have risen in the past decades, and these conditions continue to be significantly underdiagnosed. There is a need for a systematic approach to weight loss using GLP-1s, but a "first do no harm" mindset is key. With the impending FDA approval of next generation GLP-1 medications that are significantly stronger, preventing and addressing drug-induced disordered eating will only continue to grow in importance.

#5569. RMI’s Hydrogen Research Is Getting Better. Its Investment Advice Still Falls Short.

RMI has become much more realistic about hydrogen demand and competing technologies. That makes the gaps between its findings and its recommendations harder to excuse. Its latest work acknowledges that battery trucks generally have better economics than hydrogen fuel-cell trucks, that Europe needs far less hydrogen in 2030 than it originally targeted, and that low-emissions ammonia still costs substantially more than conventional ammonia. Several recommendations still seek public money to develop the very hydrogen markets the research has found difficult to justify.

I have been challenging this tension since January 2024. RMI matters because governments, investors and industrial companies use its research when deciding where to spend money. Its hydrogen program has made genuine analytical corrections. It has not made all of the accompanying strategic decisions.

Consider RMI’s February 2026 report on hydrogen trucking in India. The baseline comparisons find that fuel-cell trucks do not reach battery-electric truck ownership-cost parity through 2040, including the long-haul use case. The report also explores a much more favourable hydrogen price in an alternative sensitivity, which brings fuel-cell trucks closer to parity. Those are different findings, and the baseline matters to investment decisions today.

The report nevertheless recommends hydrogen vehicle subsidies, support for refuelling stations, production incentives and tax relief. It treats a parallel hydrogen-truck market as something to build. The case for spending public money on that market should start with evidence that a particular freight service cannot be served as well or better by batteries. The reported cost advantage of batteries does not disappear when the policy section begins.

The problem reaches beyond India. RMI’s 2025 US hydrogen report says battery trucks have greater market readiness and lower total cost of ownership, especially in the near term, yet calls for hydrogen distribution and refuelling infrastructure along freight corridors. The independent NACFE Run on Less ownership-cost work, developed within RMI’s freight research ecosystem, projects batteries becoming the lowest-cost option across its modelled duty cycles by 2035 without incentives. Hydrogen remains the most expensive option across nearly all of them. These findings support battery infrastructure as the default and a high evidentiary bar for hydrogen exceptions.

RMI already knows how to make appropriate distinctions elsewhere. Its 2026 steel research separates hydrogen used to reduce iron ore from hydrogen burned merely to supply process heat. In the illustrative plant, electric heat requires about 850 GWh a year, compared with 1,300 GWh of electricity to produce enough additional hydrogen for heating. That is the kind of direct service comparison that ought to govern recommendations throughout the organization.

Its new Green Ammonia Buyers Alliance also has a coherent industrial purpose. Fertiliser production already requires ammonia, commonly made with fossil-derived hydrogen. Purchasing lower-emissions ammonia to replace that supply addresses an existing industrial input. It does not require inventing a new energy market for ammonia combustion.

Europe shows how improved diagnosis can coexist with excessive policy ambition. RMI’s March 2025 recalibration reduced expected mandate-driven renewable hydrogen demand in 2030 to 2.2–2.8 million tons, far below the EU’s original 20-million-ton supply-and-import ambition. Its analysis identifies €13.9 billion in public support under existing mandates, plus €31.7 billion for an accelerated scenario. The combined €45.6 billion deserves a comparison with the other ways industry could obtain the same low-carbon products and services, including direct electrification and imported green materials.

That comparison changes the question for ammonia, steel and refining. A European fertiliser or chemical manufacturer needs ammonia, not necessarily hydrogen manufactured inside Europe. A steelmaker needs iron meeting its grade and emissions requirements. A mill needs process heat at specified temperatures. Governments can pay a premium to preserve domestic capacity for security or resilience, but the benefit must be valued and the public cost made explicit.

My November 2026 European hydrogen assessment applies that approach. In its central 2050 scenario, ammonia produced in Europe with on-site green hydrogen costs approximately €1,222 per ton. Qualifying imported green ammonia costs €745–755 per ton under the model’s assumptions. These are modelled values, not supplier bids. They demonstrate why an analysis that starts with hydrogen production targets can produce the wrong infrastructure plan.

RMI’s 2026 China green ammonia and methanol report acknowledges that green production costs remain two to three times conventional costs and that demand development lags supply ambitions. The report nevertheless discusses expanding ammonia and methanol as energy carriers, including ammonia for electricity. The relevant comparison for electricity is renewable generation with storage and other flexibility, not fossil-derived ammonia alone. RMI has not demonstrated that adding an ammonia combustion pathway wins that comparison.

This is a strategy problem as much as a modelling problem. Using Richard Rumelt’s framework, RMI’s diagnosis has improved, its guiding policy remains too committed to expanding hydrogen markets, and some coherent actions are missing. An economically unfavourable comparison should be able to end an infrastructure recommendation. Instead, it too often generates proposals for subsidies that would make the hydrogen route easier to sell.

RMI has the expertise to correct this. Its hydrogen recommendations should carry explicit alternative-technology comparisons, investment thresholds and exit criteria. Cross-program review should include the researchers measuring battery costs, industrial electrification, freight operations and grid flexibility. Where hydrogen is an essential chemical input or demonstrably the best means of delivering a service, support it. Where competing technologies win on cost and deployment readiness, stop trying to create demand through policy.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines RMI’s US, India, Europe and China reports side by side, including the differences between its findings and recommendations. It also links the original sources and the 2024 critique.

— Quotable quotes heard by MedPage Today's reporters

"The case count is a floor." -- Amesh Adalja, MD, of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security in Baltimore, on the likely underreporting of bird flu cases during an outbreak in Washington state.

"Having letters behind our names as physicians does not grant us any special privilege of not having an underlying mental health condition." -- N. Adam Brown, MD, MBA, discussing clinician mental health in light of a doctor's mass shooting.

"These children were thriving." -- Ania Jastreboff, MD, PhD, of the Yale School of Medicine in New Haven, on children as young as age 6 with obesity who lost substantial weight on semaglutide (Wegovy) in a clinical trial.
