#5555. Three Green Hydrogen Projects Slip Through The Trump Chopper

When US President Donald Trump swept into office last year, he set his choppers upon the $8 billion Regional Clean Hydrogen Hubs program, snuffing out plans to establish a diversified, domestic hydrogen market with a focus on decarbonization. Nevertheless, some stakeholders have continued to pursue the dream of producing green hydrogen from renewable resources — instead of squeezing it from natural gas. Now all that hard work is beginning to pay off, Trump or no Trump.

If you guessed the startup Plug Power is in the mix, run right out and buy yourself a cigar. Plug Power began life back in 1997 with a focus on electric forklifts powered by zero emission hydrogen fuel cells. In addition to replacing fossil fuels, Plug Power aimed to replace battery-powered forklifts, with fuel cells being a better fit for the fast-paced environment of shipping and logistics.

Plug Power soon pivoted into replacing gas-derived hydrogen fuel with so-named green hydrogen, pushed from water by an electrical current. After a series of ups and downs the company hit the jackpot in January of 2025, when the US Department of Energy tapped it for a $1.66 loan guarantee in support of the Regional Clean Hydrogen Hubs program, which was funded through the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. If all went according to plan, Plug Power would have used the loan to finance up to six green hydrogen projects around the US, all affiliated with the Hydrogen Hubs program.

So much for that. The Energy Department announced the loan award at the beginning of the month, when former President Joe Biden was still in office. However, by the end of the month Trump was officially installed in the White House. He soon pulled the plug on the Plug Power loan, so to speak, sending it down the drain alongside many other federally funded clean power projects.

That was not the end of the story for Plug Power. After all, it’s a big world out there, and Plug Power continued to pitch its wares overseas. Last week the company also relaunched itself back into the US market, bigly.

On November 17, Plug Power announced that its new “GenEco™ Scale” green hydrogen electrolyzer system is up for grabs in the US market while concurrently announcing that its first customer is the Texas-based firm Aracdia eFuels. Arcadia will deploy 280 megawatts’ worth of GenEco Scale modules at its Project ARC campus in the Portland/Corpus Christi area in Texas. When fully up and running, Project ARC will deploy green hydrogen from the GenEco Scale system to produce about 23.2 million gallons of fossil-free aviation fuel per year.

While green hydrogen has its fans in the decarbonization field, the stubbornly high cost of electrolysis has raised a formidable obstacle against widespread commercial uptake. Plug Power is among the stakeholders pitching modular, integrated systems to help bring costs down into parity with conventional hydrogen sourced from natural gas or coal, and that’s where the GenEco system comes into play.

“Built around a standardized 20 MW block architecture, GenEco Scale combines Plug’s proven proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzer technology with integrated balance-of-plant systems into a modular, pre-engineered solution for hydrogen production projects of approximately 100 MW and above,” Plug Power explained in a press statement last week. The company also noted that the “outdoor-ready” system avoids much of the cost and time related to the buildings and other infrastructure required of traditional large scale electrolyzer systems.

Arcadia eFuels CEO Amy Hebert also chipped in her two cents in support of the modular system. “Reducing the engineering burden on our EPC [engineering, procurement, and construction] partners and minimizing the complexity of bringing these systems together were important considerations for Project ARC,” Herbert emphasized.

Savings on land is another part of the cost-cutting plan. Unlike conventional electrolyzer system layouts, the GenEco model deploys a vertical configuration. The vertical system requires less than one acre per 100 megawatts of electrolyzer capacity, according to Plug Power.

Another Plug Power project has bubbled up in California, which was on track to host a suite of projects under the Hydrogen Hubs program with a focus on hydrogen derived from biomass as well as water electrolysis. The funding evaporated under Trump, but the state is still getting its hands on green hydrogen.

On November 19, Plug Power announced that its containerized 5-megawatt GenEco electrolyzer is up and running at a green hydrogen plant in Vernon, California, under the umbrella of the New Jersey-based firm Avina Clean Hydrogen.

Green hydrogen from this project will go to fulfill California’s plans for a zero-emission freight corridor, the plan for which includes fuel cell electric trucks as well as battery-powered trucks. “Located approximately 10 miles from the Port of Long Beach, the facility is designed to serve fleets moving freight through the Los Angeles–Long Beach port complex. It combines on-site fueling with tube-trailer deliveries to customers across the Los Angeles region,” Plug Power explains.

The station, also accommodate buses, and it can refuel a heavy-duty vehicle to more than 95% capacity in less than 30 minutes, according to Plug Power. That stacks up well against charging times for battery-powered heavy duty vehicles. On its website, for example, Tesla asserts that its new Semi electric truck can recover 60% of its 500 mile range in up to 30 minutes at a Tesla Megacharger station.

For the record, Avina has not placed all of its cards on hydrogen fuel cell trucks. The company’s roster of clean hydrogen projects also includes SAF (sustainable aviation fuel) and green ammonia, which is a key input for fertilizer among other chemical products.

Rounding out the trio of new projects is the Swedish firm PowerCell Group. The firm is better known for its work in the marine energy field, and now it is tapping into land-based markets as well. Last week PowerCell announced that its US branch is in motion to set up a green hydrogen system run by excess electricity from an existing solar array owned by a to-be-named client in the US. In effect, the hydrogen will serve as an energy storage medium. It will go to run a PowerCell PowerPod 3000 stationary fuel cell, which will kick into action at night to keep the clean kilowatts flowing after the sun goes down.

PowerCell describes the PowerPod 3000 as “a containerized power generation platform integrating our PS190 systems with power conversion equipment, cooling and DMC, PowerCell’s control and Energy Orchestration technology,” with an installed fuel cell capacity of 27 megawatts and 20 megawatts of rated power.

That’s a good question. Rather than let that excess solar electricity go to waste, the client could invest in a BESS (battery energy storage system) for daytime energy storage and night-time electricity. However, a typical BESS only lasts for a handful of hours. In contrast, PowerCell describes its fuel cell as a “long duration” storage system, which generally means eight hours or more.

PowerCell also points out that a fuel cell does something that a BESS cannot. Fuel cells generate electricity by combining hydrogen with oxygen in the presence of a catalyst. Water — H2O — is a byproduct. All else being equal, that opens up the potential for green hydrogen to serve as a water distribution medium, sucking up water in an electrolysis system at one location, then pushing it out in a fuel cell located elsewhere.

PowerCell is not making any specific promises for this particular project, though the company does emphasize that “the ability to generate both electricity and recoverable water adds another dimension of value to hydrogen-based energy storage.”

“The amount of water recovered, and its potential uses will depend on the final system configuration, operating conditions and water treatment requirements,” the company adds.

And, that’s where things get interesting. The client is a to-be-named electric cooperative, which is of interest because electric cooperatives (more specifically, Rural Electric Cooperatives) account for a large portion of the US grid, and their roots in the rural poverty fighting programs of the Great Depression provide for a distinctive public benefit mission that can, in some cases, allow more wiggle room for innovative energy solutions that generate broad benefits for local communities.

I’m reaching out to PowerCell for more details. If they can’t divulge the name of the client yet, perhaps they’ll be able to describe what they mean by long duration energy storage, so stay tuned for an update.

Photo: The startup Plug Power is among the green hydrogen stakeholders carving out more space for renewable energy in the US market, despite last year’s sharp U-turn in federal energy policy (cropped, courtesy of Plug Power).

#5554. UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings

UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealth Group is joining the ranks of insurers that are suing the feds over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings calculations.

Much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations. Over the summer, a Georgia federal court sided with MA plan Clover Health, and tossed 20 measures that were used in its 2026 scores.

That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.

UnitedHealth said in its complaint that it is bringing the lawsuit to ensure "that their 2027 Star Ratings are calculated in accordance with CMS’s statutory authority and procedural obligations."

The star ratings are tied to quality bonus payments for Medicare Advantage plans and listed on the Medicare plan finder to help individuals identify high-quality coverage. When those payments are lower due to a decline in scores, the insurer may not be as nimble in lowering premiums or enhancing benefits.

"The Star Ratings carry real consequences," UnitedHealth wrote in the complaint. "A plan’s Star Rating thus directly affects the benefits and healthcare offerings that Medicare beneficiaries receive."

Elevance Health is the latest insurer to sue the feds over its performance in the latest round of star ratings for the Medicare Advantage program.

The company sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in District of Columbia federal court on Friday, arguing that the 2027 star ratings calculations violated the Administrative Procedure Act in using 11 measures that it says were adopted unlawfully.

In the lawsuit, the company said that the harm from including these measures is "concrete and substantial." If they were excluded, it would increase the scores for 12 of its Medicare Advantage contracts and generate $516 million in additional quality bonus payments.

"Their inclusion therefore does more than violate statutory requirements in the abstract: it depresses Elevance Health’s ratings and reduces the funding available for the following payment year," per the lawsuit. "That funding could support broader supplemental benefits, lower premiums and cost-sharing, and improved care coordination."

"CMS’s unlawful methodology puts those resources out of reach," the company said.

In addition to the financial impacts, Elevance argues that the star ratings scores can also lead to reputational damage that makes it harder for them to compete in the MA market. It also provides prospective enrollees with inaccurate information, the company said.

"Beneficiaries cannot make informed coverage choices when the government’s own comparison tool conveys a distorted assessment of the plans available to them," Elevance said.

"An artificially depressed rating does not merely place Elevance Health at a competitive disadvantage; it undermines the very comparison the program is supposed to enable," the company continued. "A rating lowered by unlawful measures presents beneficiaries with a misleading signal of relative quality, rather than a lawful basis for distinguishing among competing plans."

CVS Heath's Aetna is joining the ranks of insurers suing over its results in the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

The insured filed suit Monday in Georgia's Southern District Court, and argues that 28 measures used by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to calculate its scores were "unlawfully adopted" and should have been excluded.

The court is the same venue that ruled in favor of Clover Health over the summer, and set aside 20 measures that were used to determine its 2026 scores. That decision, which the feds have appealed, kicked off a broad recalculation of 2026 scores that looked different for insurers outside of Clover, triggering a wave of litigation.

In its lawsuit, Aetna cites the Clover decision in finding that CMS extended beyond its statutory authority in deploying those 20 measures.

The company said that calculating its scores using the 28 measures in question will likely cost it $2 billion in 2028 quality bonus payments and rebate retention. Those are funds that the insurer could "apply toward expanding member benefits, reducing premiums and investing in quality improvement."

Aetna adds that in addition to the monetary loss, having lower scores negatively impacts the company's reputation and its ability to attract potential members.

"The harm to CVS Health is not exclusively financial; lower ratings carry meaningful reputational harm, which can in turn impact membership," per the lawsuit. "By incorporating unlawful measures into the 2027 Star Ratings calculation, CMS cast CVS Health’s ratings in a poorer light in the eyes of Medicare Advantage consumers relative to peer MAOs, undermining CVS Health’s ability to compete for Medicare beneficiaries through enhanced benefits and the like."

Aetna did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Based on an analysis from Stephens, 69% of Aetna's MA members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 81%. That threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments.

Aetna's complaint follows others focused on the 2027 scores from Centene and Alignment Healthcare (see those stories below).

Centene has become the latest insurer to sue the federal government over its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

In a lawsuit filed Thursday in Georgia's Southern District Court, the company argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act in determining its latest scores. Centene says that CMS ran afoul of "core statutory safeguards" in deploying 17 measures.

The use of those measures ultimately caused "significant injury" to the company, according to the complaint. For 2027, 9% of Centene's members are enrolled in plans with at least four stars, which declined from 18% in the prior year.

"In implementing each of the individual Star measures that Centene challenges, CMS violated applicable law and thereby caused Centene to lose out on hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that Centene could use to strengthen benefits, reduce premiums, and improve health outcomes," the company said in the lawsuit.

CMS argues that the court has already sided with a similar argument in its decision in favor of Clover Health earlier this year. In that case, which led to a broad recalculation in scores, the courts set aside 20 measures that were used in determining Clover's star ratings for 2026.

If the 17 measures in question had been excluded in calculating Centene's scores, the company estimates it would receive $448 million more in quality bonus payments for the 2028 plan year, funds it would deploy to expand benefits, lower premiums and enhance programs like care coordination.

In addition to the financial impact, a drop in star ratings also carries a reputational hit, Centene said.

"Beyond the financial impact to the company and its members, depressed ratings also inflict significant reputational damage and diminished membership," the company said in the complaint

Centene had not returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Alignment Healthcare sued federal regulators, alleging that its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings were determined "in flagrant violation" of statute.

In the lawsuit filed Friday in District of Columbia federal court, the insurer says that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services "has completely departed from Congress’s vision of leveraging predictable, valid measures developed with input from providers, plans, and the public" in establishing the methodology for the star ratings.

The company argues that rather than establish "consistent, stable specifications" for metrics through the traditional rule-making process, the agency instead detailed key measures through a series of "technical notes." This violates the Administrative Procedure Act, per the lawsuit.

The program's star ratings are the critical determinant in quality bonus payments to insurers as well as a tool that aims to make it easier for enrollees and brokers to identify benefits with the highest quality.

"Consistent application of the statutory requirements governing Star Ratings is therefore essential not only to plan payments and competition but also to ensuring that beneficiaries can rely on the Star Ratings as meaningful and comparable measures of plan quality," Alignment said in the lawsuit.

The company adds that multiple recent court decisions have set aside CMS' star ratings methodology, notably a ruling over the summer in favor of Clover Health that tossed 20 metrics used in the 2026 calculations. A Georgia federal judge determined that 10 measures utilized exceeded CMS' authority, while 10 other measures were promulgated inappropriately.

CMS recalculated the scores across the board following the ruling, but only set aside the 10 measures that the courts determined were outside the bounds of its regulatory authority. The agency maintained that approach in the 2027 calculations, Alignment argues.

"Congress created the Star Ratings program to allow Medicare Advantage beneficiaries to make informed decisions about plan enrollment based on clinically validated measures of plan quality that had been subjected to notice and comment," the company said. "CMS’s contrary approach fails to carry out the vision that Congress set forth by statute."

The Trump administration has appealed the Clover decision, so that legal case remains ongoing.

In addition, Alignment argues it suffered reputational and financial damage as a result of its 2027 scores, which plummeted compared to the prior year. Just 25% of its members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 100% in 2026.

Shares in the company tumbled following the release of the ratings, though stock prices have rebounded since.

Alignment sued the feds following the Clover decision to secure a recalculation for its scores that aligns with the court's decision, and in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, said that the lawsuit aligns with that perspective.

"Our lawsuit seeks to ensure that the Star Ratings program operates as Congress intended and that Alignment is properly compensated for the care we provide," Alignment said in the statement. "We respect the judicial process and will present our case in court. Because this matter involves pending litigation, we will not comment on the specific legal arguments beyond our filings."

"Our focus remains on delivering exceptional care, improving health outcomes and advocating for a stable, lawful regulatory framework that supports seniors and strengthens the Medicare Advantage program," the company said.

#5553. Jensen Huang Reinstated As Nvidia CEO Following  Affair With Alleged Chinese Spy, Several Employees

Good morning! It's Monday, November 23, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition, Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia after resigning following affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and several employees, a handful of automakers are suing the great state of New Jersey to block an "extortionate" vehicle recall repair law, 1.6 million Hondas and Toyotas are impacted in the latest round of Takata airbag recalls and Amazon Autos is becoming a behemoth.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

Nvidia's board of directors announced Monday morning that it would be unanimously reinstating Jensen Huang, who resigned in disgrace on November 12, as president and CEO following affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and at least two Nvidia employees. In a statement, the board said the decision was made following a "series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead NVIDIA." Great.

What's far more likely is President Trump stepping in, or, at least putting his thumb on the scale. The decision came just hours after the President wrote on social media, "I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A." I mean, the board pretty much said that was the case, with the caveat of "national security, saying Huang's reinstatement came after "input from senior levels of the United States government." It added that, based on the input, it was "confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk." I'm sure the fact the stock dropped 46-ish% during this whole fiasco didn't impact the decision, either. As of publication, Nvidia's stock is up 33% today, and the S&P500 is up 5%. From NBC News:

In his own statement, Huang said he was "honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution."

Huang has served effectively as the unofficial ambassador for the artificial intelligence boom, the companies backing it and the trillions of dollars being spent in the sector.

"I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support," Huang added.

The reversal was a dramatic turn, after Nvidia's newly installed chairman Harvey Jones on Nov. 17 said, "Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as President, CEO and Board member. The Nvidia Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Nvidia's inerim CEO Collette Kress also said that the company would not be reinstalling Huang in an interview the same day.

Huang's removal from Nvidia came after The New York Times reported that Huang had a close relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies believed was a Chinese spy. The Financial Times followed that report, saying that Huang had an affair with the woman.

In a memo to Nvidia's workforce on Nov. 8, Huang said, "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

The New York Times also reported Huang had an extramarital relationship with a senior leader at Nvidia who reported directly to him.

After Huang's removal, the board of the company initiated a search for a new leader, reportedly seeking out Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas. However, Haas earlier Monday announced that he was remaining at Arm, with a contract extension through 2033.

Nvidia also set up a new "national security and export control oversight" panel in light of the revelations about Huang.

President Trump has already weighed in, saying on social media that the government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security. Attorney General Todd Blanche also confirmed that the government doesn't feel he broke any laws.

Still, Nvidia and Huang aren't out of the woods.

The return of Huang raises many questions for Nvidia, including the status of its dealings with overseas companies purchasing its high-powered chips, and Huang's relationships with his subordinates at the company.

Despite Trump's statement that the U.S. government believes that Huang poses no national security risk, the company could still face legal exposure on other fronts. The Wall Street Journal and Reuters both reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is probing the company. The Journal said the probe was focused on the firm's accounting practices.

In any case, Huang and his leather jackets are back. I'm sure everybody (the shareholders) is thrilled about that.

Ford, Honda, Stellantis and Volkswagen are suing the Great State of New Jersey (read: God's Country) in an effort to block a new state law that they say would increase the amount of money automakers would have to pay franchised dealers for warranty and recall repairs. Boohoo!!!!

In a complaint filed in Trenton, the capital of the world, the automakers said the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Open Recall Notice and Fair Compensation Act gives dealers a "blank check" to set prices for warranty, recall and other repair services. They also contend that it prohibits them from avoiding "extortionate" results for recovering the costs. From the Detroit Free Press:

New ⁠Jersey's law will shift more than $375 million a year to dealers from automakers, giving ​dealers a "windfall" by imposing no obligation to use the money to improve customer service or ​boost compensation for employees, the automakers said.

"In short, the act rewards dealers for charging their customers more," the automakers said.

New Jersey's law took effect on April 1, after ​former Governor Phil Murphy signed it in September 2025.

The automakers objected to letting dealers charge ‌a "labor multiplier" ⁠based on samples of repair orders, saying it lets dealers bill for substantially more labor time than they actually work.

They also challenged provisions requiring automakers to pay marked-up prices on parts that the dealers received at reduced cost or for free, and preventing automakers from ​providing less expensive ​parts even if supply, ⁠demand or other factors justified price cuts.

Ford, Honda, FCA — which includes Fiat and Chrysler — and Volkswagen said that since the law took ​effect, each has received dozens of bills requiring payment "for hours that ​no technician ⁠works, that surpass what comparable dealers charge for the same work, and that exceed what retail customers pay."

They said the law violates the U.S. Constitution's Commerce Clause and Taking Clause, and it is preempted by federal laws governing recalls. They also contend it violates New Jersey's Constitution. How dare they invoke New Jersey's Constitution? This thing of ours.

The Takata airbag disaster is a saga that will clearly never end, as evidenced by the fact that a further 1.6 million Hondas and Toyotas have just been recalled over airbag inflators that could rupture. Both automakers said that no serious injuries or crashes have been tied to the recalled vehicles, and no ruptures have been reported, but out of an abundance of caution, they are replacing the inflators anyway. From Reuters:

The recall includes 810,592 older Honda cars and ​SUVs in the United States and 790,000 Toyota vehicles worldwide, including 314,000 in the United States.

The Toyota recall includes 2002-2010 Lexus SC430, 2011 ‌IS250, ⁠2017 GX460, 2003-2008 Toyota Corolla, 2005-2006 Tundra, 2005-2007 Sequoia and 2016-2017 4Runner. The Honda recall covers some 2013 Honda Accord, 2012-2013 Honda Civic, 2012-2013 Honda CR-V, 2013 Acura ILX and 2013 Acura RDX vehicles.

The Honda recall covers vehicles originally sold or registered in 14 states or territories known for high temperature, humidity and large temperature fluctuations.

The vehicles ​in the current recalls have airbag inflators that contain a moisture-absorbing material — unlike the millions of vehicles recalled previously.

The National Highway ​Traffic Safety Administration said analysis and inflator degradation simulation models conducted by independent testing groups allowed the automakers to act ahead of potential risks.

"Honda and Toyota saw early evidence of degradation risk in certain of their vehicles and are currently conducting proactive recalls of vehicles," NHTSA said ​late Friday, adding that other automakers continue to conduct inflator analysis and testing.

Honda said long-term ⁠monitoring and analysis revealed potential propellant degradation in certain inflators within specific geographic regions.

Toyota warned that degraded propellant could cause the inflator to rupture if the airbag deploys and cause serious injuries.

The Honda recall applies to vehicles sold or registered in Alabama, California, ⁠Florida, Georgia, ​Hawaii, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas, Puerto Rico, US Virgin Islands, Northern ​Mariana Islands (Saipan), Guam and American Samoa.

Toyota did not specify in which US states the recall applies but said it expects the replacement inflators will be ​ready by early 2027.

At least 28 people have been killed and over 400 have been injured by defective Takata airbag inflators since 2009 that send metal shrapnel inside the cars or trucks during inflation. It's an issue that prompted the largest automotive recall in U.S. history. All of those deaths involved airbag inflators without a dying agent, and at least 20 of those deaths were in Honda vehicles. Over the past decade, over two dozen automakers have recalled 100 million vehicles around the world, with about 67 million in the U.S. alone.

Amazon Autos streamlined its process to get dealers on its platform by more than 85 percent, replacing a one-size-fits-all signup page that left some dealers spending as much as a week registering for the digital sales platofrm. It helped overcome earlier problems that the platform has had since it launched at the end of 2024 that forced large dealership groups signing up on the same standarized page developed for standalone sotres and smaller groups. Now, there's a new signup process for larger dealer groups, and it's causing the platform to baloon. From Automotive News:

Amazon Autos initially launched with Hyundai and now includes 13 other brands listing new vehicles: GMC, Buick, Chevrolet, Cadillac, Audi, Volkswagen, Ram, Chrysler, Kia, Dodge, Subaru, Mazda and Jeep, according to the company. These brands also list used or certified preowned vehicles, along with 21 other vehicle makes.

Amazon Autos now has more dealers in the pipeline than they have live, [Amazon Autos director and global general manger Fan] Jin said, and the company continues to work through the backlog.

Dealerships are coming around partly because they now see Amazon as a reliable lead generator, rather than a competitive threat, said David Whiston, U.S. autos senior equity analyst at Morningstar Equity Research. It also helps, he said, that Amazon positions itself as assisting dealerships in selling vehicles rather than selling them directly to consumers.

Rohrman Automotive Group, with 20 dealerships in Indiana, Illinois and Wisconsin, sold 51 new and used vehicles through Amazon since it joined the partnership in April, said Jeremy Nowling, the group's sales and digital retailing director.

Amazon, for as big a company as it is, also doens't seem too worried about how people use Autos. Some customers use the platform from start to finish, visiting the dealership just to puck up the vehicle. However, some start the process on Amazon and the visit the dealership to apply for financing or finish the process.

#5552. Virginia Reports Young Child Is the State's First Measles Death in 2026

— The state has reported 220 cases overall this year, most of them among people not vaccinated

A young child has died in Virginia after testing positive for measles, officials said, the first deadly case in the state this year.

The Virginia Department of Health reported the death Friday, saying only that the child was under 5 years old.

Just days earlier the U.S., along with Mexico and Bolivia, lost its designation as having eliminated the highly contagious virus.

States have reported at least 12 measles-linked deaths in 2026. Eight of them, including one last week, have been in Pennsylvania, one was in New York, and two were in Wisconsin.

Virginia has reported 220 cases overall this year, most of them in the central part of the state, and the vast majority were among people not vaccinated against the virus.

The CDC has tracked more than 5,800 cases nationally in 2026, by far the most of any year since 1991.

There has been some concern about the virus spreading as families and friends gather for Thanksgiving next week and for Christmas and other holidays in December.

But experts say most adults do not need a booster shot, though some are good candidates for one.

This month the CDC put out new guidance on measles and pregnancy noting an increased risk of miscarriage and babies born with congenital infections, as well as health problems such as pneumonia for pregnant women.

The vaccines are not given to pregnant women but are recommended before pregnancy.

#5551. Pondering The Potential Of Plug-In VPP

I recently discussed the potential of the plug-in VPP from Jackery and Every Electric to transform urban energy storage. But the current program could be just the start. The more I discussed it at RE+, the more it started making me thing about where it could go in the future.

Essentially, customers of the plug-in VPP receive a battery, plug it into the wall and their window air conditioner, and connect to Wi-Fi. Then they use AC as they normally would, the VPP shaves off demand peaks on the grid, and the customer gets paid. It is likely the fastest, easiest and cheapest way to implement urban BESS in the US. And regular people living in apartments benefit. You can read more about the plug-in VPP in my previous article for context. Or you can watch the video below.

Both Jackery and Every Electric are collaborating and working to create innovative solutions for customer needs. Plug-in VPP makes the benefits of battery storage accessible to people in apartments. However, the potential could go much farther. Of note, much of what I am discussing here is not available yet. But the plug-in VPP sparked my imagination, and I wanted to expand on what might be possible.

Initially, the system is being deployed in New York City, which has a large number of apartments that can be aggregated to create a meaningful amount of combined storage. Of course, the potential can be realized in areas outside of NYC. Every Electric is already looking to expand into the Boston area. There are several other areas where the existing system based on window air conditioners in urban areas could apply, particularly along the Northeast corridor. However, as the program evolves, there is tremendous potential outside of the region.

In Jackery’s home state of California, 4.5 TWh of solar and wind power was curtailed in the first half of 2026. More electricity wasted in six months in one state than many developing countries consume in an entire year. Residential solar often feeds into the grid when it just leads to curtailments elsewhere. Even with recent ESS installations, the Duck Curve is still deepening. If home batteries can help “decapitate the duck,” customers and the utility both stand to benefit. And all that renewable energy currently being wasted can contribute to reducing emissions.

In addition, every Jackery battery can operate as a solar generator, with a DC input. People can simply plug in a solar panel or two to recharge the battery. No additional inverter needed. As it does not send energy back into the grid, it also avoids the cost and complication of traditional grid-tied systems. Sending solar power directly to the battery would avoid having excess solar generation fed into the grid that contributes to overcapacity, deepening the back of the duck curve. Demand response could then come from a battery charged largely from solar, rather than from the grid. As the US is still trying to figure out balcony solar regulations, this would let people enjoy many of the benefits of small scale, plug-and-play solar now. No electricians needed.

Of course, when balcony solar regulations are figured out, Jackery has solutions like the SolarVault3 that I saw at IFA Berlin. Potentially, this system could integrate with point of use battery storage to form a kind of hybrid plug-in system. In the process, solar power could be utilized when it does the most for the grid and offers the greatest potential payback for the customer.

There is also a lot of potential for this concept to work outside of the US. In many parts of the world, most people live in apartments. As the planet warms, world cooling needs recently overtook heating for the first time. As the VPP is monitored via a Wi-Fi connection, there is no need to upgrade to a smart meter to take advantage of the capability. As the storage is already distributed, there is also reduced need to provide the grid upgrades to distribute the energy stored in a large battery during peak energy demand.

Currently, the plug-in VPP is only working with one model of battery in one application. That makes the deployment and scaling of the plug-in VPP easier. Large urban areas offer the clearest path to aggregate the storage needed for a plug-in VPP to work.

However, Jackery has sold over 8 million units over the past 15 years. This has established a level of customer trust and a reputation for reliability. Many of those portable power stations and solar generators can connect to Wi-Fi. That is potentially GWh of deployable storage.

In addition, portable power stations are very popular now. Many Jackery models are selling out. Preparedness is a major driver. Climate-related disasters amplify the fear and uncertainty. However, the batteries that people are buying to be prepared for emergencies offer far greater potential capability. The more batteries that are out there, the greater the potential.

As the software and capability of the VPP develop, multiple batteries have the potential to connect to amplify value, even if that capability isn’t being offered yet. Those batteries, in coordination with a VPP, could earn people money. Currently, the system is being run with one battery model, but Jackery offers a wide range of batteries with Wi-Fi connectivity that might be able to participate in the future. Once the program has proven itself with the initial application in urban areas, there is potential for expansion.

As people start earning money, even if they purchased the battery out of preparedness concerns, they would also start to see the broader benefit. When they gain both confidence and financial benefit from battery storage and renewable energy, they will tend to rationalize that benefit. That can lead to a broader shift in mindset. When you try to start with a rational argument, especially when that argument involves added costs, people are less likely to be supportive than if you start with the benefit.

Many of the pieces to make this happen have already existed. People have the ability to program Jackery batteries through the app to charge and discharge during certain parts of the day. This can work with TOU utility plans, where available. But it doesn’t take full advantage of the capabilities of a VPP. Customers do not get full credit for the storage capability. The true innovation comes from putting the pieces together, between the Jackery hardware, Every Electric software and the utility. If one of those pieces of the collaboration was missing, a plug-in VPP wouldn’t have the same potential.

One of the things that has impressed me about Jackery since I was first introduced to the company was their focus on solving customer problems. However, to create solutions, they also recognize that collaboration is often necessary. I already saw this with the flexible solar panels of SunBooster at IFA Berlin for balcony solar applications, and then again with Every Electric for plug-in VPP.

#5549. CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition

CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has proposed a slew of changes to Medicare Advantage and Part D designed to "revitalize care" in these markets.

For one, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said late Friday that it will update application and network adequacy requirements to make it easier for new entrants. The agency proposed to require organizations to demonstrate network adequacy during their first year in operation, rather than during the application process.

This shift would eliminate a significant barrier for new entrants, driving greater competition in the market.

CMS has also proposed combining three specialty areas in behavioral health—clinical psychology, clinical social work and outpatient behavioral health—into one specialty group for the purposes of network adequacy. The changes will give plans greater flexibility in building out behavioral health networks.

CMS will also make adjustments that seek to boost competition for special needs plans.

In addition, the agency said it will make adjustments to the star ratings program, focusing its ratings on 15 measures. The proposed measure set would emphasize "clinical outcomes and patient experience while retaining select process measures in high-priority areas where performance remains low."

CMS is also aiming to update the calculation methodology that will "raise the bar for achieving high ratings," and thus quality bonus payments.

"People with Medicare should be able to choose coverage based on what matters most to them—quality, affordability and access," said CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These proposals are about creating a Medicare Advantage marketplace that rewards better care and better value while empowering beneficiaries with the options and knowledge they need to make informed decisions about their health."

The proposed rule also includes provisions that align with Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again agenda by setting a "healthy food" standard that MA plans should follow for supplemental benefits.

The goal, CMS said, is to ensure that Medicare dollars are spent on food benefits that align with MAHA.

"Medicare food benefits should pay for nutritious food that helps people improve their health and manage chronic disease," Kennedy said in the announcement. "This proposal would require those benefits to meet the Dietary Guidelines for Americans while preserving access to foods and nutritional products that providers recommend for patients’ specific medical needs."

"Under President Trump, we are putting prevention at the center of health care and demanding more from every Medicare dollar," Kennedy said.

#5548. Five Fuel-Sipping Tips That No One Else Has The Guts To Suggest

America's affordability crisis doesn't seem to be going away any time soon, with everyone's budgets getting battered left and right by inflation, record-high housing costs, war-driven fuel price hikes, and sky-high automobile operating costs. It's starting to feel a lot like the 2008 financial crisis out here in the streets again. I distinctly remember everyone suddenly caring about their fuel economy back then, scrambling for more fuel efficient cars. With new car prices higher than ever, that might not even be an option for you. So let's look into a few measures you can implement on any car to make it more efficient.

Obviously, the most fuel-efficient thing to do in a cash crunch is to drive less, take public transit, or get there without burning fuel on foot or by bicycle. If those aren't viable options for you, even the least efficient transportation machine can benefit from these five suggestions. And if you're getting 12 miles to the gallon right now, bumping that up to 13 or 15 could make a pretty significant difference to your weekly budget.

For example, at the current national average fuel price of $3.81 per gallon, a vehicle that gets 12 mpg combined and travels 15,000 miles a year (the EPA's annual estimate), would spend $4,762.50 a year on fuel, while bumping that to 15 MPG would mean spending $3,810 per year — that's a big annual savings.

Here are five great ideas that you should definitely implement for your car to achieve better fuel economy. Some are more, um, involved than others, so before you dive into a project, make sure you have the necessary tools, skills, materials, time, space, and mental fortitude. You can absolutely do some of these projects yourself, but others might be best reserved for a professional, at which point you'll have to weigh the cost of modification against savings.

Here in the United States, the midterm elections finished up, and if you live in a swing state, as I do, you were probably bombarded with political ads, and seemingly every yard had signage for an election campaign or a ballot measure. Most of those signs are made from a corrugated plastic material called coroplast, which is significant for its low weight and high strength. That combination makes them great for constructing your own DIY aerodynamic modifications. Getting the materials for free is just an added benefit.

If you've been under a car before, you know that it's a lot less smooth than the shiny side you look at every day. There are exhaust pipes, suspension, driveshafts, and jacking points. If you manage to get a couple of the really big (and really obnoxious) yard signs, you could build a nice aerodynamically efficient flat floor tray for your car, improving the efficiency of airflow between the bottom of your car and the road. Tie it in to your rear bumper, and you'll help prevent a lot of turbulence.

It should go without saying that your car's exhaust gets pretty hot under normal operation, hot enough to melt coroplast. You should build your flat floor in a way that the inexpensive plastic material is mounted far enough away from the exhaust to prevent melting, perhaps even with a heat shield material to protect the edges. It's also possible that political signs in your area aren't made of coroplast, so be careful when you're using unconfirmed plastic to block off your engine bay from airflow or releasing heat. To get a proper flat floor around the exhaust pipes, you can use sheet aluminum in hot spots to keep the airflow clean and prevent melting.

After your flat floor, if you have some more coroplast laying around, you can build for yourself a grille block off. Because your car was built from the factory to operate in any temperature range, it has to have a larger grille opening and radiator than you need for light duty operation, particularly in the colder months.

Not only does selectively blocking airflow through the grille help improve the aerodynamic efficiency of your car at highway speeds, it will also help your car's engine warm up faster than it would with the radiator exposed to cold air. A cold engine consumes far more fuel than a warm one, so a faster warm-up time and maintaining heat within your engine compartment during trips with multiple stops is more beneficial to fuel economy than you might think.

You may have seen this sort of modification on diesel trucks and big rigs, especially in extremely cold temperatures. This is an easy one to get wrong, particularly if you forget you have a grille blockoff and leave it in through summer, so you'll have to pay attention to your car's gauges to avoid overheating. If you use them properly, you'll gain some winter MPGs. Again, it's important you know what you're doing with this project, as it is extremely easy to implement, but just as easy for it all to go awry.

Many automakers have employed expensive motorized grille shutters in an effort to improve efficiency. If you're really smart with electronics, you might even be able to craft your own motorized grille shutters with thermostatic controls that can potentially help improve your fuel economy in all seasons.

Chopping a section out of the middle of a car's height to lower the roof is a tried-and-true hot-rodding mod. While primarily used for looking cool, chopping the roof a few inches helps in many aspects of performance driving. Not only does it lower the car's center of gravity, but it reduces the frontal area of the vehicle, making it slip through the wind better. Improved aerodynamics are good for going fast, as your top speed improves, but it's also good for efficiency, as the car's overall aerodynamic drag goes down.

In the video above, the Motor Mythbusters made a dramatic chop to an old Dodge Tradesman van. Perhaps taking things to extremes is the best way to show their efficacy. It doesn't take a scientist to figure out that a Tradesman isn't very aerodynamic, isn't very fast, and isn't very efficient. By increasing its quarter-mile trap speed by several miles per hour, the team proved a chopped top was more aerodynamic.

If you can cut through the air better, you need less power to maintain a normal highway speed, reducing your fuel consumption. If you want to get really wild with it, you can reduce your frontal area even more by making your car a single-seater and cut the greenhouse of the car in half down the middle, like this Geo Metro owner did.

Obviously, there are some practical downsides to chopping your roof. For one thing, it's hard to recommend cutting the structural pillars of your car, just for the effect it might have on the car's rollover safety. Modify at your own risk.

Bulky exterior mirrors are one of the areas where automakers have sought to reduce aerodynamic drag for decades. In order to comply with government safety regulations, the mirrors need to show what's happening behind you, and for a number of different seating positions, requiring them to be quite large and adjustable. As the owner of the car, you can theoretically modify your car with smaller aftermarket mirrors, reducing the frontal area of your car further than the factory could in the development phase. But what if you could get rid of your mirrors altogether?

Audi, a few years ago, introduced its "virtual mirror" technology on the old e-Tron SUV. It wasn't permitted for use in the U.S. market, but it did go on sale elsewhere. By swapping the giant mirrors for a compact camera on an arm, Audi claimed the reduction in drag (dropping the e-Tron's cD from 0.28 to 0.27) was good enough for a couple of percentage points in overall vehicle efficiency. The camera relayed exterior images to a small real-time video screen in each door. The system, while expensive, allowed Audi to bump the car's range numbers by four miles.

Because aftermarket modifications aren't mandated to follow the same strict regulations as OEM equipment, you could theoretically suction cup some GoPros on the outside of your car and have them relay the video via Bluetooth to your phone. Or, you know, you could do something a bit nicer and with less latency. Who wants a delay when you need to know if it's safe to merge? Maybe you could 3D print a little housing for a small lens and run some wire through the mirror hole to feed a dash-mounted video monitor? I've been looking into something like this for a future project of my own.

Weight is the enemy of efficiency, and modern cars have gotten quite heavy. The U.S. Department of Energy says carrying an extra 100 pounds of weight in your car can reduce your fuel economy by one percent. One side of that is to reduce as much of the cargo you're hauling around without needing to, so if you've been meaning to donate stuff to Goodwill and it's been in your trunk for a month, you've been taking a fuel economy hit as a result. On the other side, every pound of unnecessary weight you can remove from your car makes your car more efficient.

Making your car lighter helps in every aspect of driving. A lighter car accelerates easier, meaning it'll require less fuel to gain speed at a given rate. It also means you can carry more speed through corners, reducing the need to brake and accelerate again. A lighter car is also easier on your consumable components, easing the efforts on brake pads and rotors, tires, and suspension components. An engine that isn't laboring quite as much will also wear less quickly and theoretically last longer.

So what can you do to reduce weight? I guess it depends on how much you can live without. A fully stripped interior with little more than a driver seat is going to be several hundred pounds lighter than one that's complete. If you can live without things like a center console, a stereo, a dashboard, and more, you could save a lot on fuel. If you want to be a little more pragmatic about it, there are still things you could do. You drive a minivan with a removable row of seats? You could save some fuel by removing those seats when you don't need them.

Did you always want to be a car designer when you grew up? Thanks to advances in 3D scanning technology, computer-aided design, computational fluid dynamics, additive construction, and instant-quote small-batch manufacturing, it's possible to design and build your own car's bodywork to your own exacting standards. Of course, you'll have to learn how to manipulate the software in order to make that happen, but it's definitely possible. Say you wanted to add an aerodynamic boat-tail or wheel skirts to your car, like the Volkswagen Mission Efficiency concept shown above. It's all within your reach!

A boattail shaped rear end is the most aerodynamically efficient way for a car to cut through the air. Not only does this allow air to continue to stay attached to the car, but it gives a smooth transition to clear air after the car goes through. An abrupt trunk with a blunt cutoff will create lots of turbulence behind it, which acts like a vacuum sucking the car's forward progress. By shrinking the low pressure area at the back of the car, there's much less pressure drag. Adding a five-foot boattail extension behind a semi-truck, for example, has been shown to increase fuel efficiency by almost twelve percent!

Similarly, wheel skirts help remove turbulent air from the car's trajectory through the air. Ecomodder logs show a few DIY wheel skirt projects with improvements from one to two miles per gallon, depending on application. Rear wheel skirts are much easier to install than fronts, as the front wheels need to exit the cover of the fender when turning, while the rear wheels are always covered. By filling in the gap between the fender and wheel, reducing drag, the car's engine doesn't have to work as hard to accelerate or maintain speed, improving economy.

#5547. Groups Respond to Army’s Plan to Proceed with Lead Azide Detonation in Iowa

Army says it plans to detonate degraded lead in Iowa town no later than Nov. 24, despite court stay.

Des Moines, IOWA — The Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club, and Earthjustice will continue to advocate for accountability from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the U.S. Army in the planned detonation of lead azide in Middletown, Iowa. Early Sunday morning, the groups filed declarations with the court that call out the Army’s inadequate public notice and information, and question the Army’s and EPA’s claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration.

The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a statement with the court late on Saturday, Nov. 21, indicating that the Army intends to invoke emergency provisions of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) to detonate 9,773.5 pounds of lead azide stored at the Iowa Army Ammunitions Plant, without a permit from the EPA. According to the DOJ’s court filings, the Army intends to do so no later than Nov. 24. On Nov. 20, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals granted Earthjustice’s request to put on hold a permit allowing the Army to detonate.

“People across numerous impacted communities speaking up and demanding accountability is the only reason there was an opportunity to pause and think about better ways to approach the lead azide problem,” said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau. “Yet despite claiming public safety is its top priority and public communication is essential to trust, the Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm.”

This emergency is of the Army’s own making. The Army has not publicly provided details about why the lead azide was not disposed of before it became so dangerous. The Army’s own storage and inspection practices allowed a primary explosive to sit until it reportedly degraded to the point that any alternative disposal method is now deemed too dangerous. The lack of transparency raises real questions about the scope and extent of potential impacts.

“The new information from the DOJ indicates that the problem is significantly worse than the Army originally shared. It appears that detonation may be, at this point, the only feasible option due to how long this problem was allowed to persist. The public deserves to know immediately which communities will be impacted and how residents can most effectively protect themselves and mitigate impacts on their health and homes,” said Michael Schmidt, General Counsel for the Iowa Environmental Council.

The Army knew about this stockpile of dangerous munitions waste for years, and it knew since at least March that the material was becoming unstable. Yet, just one week ago, most Iowans — including those directly in the path of a toxic lead plume, the Iowa governor, and key state agencies and officials — were unaware the Army intended to detonate nearly five tons of lead azide.

The environmental groups argue the EPA and Army permitting documents have not demonstrated, nor provided appropriate documentation that all other safer alternatives to mitigate the material were thoroughly explored.

“The Army has clearly mishandled this situation, and Iowans and residents in our neighboring states deserve a full review of all of the missteps that led us to this point. However, if detonation is now the only option, it is imperative that everyone impacted has access to the full range of testing, mitigation, and remediation resources,” said Wally Taylor, Attorney and Legal Chair for the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter.

As of 11 a.m. CST on Sunday, Nov. 22, the Army has failed to provide the public with updated weather modeling and mapping showing the path of the lead dust plume, which means people impacted have little time to take precautions to protect their families and homes. The wind patterns have shifted significantly, which means that potential community exposures have likely changed without visible effort by the Army to provide updated information to the public.

The Sierra Club is America’s largest and most influential grassroots environmental organization, with millions of members and supporters. In addition to protecting every person's right to get outdoors and access the healing power of nature, the Sierra Club works to promote clean energy, safeguard the health of our communities, protect wildlife, and preserve our remaining wild places through grassroots activism, public education, lobbying, and legal action. For more information, visit www.sierraclub.org.

#5546. Stop Washing the Turkey. If You Want a Safe Thanksgiving, Here's What to Do Instead.

— Keep food either hot or cold, because bacteria thrive in between

Ready or not, the holidays are here. It's a time when many Americans accustomed to preparing simple meals find themselves responsible for safely serving multi-dish feasts.

It's no easy task. Outbreaks of some types of food poisoning tend to rise in November and December, according to the CDC. Tainted turkey, undercooked stuffing, and germ-laced gravy from holiday buffets have all led to past illnesses -- and even deaths -- CDC investigators have found.

It can be tricky for occasional cooks to prepare big meals in a way that avoids the common hazards that can make people sick, said Donald Schaffner, PhD, a food science expert at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey.

"Cooking takes longer with big masses of food. Cooling takes longer with big masses of food," said Schaffner, who co-hosts the food-safety podcast "Risky or Not?"

Together with podcast co-host Benjamin Chapman, PhD, a food scientist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh, Schaffner outlined common ways to keep holiday meals both festive and safe.

Defrost Your Turkey Before Cooking, but Don't Wash It

Raw turkey can harbor illness-causing bacteria such as Salmonella, Campylobacter, and other germs. It must be handled safely to prevent those bugs from contaminating refrigerator surfaces, sinks, and kitchen counters.

A frozen bird must be thawed first. There are several accepted methods, including in the refrigerator, in the microwave, or in cold running water, Schaffner said.

"All of these methods pose risks," he cautioned.

A frozen turkey needs about 24 hours for every 4 to 5 pounds of weight to thaw in a refrigerator, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). If you use a microwave or the cold water method, the bird must be cooked immediately. For details about safe turkey handling, check out the thawing and cooking calculators created by the USDA.

And don't wash the turkey. It's a bad idea to rinse it in the sink, even though many cooks still insist on the practice, often out of habit, said Chapman.

"Anything that hits that surface and generates spray is going to basically spread contamination around your kitchen," he said.

Instead, pat the turkey dry with paper towels and toss them, or use a kitchen towel and disinfect it in the laundry.

Turkey needs to reach a cooked temperature of 165°F (73.8°C) before serving. The best way to tell if it's cooked is to use a tip-sensitive digital thermometer inserted in the innermost section of the thigh, not touching the bone.

Don't rely on the plastic pop-up thermometers stuck in some commercial turkeys. Chapman's past research shows that those buttons can activate well before the bird is actually done.

At the same time, don't determine doneness by relying on signs such as golden-brown skin, whether the meat is no longer pink, or whether the juices run clear.

"None of those are great indicators of temperature," Chapman said.

Keep Food Either Hot or Cold, Because Bacteria Thrive in Between

How you handle the rest of the meal -- mashed potatoes, gravy, green beans, or yams -- is just as important as the main dish. It's crucial to avoid the so-called danger zone of temperatures between 40° and 140°F (between 4° and 60°C), where bacteria can easily grow.

The key is to keep hot foods piping hot and cold foods cold -- and to refrigerate everything promptly, Schaffner said.

"The recommendation is that you get those leftovers into the refrigerator within 2 hours of when they came off of the stove," he said.

Make sure to refrigerate dense foods like sliced turkey, cooked sweet potatoes, or gravy in shallow containers to help them cool down fast. Schaffner's recent research showed that foods cooled in containers at a depth of no more than 2 inches posed little risk of growing dangerous germs.

One key way to avoid food poisoning is through scrupulous cleaning in the kitchen.

Wash your hands before preparing food and after touching raw poultry. Use separate cutting boards, knives, and other utensils when handling raw meat and fresh foods such as vegetables and salads.

Pay close attention to any surface that may be contaminated. It's important to clean first with soap and water and then sanitize with a disinfectant -- a two-step process.

While it's certainly not a one-to-one copy, I can certainly see why the folks over at Jaguar-Land Rover's legal department would be a bit miffed.

Although it has been on sale in China since last year, JLR launched the case earlier this year after BYD announced on its UK website that the seven-seater would be available to order, with customer deliveries starting in January of 2027, according to Reuters. Now, there's an injunction against its sale in the EU. The one caveat of all of this is that this court in the Netherlands has no jurisdiction over BYD's affiliate in the UK.

Until the whole intellectual property case is resolved, the court is banning BYD from producing the — admittedly good-looking — vehicle at its new factory in Hungary. It's due to spin up mass production of other vehicles next year, but the Ti7 will not be one of them unless something drastic changes very quickly.

"In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that ​the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover," Reuters reports the court ruling said. "The characteristic ⁠and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7."

Some of the more notable visual similarities are the boxy, flat-roof silhouette, its upright proportions, its side-hinged tailgate and squared-off wheel arches. The real kicker has to be the solid body-colored panel behind the rear passenger door, which is controversial on the Defender, yet BYD designers decided to include it anyway.

It's actually fairly rare in Europe for a large automaker to go to court over design rights infringement. It's also uncommon for a ruling to come down so early in proceedings for a case that is ongoing and likely to last some time. JLR, of course, is pleased with the outcome, telling Reuters, "We protect our intellectual property and take legal action when necessary."

Still, this isn't exactly the first  time something like this has happened, as Reuters explains:

Legacy automakers ​have often complained that ⁠Chinese automakers have copied designs, though little has been proven in court. In 2005, for instance, General Motors and Chinese rival Chery settled a case over the Chery QQ ​that the No. 1 US automaker said was a copy of its Chevrolet Spark.

BYD, for its part, "strongly disagrees" with The Hauge's ruling and is planning to appeal, telling the Wall Street Journal that the Ti7 is "the result of BYD's own independent design work and infringes none of JLR's rights." It added that it will "pursue every legal avenue to demonstrate that this decision ⁠is incorrect."

#5542. He Thought It Was a Muscle Strain. Then, Doctors Raced to Save His Leg.

— Skiing injury led to acute compartment syndrome, requiring urgent surgery

A 50-year-old recreational skier noticed pain in his calf after a collision with another skier, although he was able to ski down the mountain afterward. But an hour later, he presented to the emergency medical center at the base of the resort, complaining of pain and swelling in his left calf.

Ultrasound showed loss of typical muscle architecture, and a large hematoma within the medial gastrocnemius muscle, but there was no bone break on plain radiography. Later, the patient's pain worsened and numbness developed, leading doctors to be concerned about the possibility of acute compartment syndrome.

"Given this concern, as well as limitation of resources in the current clinical setting, immediate transportation to a level 1 trauma center 90 minutes away and orthopedic consultation on arrival was arranged," Morteza Khodaee, MD, of the University of Colorado School of Medicine in Aurora, and colleagues wrote in BMJ Case Reports.

There, he worsened quickly and was rushed into the operating room.

Compartment syndrome is most commonly caused by direct trauma, often in conjunction with fracture of the tibia, as with high-speed motor vehicle accidents or blunt force crush injuries like those seen in earthquake victims, the authors wrote. But in rare cases, it can also arise from non-contact mechanisms such as muscle strain.

"The patient's severe pain, along with physical findings of increased calf diameter and ultrasound-confirmed hematoma, was a key factor prompting transfer to a higher-level care facility for urgent fasciotomy," they noted.

Compartment syndrome is "a potentially life-threatening condition" typically arising after trauma or tissue ischemia, the authors noted, and can affect any myofascial compartment in the body. It's considered a surgical emergency because elevated intracompartmental pressure can compromise local blood flow and lead to decreased tissue perfusion.

"The earliest and most characteristic symptom of acute compartment syndrome is severe pain that is often described as out of proportion with the apparent injury," they wrote. It is also described as burning, deep, and made worse by passive stretching of the muscles involved. Over time, other symptoms appear, including paresthesias, sensory disturbances, and localized motor weakness. "Notably, pain may diminish or even be absent in the later stages of the syndrome, particularly in the presence of nerve ischemia," they wrote.

Confirming the diagnosis often requires measuring intracompartmental pressure using direct invasive measures like needle manometry, they noted. But while this can be helpful in more equivocal cases, it is not always necessary before proceeding to surgery, especially in the absence of a pulse in the affected extremity.

"Acute compartment syndrome is an orthopedic emergency that requires prompt surgical intervention," the authors wrote, most commonly a two-incision fasciotomy using anterolateral and posteromedial incisions to decompress all four compartments.

In this case, the patient was evaluated at the trauma center by the orthopedic team, and his condition was worsening quickly so physicians decided to go forward with surgery.

Findings during the fasciotomy included severe injury with a grade 4a tear of the medial gastrocnemius muscle, and hematoma greater than 500 mL in volume. The musculature of the superficial posterior compartment appeared viable, and while torn and contused, the gastrocnemius muscle was not necrotic, so significant debridement was not necessary, they wrote.

A vacuum dressing was applied to his incisions, and he was sent to the recovery room, the authors noted. There he showed recovery of sensation and motor function in the ankles and toes, but he continued to bleed significantly. He was sent for angiography that showed active bleeding and a pseudoaneurysm in the proximal calf from a branch of the medial sural artery, which was controlled successfully with embolization. Follow-up surgery confirmed no further necrosis, and the fasciotomy incisions were closed.

At both 8 weeks and 3 months of follow-up, his scars were well healed, his distal sensory and motor function were intact, and he was walking without a limp, the authors noted.
