#5521. Court strikes down anti-trans Ryan White funding rules 'based in animus, loathing and discrimination'

Court strikes down anti-trans Ryan White funding rules 'based in animus, loathing and discrimination'" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Medical associations and providers notched a legal victory over the federal government in a court ruling vacating federal funding requirements for Ryan White clinics involving gender-affirming care.

Those restrictions would have required recipients of Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program funds to not acknowledge the identities of transgender patients or use funds for gender-affirming care.

It was challenged by the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (HIVMA), the American Academy of HIV Medicine and the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care in June (see that coverage below), who argued that the policy was contrary to Congress' intent when establishing the program under law in 1991, lacked sufficient explanation and discriminated against transgender people in violation of the First and Fifth Amendments.

The Nov. 19 decision from Judge William G. Young, of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, prohibits the government from opposing its conditions in regard to all federal funding and permanently blocks any similar policies from being implemented by associational plaintifs' members, "which covers virtually every HIV care provider in the United States," said Lambda Legal, which acted as co-counsel for the plaintiffs.

"The ruling is a decisive and important victory for transgender people with HIV and protects the ability of physicians and other health care professionals to offer evidence-based care without political interference," Philip Bolduc, M.D., chair of HIVMA, said in a statement reacting to the decision.

Young's opinion and order opened with an acknowledgement that there are "sincere and deeply felt views" regarding transgender identity, and that the issue at question was of legal regulation rather than "the propriety of individual gender expression."

Still, the judge concluded his opinion by writing that the administration's conditions "are based in animus, loathing and discrimination. They do not stand for justice—in fact, they defy it. They are contrary to the laws of this nation and cannot continue to stand."

A group of medical associations and providers has filed a lawsuit challenging new federal funding requirements for Ryan White clinics involving gender-affirming care.

The new requirements, issued in a recent HRSA Notice of Funding Opportunity, require recipients of the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program funds to not acknowledge the identities of transgender patients or use funds for gender-affirming care. The restrictions undermine the very intent of the program, the plaintiffs say, and violate anti-discrimination components of the Fifth Amendment.

“The Ryan White Program was created as a public health intervention to address the needs of low-income, vulnerable populations who otherwise would not have access to life-saving care,” Melanie Thompson, M.D., co-chair of a primary care guidance panel for the HIV Medicine Association, said in a press release. “It is crucial that Ryan White clinicians be allowed to continue to deliver the most scientifically appropriate treatments for all patients, including transgender individuals, without discrimination if we are to improve health outcomes for all and end the U.S. HIV epidemic."

The lawsuit alleges (PDF) that HHS and HRSA violated the Administrative Procedure Act by exceeding their statutory authority and imposing restrictions that conflict with the Ryan White statute. The plaintiffs ask the court to block enforcement of the funding restrictions.

The case was filed by Lambda Legal and HSF Kramer on behalf of the American Academy of HIV Medicine, the HIV Medicine Association and the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care, plus two providers.

A preliminary hearing will likely be scheduled in a few weeks. Lambda Legal is “cautiously optimistic” about the future of the case, José Abrigo, senior attorney and HIV project director at Lambda Legal, told reporters on a webinar on Thursday afternoon. He called the administration’s actions “unlawful,” and said gender-affirming care in this context includes all types of care, including primary care and mental healthcare.

Specifically, the HRSA Notice of Funding Opportunity reads: “Discretionary awards shall not be used to fund, promote, encourage, subsidize, or facilitate … denial by the recipient of the sex binary in humans, or the belief that sex is a chosen or mutable characteristic.”

Some providers are already preemptively complying with the restrictions, Abrigo said, particularly in Tennessee and Kentucky. It is unclear how many other providers will also stop gender-affirming care. In certain cases, it’s up to individual states or departments of health to enforce the restrictions. It’s possible that medical records could be audited and reviewed for indications of pronouns, per Thompson. “It does matter what someone’s gender and pronouns are listed as,” Thompson said on the webinar, explaining that medical records are shared between providers and help ensure affirming care.

If a clinic is found to be non-compliant, the repercussions are steep, Thompson added. “The penalty for being found out is severe, and puts an entire program’s funding in jeopardy,” she said on the webinar.

Forty percent of American Academy of HIV Medicine members rely on Ryan White funding, of which 40% voluntarily report providing gender-affirming medical care. For low-income trans individuals with HIV, there aren’t many alternative options, per Abrigo. They may seek care through private insurance or potentially through Medicaid, but typically the population relies on Ryan White clinics for services.

Gender-affirming care restrictions under the Trump administration have been commonplace. Over 40 hospitals have reportedly stopped some gender-affirming care services for minors in response to pressure. Last week, the Cleveland Clinic promised the Department of Justice (DOJ) to commit $2 million to detransitioning services and a “decades-long” agreement not to perform gender-affirming care on minors. Delivering most of these services is currently illegal for minors under Ohio state law. Last month, DOJ struck a similar deal with Texas Children’s.

For months, experts have been sounding the alarm about the U.S. HIV response slipping into dangerous instability. In April, the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care (IAPAC) released a data brief finding that 61% of providers have reported at least one HIV service disruption and 68% have seen operational changes such as staffing reductions, service cutbacks and program closures. This was attributed to a combination of policy decisions, funding cuts and social determinants like loss of insurance coverage.

“It’s a catastrophe in the making," José M. Zúñiga, AIPAC's president and CEO, told reporters on the webinar. "It was already happening. This adds fuel."

#5520. First Hormone Therapy Approved for Early Breast Cancer in Over 20 Years

— Oral SERD giredestrant lands indication as adjuvant therapy for stages I-III disease

The FDA on Monday expanded the approval of giredestrant (Wilserdly) in breast cancer to include the adjuvant treatment of early-stage disease, just a week after greenlighting the next-generation oral selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD).

The new indication covers adults with stage I-III estrogen receptor (ER)-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer and an intermediate-to-high recurrence risk following surgery. With the new indication, giredestrant becomes the first hormone therapy approved for early breast cancer in over two decades.

"For patients with early-stage hormone-driven breast cancer, the goal after surgery is to keep the cancer from coming back," said Angelo de Claro, MD, director of the FDA's Oncology Center of Excellence, in a statement. "Our review focused on whether Wilserdly could reduce that risk more effectively than the hormone therapies patients already receive. The evidence showed that it could, supporting today's approval of a new option for patients at intermediate to high risk of recurrence."

In a large phase III trial (lidERA Breast Cancer), adjuvant treatment with single-agent giredestrant reduced the risk of invasive cancer recurrence or death by 30% compared with standard of care: 5 years of hormone therapy with tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor (anastrozole, letrozole, or exemestane).

Three-year invasive disease-free survival rates reached 92.4% with giredestrant compared with 89.6% in the standard-of-care arm (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.57-0.87, P=0.0014). Distant recurrence-free interval also favored giredestrant (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.54-0.89) while overall survival showed a trend in favor of the oral SERD (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.56-1.12).

"In lidERA, patients treated with giredestrant had a reduced risk of invasive disease recurrence, as well as fewer treatment discontinuations due to adverse events compared to standard endocrine therapy, thus representing a major clinical advance for patients with breast cancer," said investigator Aditya Bardia, MD, MPH, of the David Geffen School of Medicine at the University of California Los Angeles, in a press release from drugmaker Genentech.

Treatment discontinuations because of adverse events (AEs) occurred in 5.3% of the giredestrant arm versus 8.2% of the control arm. The most common treatment-emergent AEs (≥10%) included musculoskeletal pain; decreases in lymphocytes, leukocytes, neutrophils, hemoglobin, calcium, sodium, and potassium; increases in aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, triglycerides, cholesterol, calcium, potassium, and creatinine; hot flash; fatigue; headache; nausea; bradycardia; and COVID-19. Treatment-emergent AEs were primarily low grade, with a similar frequency compared with the control arm.

Bradycardia incidence -- a known class effect of oral SERDs -- was higher in the giredestrant arm (11.3% vs 3.2% among controls) and is listed in the warnings and precautions section of the drug's prescribing information, alongside a warning on embryo-fetal toxicity.

Giredestrant is also approved in combination with everolimus for previously treated ER-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer in patients with ESR1 mutations.

#5519. Florida sues The Leapfrog Group for 'misrepresenting' its hospital safety grades to consumers

Florida sues The Leapfrog Group for 'misrepresenting' its hospital safety grades to consumers" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Florida’s attorney general has filed a lawsuit against hospital safety watchdog The Leapfrog Group alleging that it misled consumers about how it determines the grades assigned to hospitals, particularly those that declined to voluntarily submit data to the group.

The complaint, which was filed late last week and lists President and CEO Leah Binder alongside her organization, follows a similar suit brought by Tenet hospitals in the state that convinced a judge that nonparticipating hospitals were being “unfairly” penalized in Leapfrog’s methodology.

The group was ordered to withhold safety grades for those hospitals and in grade releases since has voluntarily chosen not to award ratings to hundreds of others that did not submit recent quality data to its surveys. Leapfrog appealed that decision in September, and has said it is reviewing a potential methodology change for upcoming gradings to incorporate non-submitting hospitals.

The Florida Office of Attorney General James Uthmeier’s lawsuit cites that case. It argues that Leapfrog’s poor scores for “at least seven Florida hospitals” misled patients, and outlined specific cases in which patients had declined care over the perceived poor performances of those hospitals.

“The Leapfrog Group told Florida patients its hospital grades were peer-reviewed and backed by experts. That was a lie,” Uthmeier said in a Friday release announcing the litigation. “When hospitals declined to fill out its survey, Leapfrog handed them the worst scores in the country without a shred of data, and patients refused surgery because of it. Leapfrog and its CEO should expect to be held accountable.”

The office requested that the court permanently bar Leapfrog from “misrepresenting to Florida consumers … the data, sources, methods or expert approvals underlying any hospital grade or score they publish,” or from representing the scores as peer reviewed. It also seeks to limit Leapfrog’s solicitation of charitable contributions, make corrective disclosures, and pay out other relief to providers, patients or other affected individuals and groups.

Leapfrog, in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, said the office’s case “poses the specter of outright government censorship,” and was “piggybacking” on the Tenet hospitals’ case “with old allegations Leapfrog strongly refuted.”

“Leapfrog looks forward to answering in court and defending our First Amendment rights and most importantly, patient safety,” the group’s statement reads. “Too many patients are harmed or killed by medical errors and infections in hospitals, and Leapfrog will always stand up for their lives as we have for 26 years.”

The methodology change at the heart of the cases came ahead of Leapfrog’s fall 2024 safety grade publication. It more heavily weighed “imputed” scores for four of Leapfrog’s 32 safety measures that were assigned when recent safety data for the two preceding years were unavailable. The Tenet hospitals, in their case, highlighted internal communications and other testimony that questioned the validity of the changes. Both lawsuits suggest the changes were made to maximize hospital participation in Leapfrog’s survey, which would bring downstream increases to revenues it collects from allowing hospitals to advertise their grades.

Uthmeier’s office has also filed a friend of the court brief to the appellate court now considering Leapfrog’s appeal, where it similarly argues that Leapfrog’s conduct is a violation of Florida’s consumer protection laws and not protected by the First Amendment.

The new complaint comes the same week as Leapfrog’s latest hospital safety grade release, which, similar to the spring release, withheld grades for 447 hospitals.

#5517. HPV Viral Load Trajectory May Improve Risk Assessment for Cervical Cancer Lesions

— Persistently elevated viral loads tied to increased risks for any and high-risk lesions

Persistently elevated viral loads of human papillomavirus (HPV) were linked to dramatically higher rates of cervical cancer lesions, a large prospective cohort study showed.

As compared with low-stable trajectories, the likelihood of any cervical lesion increased by twofold to as much as 124-fold with persistently elevated trajectories, even those classified as moderate-declining. Patients with the highest persistent elevations had a ninefold higher risk of high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSILs), the most advanced cervical cancer lesion.

The study is one of the first to link longitudinal trajectories of HPV viral load to "clinically distinct risk phenotypes," reported Lina Zhang, MD, of Nanjing Medical University in Changzhou, China, and colleagues in Cancer.

"Among the 624 women with persistent infection, four distinct longitudinal viral-load trajectories were identified," the authors wrote. "The moderate-increasing and persistently high trajectories were associated with a markedly greater cervical lesion burden than the low-stable and moderate-declining trajectories, and these associations remained after multivariable adjustment. Longitudinal viral-load information also improved predictive performance beyond baseline characteristics and baseline viral load."

"Trajectory analysis further showed that persistent HPV infection is heterogeneous," they added. "The contrast between the moderate-declining and moderate-increasing groups was particularly informative. Although the moderate-declining group had a higher mean baseline viral load than the moderate-increasing group, its lesion prevalence was substantially lower. This contrast suggests that a single baseline viral-load measurement may not fully reflect subsequent disease risk."

The findings indicated that two women with similar baseline viral loads might have different clinical courses, a difference that has potential implications for clinical management, Zhang and colleagues noted. Additional studies in different populations are needed to validate the findings before implementation in clinical practice.

The results added to a large volume of evidence linking HPV infection and cervical cancer. A recent systematic review of 85 studies and 173,746 women showed that higher HPV viral load was associated with greater cervical cancer severity and worse clinical outcomes. Another recent study showed that higher viral loads had a significant association with higher-risk cervical lesions, specifically HSILs. Yet another study suggested that evaluating genotype-specific viral loads might help distinguish transient infections from persistent, transforming infections.

The authors cited multiple other studies showing associations between HPV persistence and higher viral load with high-grade cervical disease.

"Together, these findings suggest that viral load, genotype, and infection multiplicity may provide complementary information about the clinical course and risk associated with HPV infection," Zhang and colleagues wrote.

Previous longitudinal studies have relied on repeated-measures approaches to determine changes in viral load over time, which might not fully capture between-patient heterogeneity in longitudinal viral-load patterns, the authors noted. For the current study, they used latent class growth analysis (LCGA) and group-based trajectory modeling to describe heterogeneity in HPV viral-load patterns over time.

The study involved 1,170 women with HPV infection and classifiable outcomes, followed at 6-month intervals. Of these women, 624 patients had persistent infection, 471 with clearance, and 75 with reactivation. Baseline viral load differed significantly across the groups (4.75 log10 for persistent infection vs 4.07 for the clearance group and 4.41 for the reactivation group, P<0.001). Median follow-up also differed significantly (P<0.001) between the persistently high (23.2 months) and clearance (14.9 months) groups. Median follow-up in the reactivation group was 19.8 months among those patients with follow-up time data.

The investigators used LCGA to follow the patients with persistent infection, which was divided into four viral-load trajectories: low stable (39.6%), moderate declining (18.9%), moderate increasing (29.8%), and persistently high (11.7%). Prevalence of any cervical lesion increased with the trajectory of viral load persistence:

As compared with the low-stable group, adjusted odds ratios increased with trajectory: 1.95 for moderate declining (95% CI 1.02-3.74), 29.66 for moderate increasing (95% CI 16.75-52.51), and 124.29 for persistently high (95% CI 47.30-326.60). The persistently high subgroup had an HSIL odds ratio of 9.47 (95% CI 3.18-33.09).

"Trajectory group membership remained strongly associated with any cervical lesion after adjustment for HPV type, infection multiplicity, and socioeconomic, behavioral, and reproductive factors," Zhang and colleagues wrote. "The very large ORs observed for the moderate-increasing and persistently high groups should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously because they partly reflect the marked separation in lesion prevalence across trajectory groups, and the confidence intervals were relatively wide."

#5516. Own, don’t rent: Why agentic AI is pulling cloud computing back on-prem

Agentic AI is reviving an argument over renting versus owning compute, and the model plane — the layer that decides where AI models run — sits at the center of it. Open-source efforts such as Upbound Inc.’s Modelplane route inference across clouds, but many enterprises want the models on hardware they control.

That shift favors companies that built early for on-premises cloud infrastructure. Oxide Computer Co., which raised $445 million in October to expand rack production, built its business on the idea that enterprises at scale will want to own their computers, according to Bryan Cantrill (pictured), co-founder and chief technology officer at Oxide.

“Cloud computing is great, but the model shouldn’t be exclusively to rent it. You get to a certain scale, as it turns out, you want to own your own computer,” Cantrill said.

Cantrill spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed renting versus owning compute, why agentic workloads are moving on-prem and multi-tenancy for isolating those workloads.

Agentic workloads are driving an explosion in compute demand, and much of it is CPU-heavy work that enterprises would rather own than rent. Economics remains the main reason to bring it in-house, but where models live is a close second, Cantrill explained. That makes the model plane as much a data governance decision as an infrastructure one.

“There is a real enterprise drive towards open-weight models, and I think you’re going to see more and more of that as people want to run the models on-prem and allow their data to not actually leave,” Cantrill said.

Security is the other half. Oxide stripped the UEFI BIOS and baseboard management controller out of its rack to shrink the attack surface, and built public cloud-grade multi-tenancy in from the start. Those early design choices give enterprises a perimeter for isolating agentic workloads, according to Cantrill.

“I think multi-tenancy means you’ve got potentially adversarial tenants that are going to be on the same resource,” Cantrill said. “They’re going to be sharing the same computer, sharing the same network, and they need to do that … without violating the confidentiality, without breaching one another.”

The same racks can take on legacy virtualization workloads from customers unhappy with pricing changes at Broadcom Inc.’s VMware business. That lets enterprises run old and new applications on one general-purpose platform, Cantrill noted.

“You want all that flexibility that you get from elastic compute, but you need it for economic reasons, security reasons, latency reasons,” Cantrill said of the case for on-premises cloud computing. “You need it in your own data center. You want to control your fate.”

#5515. Unpacking the implications from CMS' latest proposed Medicare Advantage changes

Unpacking the implications from CMS' latest proposed Medicare Advantage changes" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Late last week, the Trump administration released a proposed rule that includes a slew of technical changes in Medicare Advantage for 2028, citing enhanced competition as a key goal.

Analysts dove into the beefy regulation and projected that changes to MA's star ratings program would likely cull more than $100 billion in federal spending over the next decade.

Per a note from Leerink Partners, estimates from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services suggest that the changes would cut federal spending by $11.5 billion in 2031 and $107 billion through 2037.

The Leerink analysts estimate that about 58% of Medicare Advantage contracts would see lower scores using the newly proposed methodology, with about 20% of contracts losing quality bonus payments, which are tied to star ratings performance.

In the rule, CMS proposed moving to a set of 15 measures to determine the star ratings scores, which are focused on member experience and outcomes. The proposed rule would also eliminate the Reward Factor, and in tandem, these changes "would remove a cushion for contracts sitting at the critical QBP threshold, while concentrating performance across fewer measures," according to the Leerink report.

The analysts said that the potential impact of these proposals "reminds us just how many plans have been living at 4 stars for years with the hugely important Reward Factor."

The report estimates that the changes to the star ratings, if finalized, would have an uneven impact on insurers. For example, Humana would see the number of contracts earning four or more stars decline from 95% to 82.9%. Clover Health, meanwhile, would likely maintain 100% of its contracts, earning at least four stars.

UnitedHealthcare, by comparison, could see a drop from having 67.9% of its contracts in plans with at least four stars in 2027 to just 8.8% under the new methodology. For Aetna, the Leerink analysts project a decrease from 70% to 0%.

Given the scale of the changes, the Leerink analysts write that the rule sets the stage for a significant overhaul of the policies and rules that govern Medicare Advantage. The proposal is "almost overwhelming in size, scope and the impact on the industry."

Molly Turco, a policy analyst at TD Cowen, wrote in a note Monday that the proposed rule "is more significant than expected, in both revenue impact and scope and touches most core aspects of MA."

"It appears CMS aimed to reform long-standing concerns, especially Stars, in a way that takes money out of the program, while also loosening regulation on things like agents/brokers, seamless enrollment, network adequacy, etc. to help the program grow," Turco wrote. "However, we think these growth/deregulation policies are unlikely to offset the headwinds for MA."

She noted that while most of the most painful changes wouldn't impact plans until 2031 at the earliest; the delay does suggest CMS may be comfortable including more significant short-term changes to risk adjustment in the forthcoming 2028 Advance Notice, which is expected in January.

Ryan Langston, an equity research analyst at TD Cowen, wrote in the note that the proposed rule would likely be net negative for insurers with large, multi-state contracts and more people enrolled with plans earning at least four stars.

The delayed timeline of at least four years does grant plans time to adapt, Langston wrote, but the financial impacts would likely force benefit changes. The proposed rule could also spook investors concerned about what's included in the 2028 rate notice, he said.

"The combination of a smaller measure set, elimination of reward factors and reduced improvement measure protection likely lower Star ratings across the industry and force plans to mitigate lost revenue via benefit revisions," Langston wrote.

The Leerink analysts wrote that health plans are almost certain to fight the regulation. Lawsuits have become commonplace in the stars space, with multiple payers suing the feds over the most recent round of scores.

"We believe a lot of what has been proposed will change and/or not be implemented at all," they wrote. "Expect industry litigation."

#5514. Neonatal Deaths Rose After Abortion Bans, Study Suggests

— Analysis examines longer-term data and more states than previous research

Newborn deaths rose after states implemented abortion bans, partly driven by a rise in severe congenital malformations, a retrospective population-based analysis showed.

Deaths among neonates were 5.5% (95% credible interval [CrI] 2.6-8.5%) higher than expected in abortion ban states, equating to about 745 excess neonatal deaths (95% CrI 367-1,139) in those states, reported Nansi Boghossian, MPH, PhD, of the University of South Carolina in Columbia, and colleagues.

While there was a 1.8% (95% CrI −0.2% to 4.3%) higher-than-expected increase in infant deaths -- or about 288 (95% CrI −25 to 658) excess deaths -- it was not statistically significant, they wrote in JAMA Network Open.

"Our findings suggest that abortion bans may have meaningful downstream effects on infant health outcomes," Boghossian told MedPage Today, adding that this study further suggests "that the link between bans and these deaths operates mainly during pregnancy and at birth, rather than through postnatal care."

The 2022 Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Supreme Court decision overturned the federal right to abortion, sparking a flurry of abortion bans. Past research has shown that birth rates and infant mortality increased in abortion ban states following Dobbs. In Texas, the largest state to ban abortion, infant and neonatal deaths rose after the early pregnancy ban was instated in 2021.

Boghossian said the team wanted to look at a longer time period after bans and include states that more recently banned abortion to get a fuller picture, so they followed neonatal deaths for about 3 years after most bans, and infant deaths for about 2 years.

Estimated rates of both neonatal (2.2%, 95% CrI −0.5% to 5.2%) and infant (0.2%, 95% CrI −1.2% to 2.0%) deaths were attenuated after Texas was excluded. When assessed by state, both Texas and Alabama had the greatest increases in neonatal mortality, they reported.

In subgroup analyses, the highest mortality increases were observed among Black infants (8.8%, 95% CrI 3.3-14.2%), they found.

"Black infants in the U.S. already die at more than twice the rate of White infants," Boghossian noted. "Abortion bans may make that gap wider."

When analyzing by timing, deaths were concentrated in the neonatal period (5.0%, 95% CrI 1.7-8.4%) and by cause of death, infant mortality due to congenital anomalies was higher than expected (6.9%, 95% CrI 1.8-12.5%).

"This distribution suggests that the primary mechanisms linking abortion bans to mortality may operate during pregnancy and at birth, rather than through postnatal care," the researchers wrote. "Neonatal deaths are more likely to reflect conditions originating in utero, including congenital anomalies, consistent with our findings of increased mortality from these causes."

Bans may "increase the continuation of pregnancies affected by severe fetal anomalies that would otherwise have been terminated," they wrote.

Catherine Coughlin, MD, MPH, of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, noted in an accompanying editorial that this study "adds to the growing body of literature supporting an association between abortion bans and higher-than-expected infant mortality."

Several of the top drivers of infant and neonatal mortality are directly impacted by abortion bans, Coughlin wrote. While some abortion ban states have exceptions to save the life of the mother, physicians have reported "ambiguity in how laws are enforced in a clinical setting, leading to confusion in how to best care for patients," she wrote.

Moreover, she argued that comprehensive reproductive healthcare is a tool to combat both neonatal and infant mortality and disparities.

For this retrospective cohort study, researchers used aggregate birth and death certificate data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), which covers all 50 states and Washington D.C.; from January 1, 2012 to December 31, 2024 there were about 53 million births.

There were 198,967 neonatal deaths through 2025 and 281,873 infant deaths through 2024. Among these deaths, 29.0% were Black infants, 21.8% were Hispanic infants, 42.1% were White infants, and 7.1% were other racial and ethnic groups.

The authors compared 16 states with abortion bans to the 34 states and D.C. that don't have bans. A statistical model estimated how many neonates and infants would have died if the ban hadn't happened, which was compared against what actually happened.

The primary outcomes were neonatal mortality, defined as death before 28 days old, and infant mortality, defined as deaths before 1 year of age, per 1,000 live births.

There were several limitations, including limited sample sizes, that the 2025 data is provisional, and that using aggregate data precluded them from examining individual pregnancies or pinning down a single mechanism. Boghossian said that future work should analyze individual-level data. Plus, COVID-related Medicaid unwinding began in 2023, which overlapped with the ban periods, and researchers assumed no interstate spillovers, though some people do travel for abortion care.

#5513. HHS: Medicaid state-directed payment savings 'primarily' stem from slowing growth

HHS: Medicaid state-directed payment savings 'primarily' stem from slowing growth" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Rural hospitals claim a relatively small portion of the state-directed payments being squeezed in coming years by 2025’s H.R. 1, with much of the legislation’s projected spending reductions the result of holding funds for those hospitals from growing beyond fiscal year 2025 levels, Department of Health and Human Services policy heads wrote in a new report.

The analysis, released Monday, paints a softer picture of the rate limits Republicans imposed on a supplemental Medicaid payment stream in last year’s broad budget reconciliation law, also referred to as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act or the Working Families Tax Cut Legislation.

Hospitals and other healthcare industry groups, as well as advocates and Democrats, have said the law’s billions in projected savings—from state-directed payment changes as well as other policy areas like Medicaid work requirements—are likely to devastate providers already operating at thin or negative margins.

Specifically, the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation (ASPE)’s analysis showed that an estimated 7.8% of Medicaid state-directed payments reached rural hospitals in FY2025, or $11.5 billion out of $148.3 billion. That rate is slightly above rural hospitals’ 7% share of total Medicaid hospital spending for that same fiscal year, as estimated by the CMS Office of the Actuary.

Scaling from that baseline in line with H.R. 1’s multi-year payment rate phasedown, with some cumulative adjustments, showed that total nominal cumulative spending on rural state-directed payments would decline by 42.9%, or $81.6 billion, from 2026 through 2035 under the bill. This rate is again slightly higher than the CMS Office of the Actuary’s 40.8% estimate for all affected hospitals, which ASPE said is the result of the higher average dollar weighted payment rates rural hospitals currently receive, “which means that rural providers have more room to reduce rates to meet the new limits of 100% to 110% of Medicare.”

The ASPE report’s bottom line, however, is that $75.2 billion of the $81.6 billion reduction rural hospitals face, or 92.1%, reflects projected increases over the FY2025 baseline of $11.5 billion. The remainder, about 7.9% of the projected change, is a reduction below FY2025’s estimated state-directed payments to rural hospitals.

HHS, in a release highlighting the report’s findings, said that the language used in government reports describing the full $81.6 billion 10-year spending reduction as “savings” misses the government’s primary goal of capping future growth.

“Counting every dollar of projected savings as a cut below existing funding gives the public the wrong picture. Most of these savings are not reductions below what the program spent in 2025,” HHS Chief Economist and Chief Regulatory Officer Casey Mulligan, who was one of the report’s coauthors, said in the release. “They reflect future spending increases that will no longer occur. Our analysis makes that distinction clear.”

H.R. 1’s multi-year scale down in state-directed payment rates is set to begin in 2028, and are expected to slash some hard-hit states’ Medicaid spending by up to a quarter of their total annual Medicaid spending, per one analysis. Hospitals have broadly criticized the policy changes while spending much of this year adjusting their operations to contend with the future limits supplemental revenue, expectations of increased uncompensated care costs and year-to-year expense pressures like wage and supply inflation.

Additionally, CMS earlier this year proposed state directed payment caps substantially more extensive than what was outlined in H.R. 1 and used as the basis for Monday’s ASPE report. That proposal would extend rate limits beyond the bill’s four outlined service areas (inpatient hospital services, outpatient hospital services, nursing facility services and qualified practitioner services at an academic medical center) to “all [state-directed payments]s for all services in all states.” Hospital groups have flatly opposed the proposal, which more than triples the 10-year estimated savings.

Lawmakers last year, when seeking votes, blunted H.R. 1's funding reductions for rural hospitals by inserting a five-year, $50 billion rural health fund into the legislation. Those funds have come with usage restrictions for states and providers, with critics also noting transparency concerns and the fund's relatively small scale compared to the bill's total projected impact on hospitals.

#5511. Is 'Looksmaxxing' to Blame for Rising Gout Among Young People?

— Dietary trend raises clinicians' concerns

Welcome to Culture Clinic, MedPage Today's collaboration with Northwell Health to offer a healthcare professional's take on the latest viral medical topics.

As more young men turn to "looksmaxxing" to try to improve their physical attractiveness through diet, exercise, and supplementation, one trend has clinicians concerned that they may be putting themselves at risk for gout.

A "carnivore diet" involves eating lots of red meat to support muscle growth, but this can also raise the risk of this painful inflammatory arthritis once thought of as the "disease of kings."

And indeed, gout is on the rise in young people. A 2025 study in PLoS One found that from 1990 to 2021, gout among young people ages 15 to 44 rose from 194.23 to 245.07 per 100,000.

While these data ended before "looksmaxxing" exploded in popularity, eating too much of foods that contain purine is a major risk factor for developing gout, said Adam Bitterman, DO, chairman of the department of orthopedic surgery at Northwell's Huntington Hospital in Huntington, New York.

Purines are compounds that naturally occur in red meats, organ and game meats, some seafood, and some alcohols. When bodies break down purines, uric acid is created as a waste product. Gout is caused by crystalline deposits of uric acid, Bitterman said.

"From a high-red meat diet, you get an increase in purines ... which can ultimately lead to the uric acid buildup, which can then become crystals in the joints," he told MedPage Today. This then leads to "the pain, swelling, inflammation, and ultimately the inflammatory arthropathy."

He noted, however, that there isn't a cut-and-dry threshold for how much purine is too much.

Gout generally starts "as red, hot, swollen big toe joints" at the metatarsophalangeal joint, Bitterman said, but it can also develop in other locations and bigger joints, like the ankle or knee. As gout progresses, it can become painful for a patient to walk or put weight on the extremity.

At these early stages, patients should come in for an evaluation, he said. If someone has early signs and symptoms of gout, and through conversations with their doctors are able to determine that their diet is the culprit, cutting back on purine-rich foods can help significantly.

Otherwise, Bitterman said treatment usually begins with anti-inflammatory medicines like colchicine, ibuprofen, or naproxen sodium. Steroids, like methylprednisolone or prednisone taper packs, are another strategy to manage gout, as is the urate-lowering medication allopurinol.

Gout can mimic an infection, Bitterman said, so sometimes advanced imaging is needed to ensure something else isn't going on. X-rays confirm that the patient doesn't have a fracture, and dual-energy CT scans and MRIs can visualize uric acid crystal deposits. Plus, health histories and physicals can confirm there are no other signs of infection in the bloodstream.

Over time, if uric acid builds up in the joints and isn't excreted properly, "you can have a breakdown of the bones of those joints" and "the cartilage can get worn down," Bitterman said.

"If the buildup of crystals becomes so severe, it can lead to a 'toothpaste' accumulation inside the joint that needs to be drained and or washed out," he added.

For that, a surgeon makes a few holes in the skin overlying the joint and through either arthroscopic or a more open approach evacuates the crystals. After recovering from surgery, patients have "significant improvement" but still need maintenance to prevent uric acid from building up again.

"If gout got to a critical level where a surgery is involved, then you know you've essentially failed the maintenance protocol, and so you have to revisit that with your rheumatologist or your primary care doctor," Bitterman said.

As a surgeon, Bitterman said he most commonly sees gout in his male patients between the ages of 55 and 70. But in general, the two groups most at risk for gout are those who have increased uric acid buildup in their blood from intake -- like lots of purine-containing foods -- and those whose kidneys struggle to get rid of uric acid.

Some young men have leveraged social media to share their experiences with gout and remind their peers that even young people can develop gout -- and urge them to take precautions to lower their risk.

#5508. AI deals shrink to as little as 30 days as the data layer sets the pace

Artificial intelligence has turned data infrastructure from a back-office purchase into the bottleneck that decides how fast GPUs pay off. As hyperscalers, neoclouds and enterprises race to expand their data layers, the way that infrastructure gets bought is changing just as fast.

The storage industry’s longtime performance specialist sees that shift as its opening. DataDirect Networks Inc. built its reputation on scale and speed, and those traits now carry more weight in AI infrastructure, according to Kevin Delane (pictured), president and chief revenue officer of DDN.

“When you look at the data layer, performance in the data layer drives value. So yes, it has to be simple, it has to be reliable. Those are table stakes, but performance drives business value,” Delane said.

Delane spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI infrastructure sales cycles have grown more complex and faster, DDN’s tighter ecosystem work with partners such as Nvidia Corp. and Super Micro Computer Inc., and the company’s hiring for a direct, results-driven culture. (* Disclosure below.)

The way companies buy AI infrastructure has changed along with the technology. Deals at neocloud providers no longer go to a single enterprise buyer. They now involve the off-taker renting the capacity, the cloud operator and the integration software layer, Delane explained. Timelines have shrunk just as sharply, from six months to a year for a traditional enterprise sale to as little as 30 days.

“The sales cycle is more complex for sure. The speed is insane,” Delane said. “Sometimes these things are 30 days and you have to be ready to turn things around and really work with your customers and partners quickly.”

DDN is answering with tighter ecosystem work. Its decade-long partnership with Nvidia anchors the strategy, and joint offerings with Super Micro, such as the Enterprise AI HyperPOD, aim to replace a data center buildout with a ready-to-run AI stack. At SC26, DDN also introduced software-defined EXAScaler deployment to give enterprise AI customers more choice of hardware.

“It takes the complexity out of it, allows an enterprise to set up an AI pod within 3 hours,” Delane said.

The performance case holds up in the public cloud too. On Google LLC’s Google Cloud, customers using DDN’s Managed Lustre service saw 70% better training performance and a 40% gain in overall GPU efficiency, Delane noted.

DDN is growing threefold this year while adding only a few salespeople, leaning its hiring toward technical and implementation staff who can get customers up and running faster. Delane looks for grit and a fit with a direct, results-driven culture.

“If people can fit that culture, want to come in, want to grow this company to multiple billions, we have a place for them,” Delane said.

Isabella is a chronic disease reporter writing about how the Trump administration is tackling the nation’s health epidemic — or not. You can reach her on Signal at isabellacueto.03.

WASHINGTON —The MAHA Institute, a nonprofit “think tank” launched to support Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s health agenda, burned over $1 million in 2025, leaving it with little cash on hand to continue operating, tax documents obtained by STAT show.

The group started 2025 with nearly $1.3 million in its coffers, but ended the year with just $171,000, per its latest IRS return, filed this week. That 86% drop was hardly offset by the group’s revenue, which was just shy of $67,000 for the year.

“To have lost over $1 million is pretty notable to me,” said Brian Mittendorf, a professor at Ohio State University who specializes in nonprofit accounting.

#5506. Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer

Women with higher blood levels of two common "forever chemicals" may face an increased risk of developing a particularly aggressive form of breast cancer, according to new research from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).

The study identified a connection between estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer and two widely encountered chemicals: perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS). Women with greater concentrations of these substances in their blood were more likely to develop this type of cancer. However, researchers found no clear link between either chemical and breast cancer risk overall.

Both substances belong to a large family of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly called PFAS. These chemicals have been used in numerous everyday consumer products and are often described as "forever chemicals" because they resist breaking down in the environment. They can also accumulate in the human body and remain there for years.

"Women deserve clear answers about how chemicals in their environment may affect their health," said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. "This NIH study links two forever chemicals to a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer and demands further investigation. Under President Trump's leadership, we will pursue the evidence, confront environmental health risks, and give women the information they need to protect their health."

Why This Aggressive Breast Cancer Is Concerning

ER-negative breast cancer differs from more common forms of the disease because its tumor cells lack the receptors that allow estrogen to stimulate cancer growth. These cancers are often more aggressive and generally have poorer outcomes than tumors that respond to estrogen.

Despite their severity, researchers still have relatively little information about what makes someone more likely to develop ER-negative breast cancer. The new findings suggest that exposure to certain persistent environmental chemicals could be one contributing factor.

"Our findings, which we confirmed using a meta-analysis of prior research, indicate that certain legacy PFAS, including PFOA and PFOS, are associated with a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer, a more aggressive tumor type with few known risk factors," explained NIH Stadtman Investigator Alexandra White, Ph.D., who led the study.

The findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

Higher Forever Chemical Levels Linked to Greater Cancer Risk

To investigate the possible connection, NIH scientists and their collaborators examined blood samples that had been collected years before participants received a cancer diagnosis. The researchers measured concentrations of 17 different PFAS chemicals, allowing them to compare earlier exposure levels with subsequent breast cancer outcomes.

The results revealed substantial differences for two chemicals. Women in the highest PFOA exposure group had a 67% higher rate of ER-negative breast cancer than women in the lowest group. The association was even stronger for PFOS, with the highest exposure group showing a 93% higher rate, nearly twice that of the lowest group.

These percentages represent relative differences between groups rather than the absolute probability that an individual woman will develop breast cancer. The findings also establish an association, not proof that the chemicals directly cause the disease.

The analysis used data from the Sister Study, a major research project conducted by NIH's National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS). Between 2003 and 2009, the study enrolled 50,884 women ages 35-74 from across the United States and Puerto Rico.

All participants were free of breast cancer when they enrolled, although each had a full or half-sister who had already been diagnosed with the disease. For the PFAS investigation, researchers analyzed information from 1,609 women who subsequently developed breast cancer and a comparison group of 2,269 women.

Could Reducing PFAS Exposure Lower Cancer Risk?

Although PFAS can remain in the environment and the body for long periods, researchers emphasize that exposure is not necessarily unavoidable. The findings could eventually help identify new ways to reduce the risk of aggressive breast cancer.

"These findings matter for women's health broadly," said first author, Che-Jung Chang, Ph.D., who previously worked as an NIH research fellow and is now a researcher at DLH, a scientific research organization. "Although PFAS are persistent in the environment and in our bodies, exposure to them is still potentially modifiable, meaning people can take steps to reduce their exposure, and these findings could open new avenues for prevention."

The researchers are also interested in understanding how these chemicals might influence cancer development. Because the strongest associations appeared in tumors that lack estrogen receptors, the findings suggest that PFAS could act through biological processes unrelated to hormonal signaling.

Potential explanations include changes in gene activity or alterations in the immune system. However, the study did not directly investigate these mechanisms, so their involvement remains uncertain.

Newer Forever Chemicals Raise Unanswered Questions

Although PFOA and PFOS have largely been phased out and replaced with other PFAS compounds, measurable amounts of both substances are still present in most people's bodies. Their persistence means that exposure to these older chemicals remains a potential public health concern.

The researchers say additional investigations should focus on populations with greater PFAS exposure, as well as groups that experience higher rates of ER-negative breast cancer. Such research could help clarify the strength of the observed associations and identify whether certain populations face greater risks.

Scientists also need to determine whether the newer chemicals introduced as replacements for PFOA and PFOS carry similar health concerns.

"More research is needed, particularly evaluating the risk of breast cancer associated with newer replacement PFAS chemicals," White said.

The findings add to growing questions about the long-term health effects of forever chemicals and highlight the importance of understanding how environmental exposures may contribute to aggressive forms of breast cancer.

The research received support from NIEHS grants Z01ES044005; Z1AES103332; and R01ES032831.

#5505. ICE detention of Princeton scientist rattles academia

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Anil Oza is a general assignment reporter at STAT focused on the NIH and health equity. You can reach him on Signal at aniloza.16.

A graduate student who is a scientific researcher at Princeton University was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement earlier this week while traveling home after presenting research at the annual Society for Neuroscience conference in Washington, D.C.

The researcher, Eva Yi Xie, was detained Thursday. Although she has lived in the U.S. since 2016 after moving to the country from China, her visa had expired, according to The New York Times. Her lawyers told a reporter Xie had a pending asylum application and was thus allowed to remain in the country legally.

The news, first posted by a mentor of Xie’s on X, ricocheted across academic circles on Friday, in part because it seemed to crystalize pervasive fears of non-U.S. academics and international students that traveling to conferences to present new research and network with colleagues may be too risky during a second Trump administration that has cracked down on immigration.

“There’s, I think, an open question about whether or not it’s safe for people who are international students on visas to travel, because there have been these detentions, and that’s a very scary prospect,” said Caitlin Rivers, a John Hopkins academic who said a staff member of hers was detained by ICE earlier this year. A number of U.S. conferences have reported smaller attendance over the past two years, and some have considered hosting in other countries.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment as to why Xie was detained. But the administration has been vocal in its desire to reduce the number of foreign-born graduate students in the U.S. In its science blueprint released earlier this year, the White House wrote “America’s over-reliance on foreign students also creates a security challenge.”

Xie is not the first graduate student to be detained. In one notable instance, Tufts researcher Rumeysa Ozturk was detained by ICE last year in Cambridge, Mass., and later decided to leave the country. A report released earlier this week found that international graduate student enrollment is down by a third at academic medical centers.

“News of Eva’s detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” Rodney D. Priestley, the dean of Princeton University’s graduate school, wrote in a statement, adding the university has provided Xie with legal representation. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”

Xie’s work lies at the intersection of neuroscience and artificial intelligence; she uses a combination of experiments on mice and large datasets of neural recordings to understand how different portions of the brain work together to make decisions. A third-year PhD student, she is viewed as a rising star by some of her colleagues.

“I think it speaks to how exceptional of a researcher Eva is that she can work on projects that really span multiple disciplines, that require that she go and learn the foundations, not just of AI and machine learning, and not just computational models of the brain, but also understanding how do you run the experiment on the mice. She’s in the lab actually doing the surgery on the mice, gathering the data from the mice, analyzing those data, and running the AI experiments,” said Benjamin Eysenbach, a computer scientist at Princeton and one of Xie’s advisers.

As an example of the respect she commands among peers, Eysenbach cited a workshop she convened at last year’s NeurIPS conference, one of the premiere machine learning conferences. Xie presented research of her own, and also brought together leaders in AI and in neuroscience to see how they could collaborate.

It was an opportunity both to “introduce these important questions about the brain to folks in AI that might be equipped with new methods, and to help folks working on neuroscience questions define what are the right AI tools,” Eysenbach said.

Krithik Ramesh, a fellow researcher, is among those who has benefitted from her guidance. The two had overlapped at science fair competitions throughout high school, and when Ramesh was considering transferring to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where Xie had completed her undergraduate degree, he turned to her for counsel. He learned about Xie’s detention after a friend saw a post on social media. His immediate reaction was disbelief, followed by a sense of unmooring as a fellow researcher.

“We academics exist for the benefit of the public,” he said. “We are very privileged as a country to have people like Eva continue to pursue academia at the highest level, and to share that with other people. That’s literally the nature and reason why we go to conferences to present stuff. It is appalling to me that she cannot do that with reasonable certainty that she can’t be detained.”

Anil Oza is a general assignment reporter at STAT focused on the NIH and health equity. You can reach him on Signal at aniloza.16.

#5503. WTW: Global health insurance costs set to rise 10.2% next year

WTW: Global health insurance costs set to rise 10.2% next year" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Global health insurance costs are set to rise by double digits in 2027 for the second straight year, according to a new survey.

WTW released its latest Global Medical Trends Survey, which estimates that the average gross cost for medical benefits will increase by 10.2% in 2027. This follows a 10.1% increase in 2026 and a 9.8% increase in 2025, according to the report.

In the United States, the cost for medical benefits is expected to rise by 10.3% on average, on par with 2026 and up from a 9.4% increase in 2025. Across regions, the highest increases are expected in the Asia-Pacific, averaging 12.6% in 2027.

The next-highest region was North America, with a projected 10.5% average increase.

The survey was conducted in June and August 2026 and includes responses from 393 insurers offering coverage across 92 countries. Just under half (49%) of those surveyed said they anticipate elevated medical and pharmacy costs to impact them over the next three years, and likely persist beyond that window.

The WTW analysts said this likely means that insurers will remain focused on cost containment and sharing measures in the near future.

"In the US, healthcare costs remain under sustained pressure from new medical technologies, specialty pharmaceuticals, and the rising use of GLP-1 therapies, alongside higher provider costs and the ongoing demands of chronic and complex conditions," said Courtney Stubblefield, strategy and specialty leader in Health & Benefits at WTW in an announcement.

More than three quarters (76%) of the surveyed insurers named new medical technologies as the leading cost drive for both medical and pharmaceutical costs. Sixty-five percent cited provider fee increases, and 45% named pharmaceutical advancements.

Cancer was the leading condition driving costs, the survey found, with 62% naming it as the top cost condition. Sixty-one percent of those surveyed said they have seen an increase in cancer diagnoses among individuals under age 40 when compared to the past two years.

However, when looking at the conditions where costs are growing the most quickly, cardiovascular disease rises to No. 1, cited by 54% of the surveyed insurers. Cancer was second on this ranking, and named by 51%, while diabetes was third at 28%.

"To manage this, employers need a multiyear, multifaceted strategy that addresses pharmacy spending and high-cost conditions—such as cancer, cardiovascular disease and diabetes—while keeping care affordable and accessible for employees," Stubblefield said.

The Food and Drug Administration said Friday that it had rejected a cell therapy intended for patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy developed by Capricor Therapeutics.

The decision to block the treatment, called deramiocel, from reaching the market should have been an easy one for regulators to make. The targeted patient population — teenagers and young men with Duchenne who had already lost the ability to walk — have few treatment options today. Deramiocel didn’t help them either. Capricor conducted two randomized clinical trials. Both failed to show deramiocel could stave off heart failure or preserve muscle function in their arms.

But nothing is straightforward when it comes to regulating drugs for Duchenne, a progressive, muscle-wasting disease.

#5501. Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent

Vaccines may do more than protect people from the immediate effects of a viral infection. New research suggests they could also help prevent lasting damage to the immune system that remains even after the virus has disappeared.

Scientists at Pompeu Fabra University discovered that mice recovering from an acute viral infection experienced prolonged problems with their immune defenses. Although the animals had successfully fought off the virus, their immune systems remained impaired, making it harder to respond to new threats. Remarkably, mice vaccinated before infection did not develop these problems, suggesting that vaccination may provide an additional layer of protection beyond preventing illness.

Most people think of common viral infections, such as colds or stomach viruses, as temporary illnesses. A virus enters the body, multiplies, causes symptoms, and is eventually brought under control by the immune system. Once symptoms disappear, recovery is generally considered complete. The immune response also creates protection against future encounters with the same virus.

But what if the immune system continues to experience harmful effects long after the infection appears to be over?

Viral Infections Can Leave Lasting Immune Damage

Researchers from Pompeu Fabra University's Infection Biology Laboratory investigated this possibility in a study published in Cell Death & Disease.

Using mice with acute viral infections, the team examined what happened to their immune systems after the animals had recovered. They found that eliminating the virus did not necessarily restore normal immune function. Instead, the infection left behind changes that persisted well beyond the initial illness.

According to Andreas Meyerhans, an ICREA research professor at UPF, who led the research, "there is a general perception that an acute viral infection is a relatively minor and transient event: once the virus is controlled and the symptoms have resolved, the body has fully recovered and is back to normal. But this view may underestimate consequences that are not immediately visible and can persist long after the infection itself has resolved."

The researchers traced these lingering effects to significant changes in the spleen, an organ that plays an important role in coordinating immune defenses. As the immune system fought to eliminate the virus, the spleen developed fibrosis, a condition involving the buildup of scar-like tissue. The arrangement and positioning of immune cells within the organ also became disrupted.

These structural changes interfered with the interactions between immune cells that are necessary to activate T cells. These specialized cells are essential to adaptive immunity because they help recognize and destroy infected cells.

As a result, the mice remained less capable of launching effective immune responses when exposed to new challenges. Even though the original infection had been brought under control, their immune defenses continued to function poorly.

"The infection can be controlled, but that does not necessarily mean that the host has fully recovered," says Dr. Paula Cebollada Rica, first author of the study. "Our findings show that the immune-related consequences of an acute viral infection can persist beyond the period in which the virus is detectable, leaving the animals in an immunocompromised state."

Vaccination Prevented Lasting Immune System Damage

After identifying these long-term effects, the scientists investigated whether they could be avoided. They focused on vaccination, which prepares the immune system to recognize and fight a pathogen before an infection occurs.

The results revealed a striking difference between vaccinated and unvaccinated animals. Mice that received vaccination before infection did not develop the spleen damage or immune dysfunction seen in the other group.

Their spleens maintained their normal structure, and their T cells continued to function at levels comparable to those of mice that had never been infected.

This finding suggests that vaccination can protect the immune system itself from some of the harmful consequences of fighting a viral infection. In the mouse model, vaccination not only protected against the disease caused by the virus but also preserved the animals' ability to respond to future immune challenges.

"Vaccinated animals did not experience T-cell dysfunction or splenic alterations after recovering from an acute viral infection. This means that vaccination not only prevented the disease resulting from the acute infection but also preserved the immune system's ability to cope with new challenges," Cebollada Rica explains.

A Hidden Benefit of Vaccines With Public Health Implications

The findings broaden the potential benefits of vaccination by highlighting a form of protection that may not be immediately apparent. Beyond reducing the immediate effects of an infection, vaccines may also help prevent persistent changes that weaken immune defenses.

Although these results were obtained in mice and do not establish that the same effects occur in humans, they raise important questions about how viral infections influence long-term immune health and how vaccination might help protect it.

The research also comes at a time when vaccination policies and infectious disease prevention efforts are increasingly influenced by political decisions. The researchers emphasize the importance of scientific evidence in understanding the full consequences of infections, particularly when policy choices can undermine coordinated efforts to prevent infectious diseases.

Understanding the broader benefits of vaccination could therefore influence not only medical care but also how public health officials explain the value of vaccines to the public.

"The benefits of vaccination highlighted by this research are important not only for healthcare, but also for how we communicate the value of vaccination to the population at large," Meyerhans states. "It is important that people are aware of the broader protection that vaccination can provide and continue to trust in vaccines as one of the most effective tools to prevent diseases. Put simply, vaccines provide strong health benefits at a relatively low cost to society."

#5500. Opinion: How Kennedy and MAHA could help stop measles

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Adhikari is a journalist and co-host of the “Why Should I Trust You?” podcast.

A version of this article first appeared on the Substack of “Why Should I Trust You?”

On Tuesday, after the United States lost its measles elimination status, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. posted on X that he wanted to stop measles from spreading in America. “We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend [measles, mumps, and rubella] vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”

Well, Secretary Kennedy, do I have an idea for you …

It involves mobilizing a movement you helped build, a movement that has successfully organized millions of Americans around issues related to their health. I’m talking about MAHA.

Right now, the discourse is playing out like this: Medical societies are expressing alarm over the loss of measles elimination status, while many politicians blame Kennedy and the Trump administration for failing to adequately respond.

Kennedy’s defenders clap back by reminding us that other countries have lost elimination status in recent years, too, that these are all efforts to undermine Kennedy and that his administration is doing what it can.

I understand on some level that, as a society, we need to litigate what went wrong. But candidly, I’m much more interested in something else: Who might be best positioned to reach the Americans that public health officials are struggling to persuade to get the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine?

I’ll start by saying that I believe in the measles vaccine. I was vaccinated as a child. I’ve vaccinated my two kids. I don’t identify as particularly vaccine skeptical. I’ve sometimes wondered why we have so many vaccine recommendations in this country compared with others, but I generally trust my doctors and haven’t (yet) experienced any major adverse reactions that might have led me to question that trust.

Over the last two years of making the podcast “Why Should I Trust You?,” my co-hosts and I have had the privilege of speaking with many people who feel quite differently than I do about vaccines, public health, and the medical system, and what they see as blind faith in expertise.

I’ve learned a tremendous amount. These conversations have made me question my own assumptions and better understand why I trust institutions, while sometimes realizing that I, too, harbor mistrust. While some of these conversations have been with people who are unwaveringly anti-vaccine, most have been with people who have taken some vaccines and harbor doubts about others.

They’ve also given me a front-row seat to something else: the MAHA grassroots movement’s astonishing ability to organize.

I’ve watched as MAHA supporters rally around pesticides, toxic pollutants in our air and water, microplastics, and PFAS (aka “forever”) chemicals. I’ve been to conferences and meetings, and been included in many group chats and Zoom meetings, where you can practically feel the energy around you: people exchanging ideas, meeting with lawmakers to draft legislation, and mobilizing others to organize local action. I constantly hear two questions: “What do you need? How can I help?”

That energy doesn’t seem to have disappeared after the midterms. But it’s definitely looking for places to go.

MAHA is politically weak right now. Candidates backed by the movement suffered significant electoral defeats, and there’s anger at the Trump administration over what seem like broken promises on pesticides, corporate influence, and environmental health. Yet the grassroots supporters haven’t given up. They’ve already been regrouping around issues like data centers and their effects on communities, while continuing to fight toxic pollutants and corporate influence. They don’t want to wait for the government or medical establishment to fix problems for them.

Measles presents a different kind of challenge. Public health officials need to reach parents who hesitate before vaccinating their children, including families in communities that view government institutions with suspicion.

I’ve heard from public health officials that many local health departments are so underfunded, they struggle to reach these families — and even when they have the resources, they may lack the cultural fluency or trusted relationships to connect with them.

But what if some of the people who could help actually share those families’ skepticism about pharmaceutical companies, admire Kennedy, or prefer alternative medicine — yet believe the MMR vaccine is worth getting?

MAHA is not a fringe movement. According to KFF’s analysis of the 2026 midterm election, roughly 3 in 10 voters said they support MAHA, including 21% who strongly support it.

And, perhaps surprisingly, most MAHA-supporting parents vaccinate their kids. A separate KFF/Washington Post survey found that 86% of MAHA-supporting parents believe it’s important for children in their communities to be vaccinated against measles. Nearly 8 in 10 expressed confidence in the safety of the MMR vaccine. And about 75% reported that their children were up to date on routine childhood vaccinations, excluding Covid and flu.

Truthfully, very few MAHA supporters I’ve met haven’t taken MMR or vaccinated their children against polio, even if on a delayed schedule. I’ve met plenty who feel differently about Covid, flu, or the hep B birth dose, and certainly there are those who reject MMR. But among rank-and-file supporters, I’ve encountered far fewer MMR skeptics than you might expect from listening to some of the movement’s most prominent influencers. Which is important for the challenge at hand: You can believe deeply in MAHA’s core concerns about food, pesticides, water, chronic disease, and even have mistrust in flu and Covid shots — but still have confidence in the value of the measles vaccine.

We don’t acknowledge this enough. Some of MAHA’s most prominent vaccine skeptics may not speak for the broader movement when it comes to MMR.

The science on MMR is clear: Two doses are approximately 97% effective at preventing measles. But knowing the facts and trusting the person delivering them are two very different things. A fact like that can land differently when it comes from someone who has wrestled with the same doubts you have.

I think about Roberta Devers, a mother and midwife practicing in Lancaster County, Pa., whom my colleagues and I met working on an episode about the measles outbreak there.

Roberta was vaccine skeptical, a Kennedy supporter, and chose not to vaccinate her son when he was a baby. But after seeing what measles was doing to people in Lancaster County, she changed her mind. She believes MMR is effective against measles and encourages Amish families in outbreak areas to get vaccinated, too. She tells me she now gets one or two calls a week from families who want to get vaccinated.

What’s particularly interesting to me, though, is what hasn’t changed.

Roberta still admires Kennedy. She hasn’t suddenly decided the medical establishment deserves her trust. If anything, she tells me the measles outbreaks are a reflection of a lack of trust communities continue to have for health systems. One of her ongoing campaigns is to fight for home-birth midwives to receive the same recognition as those working in hospitals. She talks about holistic living, alternative medicine, eating whole foods, even using brown paper toilet paper because she believes in living close to the earth. She hasn’t changed her values or worldview. She’s simply reconsidered what she believes about measles vaccination.

Imagine a vaccine-hesitant parent hearing from someone like Roberta, who shares many of their concerns but has seen measles up close and reached a different conclusion. Roberta doesn’t need to defend pharmaceutical companies or persuade anyone that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is always right. Just telling her story could lead to a conversation that perhaps a public health official would have a harder time brokering.

I’m not suggesting this movement will suddenly lead the charge on getting Americans vaccinated for measles. Some of MAHA’s most influential voices have spent years not just questioning, but actively sowing distrust in vaccines, including MMR, using claims not rooted in scientific fact. And I expect for many, encouraging vaccination, even during an outbreak, would be a bridge too far for them, a betrayal of their principles.

And organizing a rally isn’t the same as running a public health response.

But shouldn’t we at least try to make an active effort to reach MAHA supporters who believe in MMR? Because the polling shows it looks like there are a lot of them.

In his statement, Kennedy said his department is working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. He also promised to collaborate with trusted health care providers and community leaders.

He could start by elevating voices who support MMR. People like Devers, who can speak to vaccine-hesitant families with credibility and trust that public health institutions often lack. Find more people like her.

Then encourage those MAHA supporters who trust the measles vaccine to organize conversations about measles prevention. Bring in trusted physicians or other clinicians to answer questions. But also listen to families’ fears and doubts — because chances are, many MAHA supporters have wrestled with those same questions themselves. Help families find vaccines. Connect them with parents who share their values but have decided to vaccinate their children.

Would everyone in MAHA welcome that effort? Almost certainly not. Would Kennedy face backlash from the anti-vaccine wing of his movement? Very likely.

But for the past two years, MAHA supporters have pushed back against being characterized as anti-vaccine. Instead, they say, they are concerned about mandates, informed consent, conflicts of interest, and what they see as an unwillingness to acknowledge questions about safety.

Well, guys, here’s an opportunity to demonstrate what that distinction means in practice.

If you’re not anti-vaccine, helping people make informed decisions about a vaccine that the overwhelming majority of your own supporters trust shouldn’t betray your principles. It should express them.

The public health establishment has a responsibility here, too. If people within MAHA are willing to help, officials should work with them. That doesn’t mean overlooking misinformation or compromising on evidence. But it does mean recognizing common ground.

I know some readers will think I’m naive. Doesn’t she get that parts of MAHA have contributed to the distrust that makes measles prevention so difficult? I do. But even if parts of MAHA contributed to the problem, isn’t it worth asking whether some of its supporters might be particularly well positioned to contribute to the solution?

At a moment when MAHA is regrouping after an election rout, the movement now has an opportunity to demonstrate that it truly offers a big tent. Not by abandoning its core priorities, but by directing some of its powerful grassroots energy toward a disease affecting American children and their parents — the very people MAHA claims to put at the center of its mission.

Brinda Adhikari is a journalist and co-host of the “Why Should I Trust You?” podcast.
