#5499. Inference pushes AI to smaller sites, making the data layer the deciding factor

Inference is moving to the center of enterprise AI spending, and the AI data layer is emerging as the piece that decides whether those investments pay off. As GPU costs climb and component shortages persist, the architecture behind AI is shifting from a handful of massive facilities toward a distributed web of smaller sites.

That shift is putting storage companies with roots in high-performance computing at the center of the AI conversation. Turning data into insight at an acceptable cost now depends on a resilient, secure data engine built for GPU efficiency, according to Alex Bouzari (pictured), co-founder and chief executive officer of DataDirect Networks Inc.

“As inference is off the charts in terms of utilization, the data layer is what makes a difference,” Bouzari said. “Costs are skyrocketing. GPUs are becoming more and more powerful, but also more and more expensive.”

Bouzari spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how inference, cost pressure and shortages are reshaping AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.)

The first wave of AI buildouts concentrated GPUs in large, power-hungry facilities. Inference changes that math because it needs to run close to users and their data, Bouzari explained. Communities are also pushing back on giant monolithic data centers, he added.

“Now, what is happening with inference, you need to supplement that with smaller footprints. Let’s call them data centers, 1 megawatt, 2 megawatt, 5 megawatts. And those need to reside where the action is taking place, where the autonomous driving is happening, where physical AI is happening, where the sensor data is,” Bouzari said.

Connecting small pods back to large AI factories requires a different approach to data. DDN is building a software layer that spans many types of hardware, a direction reflected in its recent move to free its EXAScaler file system from DDN’s own hardware. The goal is to squeeze more use out of very expensive gear, according to Bouzari.

“It is a software layer that needs to accommodate the different types of hardware because, look, the costs being so high, people want to be able to maximize the utilization over an extended period of time, just like it was in high-performance computing,” Bouzari said.

The scale of spending has changed dramatically. A couple hundred million dollars once funded the world’s fastest supercomputer but now buys 15 to 20 racks of equipment, Bouzari noted. Shortages of GPUs, memory and solid-state drives are colliding with tighter budget scrutiny.

“On the one hand, you have budgetary constraints and the need to extract as much value as you can from your investment,” Bouzari said. “On the other hand, you have the shortages. And so a data layer that can do a lot more with a lot less infrastructure, the smaller footprint is extremely valuable.”

That thinking extends into the enterprise. DDN’s Enterprise AI HyperPOD packages CPUs, GPUs, networking and storage into a rack that can drop into existing corporate sites with available power. Keeping the pod on-premises also gives companies tighter control over their data, Bouzari explained.

“I think we’re entering an era where we will see a blossoming of smaller footprint pods being deployed in enterprises globally,” Bouzari said.

Bouzari framed the AI data layer as the counterpart to accelerated compute, with Nvidia Corp. supplying the processing and DDN supplying the data. As inference and agents take over, the data side carries more weight, he said: “You need both to make it successful. But the data engine, I think, is becoming increasingly important as inference and agentic is really becoming the predominant way to utilize AI and get value out of it.”

#5498. Opinion: When should medical school start?

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Torie Bosch is the First Opinion editor at STAT.

First Opinion is STAT’s platform for interesting, illuminating, and provocative articles about the life sciences writ large, written by biotech insiders, health care workers, researchers, and others.

To encourage robust, good-faith discussion about issues raised in First Opinion essays, STAT publishes selected Letters to the Editor received in response to them. You can submit a Letter to the Editor here, or find the submission form at the end of any First Opinion essay.

The authors’ proposal hinges on the premise that learning the foundational sciences and learning to become a physician can be separated without compromising either. My first year of medical school was peppered with clinical exposure and taught me otherwise. I floundered with a blood pressure cuff during a wellness visit, fumbled for words as I interviewed a man waiting for a heart transplant, and listened to a patient recount her immense sorrow after multiple miscarriages. These encounters remain among my most formative.

I agree with the authors that students are often preoccupied with medical licensure exams, and that early clinical exposure might not cure this. In my experience, however, it is the strongest counterweight. After meeting those patients, I was learning for more than an exam. The proposed model would abandon that counterweight. Students would still encounter patients eventually, but we would have forfeited valuable time. Becoming a compassionate, humanistic physician is slow work, and it deserves all the time we can offer. A flashcard can teach a student what causes a miscarriage. It takes a patient to teach what it means to grieve one. And that lesson should not wait until after Step 1.

— Surya Pulukuri, Harvard Medical School student

Markovich is correct: The U.S. health care “non-system” is broken. There are many culprits, including hospitals, whose prices are set more by market dominance than by quality. He should also look at the administrative complexity driven largely by our myriad of private insurance companies. Some 25% of U.S. “health care” spending goes to administrative costs. The insurers need to agree on a single set of billing codes and procedures to cut doctors’ and hospitals’ cost of billing. They need to sit down with doctors and come up with a uniform set of procedures needing pre-authorization and a single set of criteria. They need to agree on a small number of policy options that are understandable to the public. Finger-pointing is easy, but should start at home.

— Edward Hoffer, M.D., Harvard Medical School

A chatbot can handle every conversation responsibly and still, over time, take the place of someone a person used to confide in. In their First Opinion essay, Qian Yang, Ned Cooper, and Ibrahim Emara show how easily a gradual loss of human connection can escape safeguards designed for individual conversations. They make a persuasive case for giving independent researchers access to platform data and developing tools to distinguish the effects of chatbot use from other causes of isolation. Those tools should ask whether people could reach someone they trusted when they needed help.

That question is especially worth asking adolescents, who may have fewer ways to seek help privately. Imagine two teenagers who each spend an hour every night talking to a chatbot. One used to call a friend during difficult times, but he called less often as talking to the chatbot became a habit. The other still talks to friends every day. When she wanted to discuss something she feared would get back to her parents, she asked to see a school counselor. While she waited for an appointment, she took the problem to a chatbot. Their chat logs might look very similar. The authors suggest measuring school counselor time as one way to estimate what isolation costs schools. That measure captures time counselors spend helping students. Hours, days, or weeks spent waiting leave no trace.

Researchers could ask teens to think about the last time something was troubling them. Did they talk to someone about it, try to reach someone, or decide against reaching out? If they tried, did they get to talk to someone? Did they talk to a chatbot about it?

Asking these questions regularly could help researchers distinguish a teen who reached out to people less often as their chatbot usage grew from one who turned to a chatbot only after trying to get help. The distinction matters for policymaking. When chatbot use displaces human contact, usage limits may help. When it fills a gap in support, the priority should be making help easier to reach. A usage limit might prompt one teenager to call a friend. Another may still be waiting for someone to call back.

— Brian J. Carter, J.D., Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

In her essay “How bad is healthy supposed to feel?” Kirsten Balin properly notes that medicine has a regrettable history of dismissing symptoms, particularly in women. However, she also says that health professionals tend to give an illness label to the aches, pains, and anxieties of everyday living when the symptoms have no underlying biological explanation. As examples, she lists chronic fatigue syndrome and autonomic dysfunction. In fact, there are tens of thousands of peer-reviewed publications in top scientific journals that document the biological abnormalities in these two illnesses. The same is true with several other similar illnesses such as fibromyalgia and long Covid. It now is clear that they all are “real” illnesses.

— Anthony L. Komaroff, M.D., Harvard Medical School

The authors of the First Opinion commentary on pediatric emergencies from Oct. 27 identify a growing but hidden problem: stark gaps in delivery of pediatric emergency care across the U.S. The solutions they propose — payment reform, expanding regional care coordination hubs, and incentivizing large pediatric medical centers to support smaller hospitals — all merit serious consideration.

However, such approaches risk overlooking existing strengths that we can build upon now to support emergency departments and prehospital agencies aiming to develop their own internal capacity. Pediatric readiness refers to the infrastructure and resources EDs and prehospital agencies need to provide high-quality care for children. In our roles as researchers and physicians, we collaborate in community-engaged research to identify strategies to support EDs and EMS agencies in their readiness.

This is vital: EDs with high pediatric readiness have up to 76% lower mortality for critically ill children. It would cost approximately $200 million to make all EDs nationwide pediatric ready, a tiny fraction of annual U.S. health care expenditures. Many EDs lack designated pediatric champions, knowns as pediatric emergency care coordinators (PECCs), whose presence has been shown to be closely associated with readiness. As the authors rightly point out, larger pediatric medical centers can support smaller hospitals and PECCs.

That’s why we collaborate with local, national, and international partners in readiness improvement strategies such as telehealth support to smaller hospitals, simulation-based systems-testing and medical education, developing PECC networking and mentorship models, and more. This research stems from our experiences in rural, indigenous, and urban hospital systems. This has helped us understand the importance of foregrounding community members’ concerns and supporting their local expertise and leadership in our research efforts.

The authors grounded their commentary in two stories of what pediatricians are seeing nationwide. We agree that stories from families and local providers should drive our research. For us, that means collecting stories about what pediatric emergency readiness should look like, collaborating with community hospitals and families to identify research questions and select appropriate methodologies, and finding sustainable dissemination and implementation strategies.

EDs can start their own readiness journey by participating in the National Pediatric Readiness Project’s national assessment to identify current strengths and opportunities for improvement. As we work toward a future where any child can receive high-quality emergency care when and where they need it, we recommend starting by identifying and building upon strengths already in place.

— Elizabeth Sanseau, M.D., Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) PolicyLab, CHOP Indigenous Health Unit, and the University of Pennsylvania’s Perelman School of Medicine; and Jeremy Jones, M.D., CHOP PolicyLab

As a pediatric emergency physician and clinical ethicist, I have experienced and witnessed aggression at work many times. The authors’ concern comes from a good place, but it misses the realities of the clinical setting. They write that ineffective signs would be “pointless, but not harmful.” I disagree, for three reasons.

First, the essay overstates the evidence against signage. Its claim rests on two sources: a 2006 survey of Australian nurses and a 2008 commentary on the U.K.’s zero tolerance campaign. Neither evaluates whether signs change behavior. Nor has anyone tested the claim that signs erode patient trust. Research on violence prevention is methodologically weak, though multicomponent programs show mixed but encouraging results.

Second, deterrence is not the only purpose of a sign. Even if the signs prevented nothing, they would matter. The authors acknowledge that violence against health care workers has risen. In emergency departments specifically, it has introduced a mental and physical burden that fundamentally changes what it means to do this work. Signage stating an obvious standard of behavior may seem trivial, but it can have meaning as a piece of a broader institutional commitment to health care worker well-being. It tells staff that their hospital understands the realities of their work and supports them.

Third, signs remind clinicians where their obligations end. Many clinicians, especially trainees, are unsure what they owe a patient or family who is abusing them. A hospital must screen and stabilize anyone who comes to the emergency department, whatever their behavior. Beyond that, no patient or family is entitled to further care from a clinician they are making unsafe. This is easy to forget amid the pressures of clinical care, and a visible reminder helps.

The authors worry about the message these signs send to patients and families. That concern is thoughtful, but it is aimed at the wrong signs. The signs I see in emergency departments name physical assault, threats, and harassment. A sign that polices tone or discourages complaints could deserve criticism, but those signs are the exception and should not set the terms of this debate. Even the authors want their alternative signs to make clear that violence will not be tolerated. They close by asking that the words on hospital walls communicate medicine’s values. Protecting the people who care for patients is one of them.

— Joseph Shapiro, M.D., Children’s National Hospital

Torie Bosch is the First Opinion editor at STAT.

#5497. The Rise of the House Manager: Why Busy Families Are Outsourcing Everyday Tasks

Between managing the demands of work and keeping up with everything at home, it can feel like there are never enough hours in the day.

For busy, overscheduled families, hiring a house manager may be the key to reclaiming valuable time, reducing daily stress, and bringing a little more balance to everyday life.

For those who are unfamiliar with this trending form of home support, a house manager is basically someone who keeps track of things behind the scenes so you can off-load some of your never-ending to-do list.

"A house manager takes on the parts of the household a family chooses to hand off—that means both the everyday work and the planning behind it, from start to finish," says Kelly Hubbell, founder and CEO of Sage Haus, a thriving house manager placement company. "Think meals, laundry, errands, calendars, pet care, and home projects. A house manager doesn't just complete tasks ... they anticipate what's needed and handle it without being asked."

In other words, a house manager is an added support system that helps keep a household functioning efficiently.

The simplest definition of a house manger is someone who helps facilitate everyday life behind the scenes.

"A housekeeper cleans, a nanny cares for the kids, a house manager owns whole areas of the household, from planning to follow-through," says Hubbell.

There can be overlap. A house manager might tidy, do laundry, or prepare meals, depending on what the family hands off. The difference is ownership.

"Take laundry: A housekeeper might wash what's in the basket, whereas a house manager who owns laundry knows the soccer uniform has to be clean by Saturday, without a reminder," explains Hubbell. "The work that's different is the thinking behind the household."

The best house managers have sharp judgment and the ability to plan ahead, juggle several schedules and tasks at once, manage vendors, and make good decisions within the scope a family has agreed to, according to Hubbell.

They're proactive and notice what needs attention before anyone asks. And because they're in someone's home, trust, reliability, and discretion are essential.

"People come to it from lots of backgrounds: nannies whose kids aged out of needing a nanny, teachers, hospitality and operations managers, military spouses who have set up a household in four cities, and moms coming back into the workforce after years of running their own homes—frankly, the hardest training there is," says Hubbell, whose network now includes over 7,000 house managers in the U.S. and Canada, though Sage Haus accepts only about 5% of applicants to ensure quality.

"As AI changes the jobs available, this work depends on what technology can't supply: human judgment, trust, and care," she explains.

Basically, house managers are gaining traction because people are burning out, especially women.

"Most families hit a point where their life, career, or ambitions can't grow any further without more support—I call that the support ceiling," says Hubbell. "They don't need to scale back their dreams. They need to scale up their support."

Many families already have some help, like a cleaner every other week, a nanny/sitter, or groceries on autopilot. But someone still has to hold it all together—the noticing, planning, and following up.

"That's the mental load, and research shows it usually stays with mom, even as her career and earnings grow," says Hubbell.

According to a 2024 study from the University of Bath and the University of Melbourne, mothers in the U.S. carry 71% of mental-load tasks, and while women’s employment and earnings reduce their physical household labor, it does not shrink their cognitive burden.

"Real estate has always recognized the value of a well-maintained home. What we're only beginning to recognize is the value of the work required to maintain it," says Laura Marie Rivera, a gender equity and unpaid labor researcher and host of the "Motherhood Advantage" podcast. "The rise of professional house managers puts a job title and salary on responsibilities that mothers have managed for generations—largely without either."

Unpaid household work in the U.S. is worth up to $6 trillion a year, and none of it shows up in the GDP. However, the rise of house mangers is finally putting a dollar amount on the mental load of keeping a home operational.

"Paying someone to manage a household doesn't just reveal the economic value of the work, it reveals the scope of the work," says Rivera. "We're not witnessing the invention of a new profession so much as the professional recognition of work that has been hiding in plain sight."

The good news is that having a house manager isn't only for the wealthy. In general, cost depends on where you live and what you need the house manager to take on.

"Families hire and pay house managers directly, and pay ranges from $25 to more than $50 an hour depending on location and scope," says Hubbell. "It doesn't have to be full time: 80% of families start with part-time help, averaging 15 to 20 hours per week."

For many families, a house manager can be a more practical investment than several separate kinds of help, because it brings that support together in one role. However, there are still options when budgetary constraints prohibit the employment of a house manager.

"Support doesn't have to start with a hire," says Hubbell. "It can begin with mapping out everything it takes to run your home and deciding what to drop, what to share with a partner, and where you need help most."

That being said, for those who can swing it, having a house manager can be life-changing.

In theory this all sounds amazing, but what's it like in practice? We checked in with a house manager and a family that's hired a house manager to get the inside scoop. But the short version is, both are very happy with their decision.

Before becoming a house manager, Terry Boch worked as an executive assistant, but also spent years as a stay-at-home mom raising her three children.

Once they were grown and she reentered the work force, she was enjoying being an executive assistant again but realized she wanted something less computer-focused and more hands-on. That's when she came across a job post seeking house managers. Intrigued, she pursued the opportunity, was matched with a family in New Jersey, and found it was a perfect fit for her skill set.

"I love transforming an already beautiful house into a warm, welcoming home that looks and smells inviting every day," says Boch, whose primary responsibilities include meal planning, grocery shopping and meal preparation, laundry, resetting bedrooms and living spaces, and plant care. "I work approximately 15–20 hours per week, but I like to say that I get to play house in a home I could never afford."

In reality, however, Boch says she sees what she does as much more about creating a home than maintaining a house.

"Although my interaction with the children is limited, knowing that I can contribute to an environment where they feel comfortable, cared for, and happy brings me tremendous joy," says Boch. "I love making a home feel welcoming, anticipating what a family needs, and taking pride in all the little things that make everyday life more enjoyable. I'm not a house cleaner; I'm a homemaker at heart."

On the flip side, Krissel Varela found her way to the idea of hiring a house manager online.

"Following Sage Haus on social media really opened my eyes to what household support could look like," says Varela. "I had always thought about help in a more traditional sense, like a nanny or someone full-time, but started realizing we could shape the support around what our family actually needed."

Though she'd had a nanny when her kids were younger and she was working a corporate job, once they reached school age, they didn't need that kind of assistance anymore. However, their lives didn't get less busy.

"Between school, sports, activities, keeping our household running, and now building a business of my own, there are just so many moving pieces," says Varela. The idea of a house manager made sense for her family, though they didn't need someone full time.

"Right now, we have help about 8 to 10 hours a week, and even though that's not a huge number of hours, the impact feels so much bigger," says Varela. Her house manager is usually with them on Mondays and Thursdays, with some flexibility predicated on their needs.

"Between laundry, household organization, errands, and all those little tasks that add up throughout the week, having someone share those responsibilities makes such a difference," she adds.

Though it's been only a few months, Varela says she can already feel a huge life shift.

"It's not just the actual hours saved; it's also the mental space that comes from knowing someone else is helping keep things moving without having to manage every little detail," says Varela. "It's also given me more room for the things that are easy to push aside when life gets busy, whether that's spending quality time with my husband, enjoying our weekends, or even having a little time for myself. Having that extra support has really helped me be more intentional about where my time and energy go."

And that is exactly what a house manager is supposed to do, open up space for life at home to be about more than just getting by every day.

"People should also know there's a cost to getting support and a cost to going without it, whether that's your health, your relationships, or your connection with your family," says Hubbell. "The goal isn't to outsource your life; it's to get enough support to be present for it."

Kimberly Dawn Neumann is a journalist based in New York City and the author of hundreds of articles on home-related topics for major publications, including Forbes, Real Simple, and Realtor.com. For more information, visit www.KDNeumann.com or IG @dancerscribe.

#5496. 5 Exciting Ways to Invest in Real Estate

When it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

#5495. Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch

A major new study suggests that many adults age 70 and older who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke may be able to stop taking statins without substantially increasing their short-term cardiovascular risks. However, the findings also point to a possible increase in risk over a longer period, making the decision more complicated than it initially appears.

The independent, preliminary research was presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through 9 in Chicago. The annual conference brings together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, emerging evidence, and advances in clinical care.

An estimated 25% of American adults have elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), commonly called "bad cholesterol." When too much LDL cholesterol accumulates in the arteries, it can restrict blood flow and contribute to heart attacks and strokes. Statins are widely prescribed to lower cholesterol and reduce these risks, including in people who have never experienced a cardiovascular event. This preventive approach remains a central part of the American Heart Association's 2026 joint guideline on dyslipidemia.

Do Older Adults Need to Keep Taking Statins?

Although statins are an established treatment for reducing cardiovascular risk, questions remain about how much benefit they provide when people reach their 70s and beyond, particularly if they have never had a heart attack or stroke.

"While the Association's recent joint guideline recommends lifestyle and potentially medication for people with high LDL-C at younger ages to reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, recent studies question the health benefits of continuing statins in the later decades of life," said study author Rita F. Redberg, M.D., M.Sc., FAHA, professor of cardiology and the Araxe Vilensky Endowed Chair in Cardiology at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine. "A few previous studies assessed the safety of discontinuing statins for primary prevention at age 70 and later, and they found no difference in mortality. One study suggested quality of life improvements after stopping statins. Whether it is safe to discontinue statins to prevent a first CVD event in the elderly remained unclear and the question we explored in our study."

To investigate, researchers enrolled nearly 1,900 adults aged 70 and older who were taking statins specifically to prevent a first cardiovascular event. Every participant also had at least two chronic medical conditions, such as a history of cancer or lung disease.

Participants were divided into two groups. One group stopped taking statins, while the other continued their prescribed treatment. Researchers tracked their health for approximately two years, with additional follow-up extending as long as four years. They examined rates of heart attack, stroke, and death, along with changes in quality of life, muscle pain, falls, and muscle wasting (known as sarcopenia).

What Happened When Older Adults Stopped Statins?

The initial findings were largely reassuring. After approximately two years, participants who stopped taking statins did not experience a statistically significant increase in heart attacks, strokes, or deaths compared with those who remained on the medications.

Stopping treatment also did not produce measurable improvements in the other outcomes researchers examined. Quality of life, muscle discomfort, falls, and muscle wasting were similar in both groups.

There was, however, a small difference in cardiovascular outcomes. Over the first two years, the results indicated approximately one additional cardiovascular event for every 40 people who discontinued statins compared with those who continued treatment.

The longer follow-up revealed a more concerning pattern. Over a period of up to four years, 12.7% of participants who stopped statins experienced a heart attack, stroke, or death, compared with 9.2% of those who kept taking the medications.

Longer Follow-Up Reveals a Potential Risk

Redberg explained that the higher rate of serious outcomes during the four-year follow-up represents a new finding in research on statin discontinuation among older adults. She suggested that the difference may have emerged because this trial included more participants and tracked them for a longer period than earlier studies.

These results complicate the question of whether older adults should continue cholesterol treatment indefinitely. While the findings suggest that stopping statins may be a reasonable option for many people in this age group, they also indicate that remaining on treatment could offer some protection over time.

"This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population," she said. "There should be shared decision-making between the patient and the healthcare professional to know if it is appropriate for an individual to discontinue the medication. In general, however, discontinuation is safe for most people who are in this age group and without a previous CVD event."

The trial involved 1,880 participants aged 70 and older (average age of 77; 53% men, and 47% women), all of whom had at least two chronic health conditions. Individuals with established cardiovascular disease or a previous cardiovascular event were not eligible to participate.

Researchers conducted the study between November 2021 and April 2026 across 24 medical centers in Switzerland, France, and the Netherlands. Of the participants, 938 were assigned to discontinue statins, while 942 were assigned to continue taking their medications.

Throughout the trial and subsequent follow-up, researchers recorded heart attacks, acute ischemic strokes, and deaths from any cause. Participants also completed surveys assessing their overall quality of life, muscle pain, falls, and sarcopenia.

One limitation was that some participants did not remain in their originally assigned groups. Some people instructed to stop statins eventually resumed treatment, while others assigned to continue taking statins stopped using them. Altogether, approximately 14% of participants switched from their assigned treatment approach during the study.

To determine whether these changes affected the findings, the researchers performed several additional statistical analyses. The results remained unchanged.

Taken together, the findings suggest that discontinuing statins may be an option for many adults over 70 who have not previously experienced cardiovascular disease, especially when considering outcomes over the first two years. However, the higher rate of heart attacks, strokes, and deaths during longer follow-up underscores why stopping treatment should be an individualized decision made with a healthcare professional rather than a general recommendation for all older adults.

#5494. As diabetes association’s turmoil continues, what does it mean for patients?

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Liz covers cardiovascular and metabolic disease, asking why we’re not doing better or even losing ground against the world’s leading killer. Send tips on Signal at LizC.22.

Five months after the American Diabetes Association fractured over a political protest and its extended fallout, one question remains unanswered.

What’s the bottom line for people living with diabetes?

Although any impact on patients may be hard to trace now, experts told STAT, they expressed concern that the impasse could stymie advancement in diabetes care. At the heart of the matter is the role the ADA and other professional organizations play in setting guidelines and sharing research, whether in their journals or at wide-ranging meetings that attract thousands to present and to learn.

The ADA dispute began after five members were ousted from its 2026 scientific meeting in New Orleans. The sparring continues, fueled by high-profile resignations and dismissals, a 1,221-member boycott, and the appointment of unidentified editors to manage journals. In October, an internal ADA review acknowledged some missteps but doubled down on its rebukes of members who objected to Trump administration policies decimating scientific research and proposing political reviews of individual projects.

A scheduled appearance by Jay Bhattacharya, director of the National Institutes of Health, inspired the five members to pass out copies of an editorial published in an ADA journal critical of diminished NIH funding. He did not appear, but armed security officers evicted those who shared the printouts outside the hall where he was expected to speak.

Bhattacharya was not the speaker originally suggested for the meeting, Mark Atkinson, who resigned as ADA’s 2026 scientific sessions planning committee chair, told STAT. His choice was to assemble a panel of academic experts to discuss artificial intelligence and its influence on diabetes care, but ADA leadership and its advocacy committee selected Bhattacharya instead.

These and other details regarding the dispute have accumulated, along with high-level resignations. But when asked if the continuing controversy matters to patients, the answer from four prominent voices is yes, but maybe not yet.

To illustrate his concern for the ADA’s future, Atkinson cited examples of how the ADA helped patients in the past.

“The ADA is one of many agencies that have advocated for lower insulin costs,” he told STAT. “They’re one of many agencies that have argued for increased federal funding for research. They’re advocates for standards of care.”

David Nathan, a noted researcher and founder of the Diabetes Center at Massachusetts General Hospital, is far more concerned about the broader impact of federal funding cuts on the scientific enterprise than he is about ADA tumult. Still, he’s also hearing from people who link that ongoing national crisis to what has happened at ADA.

They’re afraid of what’s going to happen to diabetes research, he said, starting with the NIH withdrawing support and then aggravated by the ADA discord.

“It’s really one blow on top of another,” Nathan told STAT. “All of this has coalesced to make everyone anxious, uncertain about the future of diabetes research. And the ADA should at this point be standing up and being something that we can all rally behind. Instead it is being fractured by its own actions.”

In a written response to STAT’s request for comment, the ADA press team said Tuesday, “The ADA has outlined the next steps that we plan to take to learn and improve based on the facts that came to bear from the review. This includes a review of event protocols, procedures, and code of conduct.”

In the near term, the 2027 ADA guidelines to be issued in December were already close to completion, physicians familiar with their production told STAT. The ADA confirmed their publication online in Diabetes Care next month. The agenda for the next annual scientific sessions, slated for June in Washington, D.C., is not yet set.

Meanwhile, the journals have been in limbo.

Since June, the ADA member boycott has erased the editorial masthead for Diabetes Care, its flagship journal. Editor-in-chief Steven Kahn, one of the five escorted out this past June, is part of the boycott, as are deputy editors. Chris Kohler, vice president of publications at ADA, resigned in protest when an interim editorial board was appointed without making their names public.

Kohler’s resignation letter said the appointment of unidentified interim editors violated editorial independence, scientific integrity, transparency, and accountability.

“I cannot, in good conscience, endorse or assume responsibility for an approach that I believe will compound the very problems it is intended to solve,” his Nov. 6 letter said.

Nathan, too, was severe about the unidentified editorial board. “To put it in strike terminology, these are scabs,” Nathan said. “I hate to tarnish them in that way, but they are working against this boycott. And the ADA has not announced the name of a single one of them. That’s weird.”

ADA told STAT the names would be made public.

“While the boycott continues, the ADA will remain relentless in our work to provide the resources that healthcare professionals are counting on. That is why we have established an interim editorial board for Diabetes Care that consists of highly experienced and respected healthcare professionals who have dedicated their careers to caring for people living with diabetes, including endocrinologists, primary care physicians focused on diabetes care, diabetes educators, and more,” the ADA press statement said. “The names of the interim editorial board will be placed on the Diabetes Care website soon.”

Elizabeth Selvin, a deputy editor at Diabetes Care who is also boycotting ADA, expressed concern that a weakened journals might dilute future guidelines.

“I worry that the CEO is treating the journal as a marketing tool for the organization rather than a scientific asset that should be protected and governed by standard publishing ethics,” she wrote to STAT about chief executive Charles Henderson. “A concern is that because typical governance structures to ensure editorial independence are not in place, we need to simply trust that ADA is not making decisions that will benefit industry more than patients.”

In its message to STAT, the ADA said the current editorial team’s term was set to end in December 2027. ADA has opened applications for a new editor-in-chief and said it will work with the selected candidate to confirm a transition plan and the appointment of deputy editors and associate editors.

In addition to the journals, large meetings are another forum for scientific exchange.

John Buse, an endocrinologist at the University of North Carolina and a former president of the ADA, is looking elsewhere.

“I am currently not submitting papers to any ADA journals, but there are many other outstanding journals to pick from,” he wrote to STAT. “It pains me, as of my 600 or so publications, no journal has published more of them than Diabetes Care historically.”

Journals are the way to communicate, Atkinson said.

“Without having medical journals, you don’t have a real way to impact how patients are treated in their care,” he said about the impasse. “This has just got to end soon because the losers in all of this are people with diabetes.”

The same holds true for scientific meetings. Buse plans to attend the Endocrine Society meeting in Toronto, which he has previously gone to only infrequently. He does regularly go to the European Association for the Study of Diabetes, which will meet this year in Budapest, calling it a strong meeting with much to offer. Another option is the American Association of Clinical Endocrinology meeting in San Diego.

“I do hope the issues are resolved soon and that I will attend the ADA, but the plan today is not to attend the scientific sessions in D.C. in June,” he wrote. “If the negotiations with ADA go nowhere and the boycott persists, there is great risk that the ADA loses its standing as the authoritative voice in diabetes. I am sure that the Endocrine Society, AACE, EASD, and others could carry the mantle in the future if the diaspora of thought leaders persists.”

Nathan said he and his colleagues are also thinking about where to present the results of their research, predicting scientists will find other venues. And so will participants and sponsors.

“Industry is interested in having a large audience at these annual meetings. If they start leaving, or if their support starts weakening, the ADA will suffer from it,” Nathan said. “As will people with diabetes. As will the scientific enterprise. I mean, this is just a colossal blunder on the part of the ADA.”

The ADA said there are plans to meet with some of the people leading the boycott to work towards a resolution.”

“They seem to be procrastinating, frankly, with us,” he said. “We have tried to get a meeting with them for easily more than four months. I think they’re hoping that this will just go away, and it’s not going away.”

#5493. Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable

A smile might brighten your mood, but new research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect. When smiling becomes an obligation, especially one tied to financial pressure, it may actually leave people feeling less happy and more irritated.

For years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier. Yet those findings never quite matched his own experiences.

"I used to work in customer service. I actually got written up for my inability to keep smiling at work at an unnamed theme park in Florida," laughed Coles, a professor of psychology at the University of Florida. "So I'm looking at all this evidence I had accrued so far that smiling boosts happiness and realizing it flies in the face of my own experiences in the world."

That contradiction inspired Coles and his colleagues to investigate what happens when people must keep smiling, rather than simply trying it once. Their findings suggest an important distinction: A brief, intentional smile can provide a small emotional lift, but repeatedly putting on a smile under pressure can undermine happiness.

Testing How Forced Smiling Affects Happiness

To explore this difference, Coles worked with researchers Annabel Dang and Joao Francisco Goes Braga Takayanagi to design an experiment that more closely resembled the demands of customer service jobs. Their findings were published on October 1 in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.

"We tried to combine the classic way of studying it in a lab with some extra ingredients that we might see in the real world. We told participants that we would pay them less if they weren't successfully smiling," Coles said. "We also controlled the number of times they have to do it, because in customer service, every interaction is another faked smile."

The online experiment initially enrolled 1,201 people, with data from 1,174 included in the final analysis. Participants were shown images designed to produce different emotional reactions. Some depicted appealing subjects, such as kittens and flowers, while others showed disturbing situations, including theft and mistreatment of animals.

During the experiment, participants either deliberately formed a smile or allowed their facial expressions to develop naturally. Depending on their assigned group, they completed the exercise once or repeated it 10 times.

To introduce an element of pressure, researchers warned half the participants that failing to follow the smiling instructions could cost them $2 from their $6 payment. However, nobody actually lost any money, and every participant received the full amount.

After completing each task, participants reported how happy they felt. The results showed that the emotional effects of smiling depended on how often people had to do it and whether they felt pressured.

When participants viewed unpleasant images, producing a single smile gave their mood a modest boost. This benefit appeared even among those who had been warned about a possible financial penalty. However, the positive effect weakened when smiling was repeated, and it disappeared when repeated smiles were combined with the threat of losing money.

The pattern was even more revealing when people looked at pleasant pictures. Smiling just once offered little additional happiness compared with allowing their faces to respond naturally. But when participants had to smile repeatedly or felt pressure to do so, their happiness ratings actually fell below those of people who responded naturally.

Further analysis revealed another unexpected consequence. In the pleasant picture conditions, forced smiling was also associated with increased irritation and anger.

"If you only force a smile once without any financial penalties, you can see the improvement in happiness. So what psychologists were seeing in their lab is right," he said. "But when you make it a little bit more like the real world, where you have to keep repeating it, and if you don't do it well, you get financial penalties, you see it completely reverse."

The Hidden Emotional Cost of Smiling at Work

These findings may help explain why expectations to appear cheerful throughout the workday can become frustrating rather than uplifting.

The issue has already sparked controversy in the workplace. In recent years, Target faced widespread criticism over a policy requiring employees to smile when customers came within a specified distance. Although the policy was intended to encourage friendly interactions, Coles argues that such requirements can interfere with people's ability to express their emotions naturally.

The problem may extend beyond employees. Customers can also feel obligated to respond positively to friendliness that is being imposed rather than offered spontaneously. According to Coles, these expectations limit the emotional freedom of both sides of the interaction.

Could Trying Less to Be Happy Make Us Happier?

After spending years investigating how people can improve their emotional well-being, Coles has begun considering a broader question. Rather than constantly searching for ways to increase happiness, might people be better off placing greater value on simply being content?

His research suggests that efforts to manufacture positive emotions do not always produce the intended results. Sometimes, trying too hard to appear happy can make the experience less pleasant.

"As a society, we have placed such an immense amount of emphasis on trying to make ourselves feel happier than we currently are," he said, "much less emphasis on just being content with what we have."

#5492. Opinion: A Chinese research entity FOIA’d my scientific work. I had to give it to them

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Duncan, Ph.D., is the Thomas J. Watkins memorial professor of reproductive science in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology in the Feinberg School of Medicine at Northwestern University.

Team science — or collaborative science across disciplines and institutions — is essential for scientific progress as modern problems are too complex for a single person, laboratory, or even field to solve alone. Some of the best work happens when scientists from different countries collaborate.

However, U.S. policies in place and in development increasingly curtail this vital foreign collaboration. There are foreign funding restrictions, visa and entry restrictions for researchers, mandatory institutional compliance and audits with respect to foreign collaborations, and tight export controls. These policies were implemented as biosecurity measures to protect from “countries of concern,” including China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.

Meanwhile, proprietary scientific research is easily accessible to anyone, including foreign actors, through a policy meant to protect Americans’ right to government information. In other words, we are locking the front door while the back window is still wide open.

The Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) is a U.S. federal law enacted in 1966 in response to concerns that the government was too broad and unaccountable. FOIA gives anyone the right to request access to records held by federal government agencies.

This means that through FOIA, anyone — U.S. citizens, noncitizens, and foreign nationals — can access U.S. government-funded science by completing a simple online form and paying a minimal fee. While FOIA is an incredibly important tool for citizens in a free society, it was never intended to allow anyone around the globe to access proprietary U.S. science.

People are readily climbing in through the open back window. As a scientist in the U.S., I personally experienced the impact of such a FOIA request. I was notified by a FOIA coordinator at an NIH institute that my scientific ideas, supported by a funded grant from the U.S. government, were being requested by a Chinese entity through a simple online request form. They only had to pay a $25 fee.

By law, I had to comply and release the grant to them. The requester was listed as a “Consultant” and identified by a generic email address and physical address in China that could not be verified.

I am not the only one to have this experience. The FOIA coordinator told me offhand that this specific individual had a track record of requesting numerous grants from different NIH institutes every year. More broadly, over a decade, the NIH received more than 13,300 requests for grant proposals through FOIA. (Meanwhile, journalists’ FOIA requests often face major delays and other hurdles.)

This loophole has significant negative ramifications on our society. Scientific grants contain unpublished scientific data and sensitive intellectual property. The release of this material could:

1) harm personal and institutional financial interests by divulging patentable ideas, product concepts, and precompetitive information;

2) mislead the public through exposure to unvetted and untested hypotheses and preliminary data;

3) ruin careers and livelihoods of U.S. scientists; and perhaps most importantly,

4) damage U.S. interests by allowing foreign nationals or foreign corporations to be the primary beneficiaries of work funded by the U.S. taxpayer.

Our policies are fundamentally not aligned to protect science. We say we are blocking competing foreign interests, yet through FOIA, anyone can access this science.

If the U.S. truly wants to protect science, Congress needs to close the open window that FOIA affords. Proprietary U.S. science should be exempt or excluded from FOIA. Failing that, those who can access our material must be scrutinized.

Almost exactly four years after receiving the FOIA request, a research team from China published findings that closely matched my team’s original hypothesis — one our own later experiments did not support. While I cannot say whether the FOIA request, my grant, and this recent publication are related, the timing has made me think more about how research, including my own, is ultimately used in these situations.

Francesca E. Duncan, Ph.D. is the Thomas J. Watkins memorial professor of reproductive science in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology in the Feinberg School of Medicine at Northwestern University. She is also an associate professor in residence at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging.  The views presented here are her own.

#5490. New York’s Luxury Rental Market Sees Influx of Cash from AI Boom

The artificial intelligence boom has expanded from the rolling hills of San Francisco and Silicon Valley to the busy streets of New York City, where an already tight luxury market is feeling the impact.

The AI wealth boom was in the spotlight this week, following Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO and jaw dropping $1.494 trillion valuation. With the tech constantly growing and producing newly minted millionaires, the impacts of deep-pocketed AI professionals entering the New York real estate market are just beginning to be felt, agents there say.

There are more than 2,000 AI companies operating in New York City, according to the city’s Economic Development Corporation, and AI companies signed leases for about 1.5 million square feet in just the first six months of 2026, the Brooklyn Daily Eagle reported.

Major AI frontrunners like Anthropic, Palantir, OpenAI, and EliseAI have opened offices in New York, contributing to the thriving commercial real estate market.

“It’s been pretty unbelievable, what’s happening in the public sphere of the AI business. We’re seeing a ton of AI leasing activity on the ground in New York,” Evan Kleinberg, co-founder of Cornelia Street Partners, a boutique commercial real estate firm, told Realtor.com. “And it’s been happening so fast, it’s almost representative of the technology itself. The companies hire immediately and they need space yesterday.”

While Kleinberg has been keeping eyes on the AI industry for the past couple of years, his brokerage worked with its first AI specific company about 12 months ago, at the end of 2025. Since then, the brokerage has secured leases for five companies developing proprietary AI models.

There are a number of reasons Kleinberg sees AI companies expanding east and planting roots in New York. The city has fully rebounded from the pandemic and has an attractive lifestyle that draws many young professionals. Plus, companies see the benefit of being close to their portfolio businesses.

“Ultimately, if your goal is to raise money from Goldman Sachs or JP Morgan or one of the major private equity groups like Apollo, they’re all here,” Kleinberg explained. “So wanting to get close to them is an underlying reason to move.”

With these new offices comes a hoard of young, newly wealthy professionals who are looking to build a home in New York, many of whom are stepping into an already fiercely competitive luxury real estate market.

“Wall Street has historically been a major driver of Manhattan luxury real estate, and now we’re really starting to see the effects of AI. It’s becoming an important engine for wealth creation and housing demand,” Michelle Griffith, a residential real estate agent in New York City, told Realtor.com. “Right now in Manhattan, we are already in a very tight rental market. Even for the last year, rents are up anywhere from 10% to 20% in Manhattan, especially for these luxury properties.”

As of November, the median sold price of a home in Manhattan is $1,150,000, a 15% year over year increase. Some Manhattan neighborhoods have had more extreme changes.

The Lower East Side, for example, saw the median sale price jump 28% year over year to $1,435,000. Rent in the Lower East Side also increased 11% year over year, for a median of $5,947 per month.

The New York City luxury residential landscape is no stranger to competition, with deep pocketed masses vying for a severely limited inventory of spaces. With the flood of AI professionals, another layer of people has been added to the market.

Griffith recalled a recent listing at 50 Gramercy Park North, which had historically rented for $30,000. While a rental like this, which is in the higher end of the market, would previously take 30 to 60 days to identify a tenant, the listing had eight rental bids after 48 hours on the market, with half above asking.

Most workers are determined to live close to work, making it especially challenging to secure an apartment in these highly sought after neighborhoods.

OpenAI’s 90,000-square-foot New York office is located in the Puck Building, which sits on the boarder of SoHo and Nolita in Manhattan.

Anthropic’s New York hub takes up the entirety of a 16-story building at 330 Hudson Street in the Hudson Square neighborhood of Lower Manhattan.

“The offices are in fantastic locations, so it’s easy to find great housing within walking distance,” said Griffith. “The challenge is finding that apartment because there is very, very limited inventory because those neighborhoods were already popular and in demand.”

For luxury agents, the challenge is no longer finding tenants with the money to rent high priced rentals, its finding the rentals for deep pocketed tenants.

When Griffith began in real estate 15 years ago, an apartment for $100,000 per month might be the biggest rental of the year. Now, rentals for $80,000 to even $150,000 are common and moving quickly, she shared.

#5489. Exercise after ACL surgery may protect knees from early osteoarthritis

A serious knee injury can cause problems that persist long after surgery, but new research suggests that the right exercise program could make a major difference. A clinical trial led by researchers at La Trobe University found that supervised exercise and education can improve knee health, reduce pain, and enhance quality of life in young adults recovering from anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. The findings also offer hope for addressing their elevated risk of developing knee osteoarthritis at an unusually young age.

Recovery from ACL surgery is often more difficult than expected. About half of patients are still dissatisfied with their knee health two years after the procedure. Even more concerning, roughly half develop signs of early-onset knee osteoarthritis within a decade, often before reaching age 40.

Medical guidelines recommend combining exercise rehabilitation with patient education after ACL surgery, yet many people receive treatment that falls short of these recommendations. One obstacle is the widespread concern, shared by some patients and healthcare professionals, that exercise could damage already vulnerable knee cartilage.

A New Approach to Recovery After ACL Surgery

To investigate whether additional rehabilitation could help, researchers at La Trobe University's Sport and Exercise Medicine Research Centre conducted the SUPER-Knee clinical trial. It was the first study to evaluate the benefits of combining exercise therapy and education more than nine months after ACL reconstruction, a time when patients are generally expected to have recovered even though many continue to experience problems.

The researchers enrolled 184 adults between the ages of 18 and 40 who were still struggling with knee symptoms one to three years after their operations. Participants were assigned to either a progressive exercise therapy program or a comparison group that received a single educational session.

The findings, published in Annals of Internal Medicine, showed that participants who completed the four-month program under the guidance of a physical therapist experienced improvements in knee health and muscle strength, along with less pain and better quality of life.

Importantly, these benefits came without evidence that the exercises were damaging knee cartilage or worsening early osteoarthritis. The results challenge the belief that physical activity necessarily makes injured knees worse.

Exercise Offers Hope Against Early Knee Osteoarthritis

Associate Professor Adam Culvenor, who led the research, said the findings provide much-needed evidence about how to help younger patients who remain at risk of knee osteoarthritis following ACL surgery.

"Currently we don't have any high-quality evidence for what treatments should be offered to young people at risk of early-onset knee osteoarthritis. Our SUPER-Knee study changes this, and addresses a globally recognized research priority," Associate Professor Culvenor said.

"Our study showed physiotherapist-supervised exercise therapy and education is safe and should be recommended to improve the knee health of young people at high risk of early-onset osteoarthritis following ACL reconstruction.

"The evidence generated by the SUPER-Knee trial can be used to update international clinical practice guidelines for rehabilitation following ACL reconstruction and could be a lifeline for young people struggling after serious knee injuries.

"The intervention is ready to be used by local health professionals with minimal specialized equipment or staff training."

The findings could influence how clinicians approach rehabilitation long after ACL surgery, particularly for patients whose symptoms continue beyond the usual recovery period. Although the trial did not establish whether the program prevents osteoarthritis over the long term, it demonstrated that supervised exercise can improve knee health without accelerating the cartilage damage or early osteoarthritis researchers were monitoring.

Years of Knee Pain After a Serious Sports Injury

For Ruby Cumming, the challenges of recovering from ACL surgery were deeply personal. In 2019, when she was 24, she tore her ACL while playing Australian rules football. Hoping to return to the sport as quickly as possible, she underwent reconstructive surgery within six weeks.

But the operation did not lead to the recovery she had imagined. Her rehabilitation continued for years, and she ultimately decided not to return to football.

"I thought if I had the surgery and did the rehab I'd be able to get back to normal. After surgery impacted my entire life - not just footy - I changed my outlook and decided I wanted to avoid re-injuring my knee ever again so haven't played contact sport since," Ruby said.

"Experiencing regular pain, not being able to walk, getting public transport to work and living independently all became really challenging for me."

Cumming remained committed to her rehabilitation, regularly attending physical therapy appointments and performing prescribed exercises. She initially exercised daily before moving to a weekly routine. Despite those efforts, she continued to experience varying degrees of knee pain every day for three to four years.

Her experience changed after she enrolled in the SUPER-Knee trial and began participating in weekly rehabilitation sessions supervised by a physical therapist.

"When I joined the SUPER-Knee program and did weekly physio-supervised rehab, this improved my pain significantly," Ruby said.

The research suggests that people who continue to struggle after ACL reconstruction may benefit from additional structured rehabilitation, even years after their original injury. Because the program requires little specialized equipment or additional staff training, researchers say healthcare professionals could readily incorporate it into existing treatment services.

The SUPER-Knee clinical trial received funding through a Project Grant from Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC).

#5488. Equifax cuts database firefighting after moving billing to Oracle on AWS

A multicloud strategy once meant deciding which workloads lived with which provider. Now database providers are moving into the clouds customers already use, and AI projects are raising the value of those migrations well beyond the back office.

Equifax Inc. is a case in point. The credit bureau has moved nearly all of its on-premises data centers to the cloud and runs workloads across Amazon Web Services Inc., Google LLC’s Google Cloud and Oracle Corp.’s cloud infrastructure, according to Avinash Singh (pictured), vice president of technology services at Equifax.

“Their performance optimizer is so advanced that we don’t need to tune a single query,” Singh said. “Just think about that. Fifteen to 20 tickets per day turns into one to two tickets per month.”

Singh spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how a multicloud strategy is helping Equifax cut billing database tickets. (* Disclosure below.)

Equifax’s global billing system runs on Oracle’s billing and revenue management software, rating and invoicing billions of transactions each month. The database behind it ran on Amazon Relational Database Service for Oracle until it hit a 65-terabyte ceiling. Oracle Autonomous AI Database on AWS, built on Exadata hardware, has room for petabytes of data inside the same cloud, as enterprise adoption accelerates. Because the application stack stayed on AWS, only the database service changed, Singh explained.

“There is zero code writing because it is just about migrating the data from one database to another,” Singh said. “We achieved this migration without any downtime.”

The results showed up quickly after the system went live in April. Gathering database statistics on nearly 100 terabytes of data dropped from three to four days to three to four hours. After some configuration tuning, batch jobs that once handled 100 to 200 rows per transaction now process 15,000 to 30,000, according to Singh.

“Our rating improved almost 200% to 300%,” Singh said. “We are able to close our books way before what we have been closing.”

#5487. Opinion: If the AI bubble bursts, it could create a serious problem for health care

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Adler is chief scientific officer at the PATHORA Institute of Pathology & Tissue Medicine.

The Oct. 30 sell-off on Wall Street ignited doubts about whether the huge investment in artificial intelligence will earn the returns investors expect. Those concerns have persisted, with even Anthropic’s initial public offering on Nov. 19 failing to halt the broader tech sell-off.

If the AI bubble bursts (assuming it is a bubble) and takes some medical AI companies down with it, health care will face a serious problem. A health AI company’s market value and the medical value of its technology are two different things. If funding runs out because investors decide to walk away, hospitals could lose the chance to complete evaluations of potentially useful medical tools. Giving up on medical AI would be a financial decision — but it may look like a clinical one. The financial markets will decide which medical AI technologies survive before hospitals have had the opportunity to establish whether these technologies benefit patients.

If investment in medical AI technologies experiences a sharp fall, companies will lose funding, forcing them to reduce their activities or stop supporting their technologies completely. The impact of such an event could be felt across the entire health care system: Companies are developing AI tools ranging from interpreting scans to identifying patients at risk of developing medical complications due to treatments. Clearly, some of these tools will eventually prove useful in clinical settings, while others will not. The point is that neither an impressive AI tool nor a falling stock price tells us which AI tool deserves a place within the health care system.

To illustrate this point, let’s take cancer clinical trials as an example. In one study, researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Emory University examined electronic medical records using AI systems to identify patients who may meet the eligibility criteria for inclusion in clinical trials. Determining eligibility involves a demanding manual screening process examining things like tumor characteristics, previous treatments, and lab results.

Interestingly, the findings revealed that using the AI system improved accuracy of assessing enrollment eligibility for the cancer clinical trials, but it didn’t reduce screening time significantly. It’s not clear whether such improvements would lead to an increase in patient enrollment. In another study, researchers in Australia from the Victorian Cancer Registry at Cancer Council Victoria and Monash Health utilized an AI system to analyze pathology reports with the goal of identifying patients eligible for enrollment in cancer clinical trials. The AI system was able to successfully identify more eligible patients when compared to standard screening procedures, but ultimately utilizing the AI system didn’t result in increased patient enrollment into the clinical trials. The study didn’t establish why, which brings to focus that screening improvements doesn’t necessarily lead to higher clinical trial participation.

Taken together, these two studies illustrate the potential utility of AI systems in health care. They also make clear that improvements are needed before such AI systems become an integral part of health care system.

Based on my experience in senior leadership in oncology drug development, I think that medical AI systems should be developed and evaluated based on the general framework that we currently apply in the research and development of new innovative cancer drugs. What I mean by that is when it comes to the AI systems promising early results are important, but it is critical not to celebrate a success too early. Ultimately the value of the AI system depends on whether it eventually benefits the patient. We need to determine whether using a particular medical AI leads to better clinical decisions, better patient identification, reduction of unnecessary work, or improved access to treatment.

If the AI bubble bursts, these success metrics could become more difficult to achieve. Companies developing medical AI systems may lose their funding, downsize, or even withdraw support for their products. Worst of all, they could close before hospitals have finished assessing their AI systems.

Clinicians could, of course, return to doing their work as they did before the introduction of the medical AI system. But that would mean the health care system loses the opportunity (and valuable data) to determine whether such medical AI tools could have offered meaningful improvements and patient impact.

The clear answer is not to try and save each struggling AI company, but to make sure that hospitals and health care system are able to complete their assessments of medical AI systems even if a given company reduces its services or even goes out of business.

Before adopting such medical AI systems, hospitals should establish clear success criteria and build systems in place to track, store, and ensure that the research data generated about the medical AI systems are available for independent evaluation even if the AI company supporting such a system no longer exists. Such plans would make sure that any financial difficulties that may affect a relevant AI company would not prevent the hospital or the health care system from determining whether a given medical AI system could benefit patients.

David Adler is chief scientific officer at the PATHORA Institute of Pathology & Tissue Medicine, with more than 15 years of experience in oncology research and drug development.
